title: German B2
description: The fourth step in German, from B1 to CEFR level B2, the level of the Goethe-Zertifikat B2. Lessons cover reporting what others said with the Konjunktiv I, the passive and its alternatives (sein + zu, sich lassen, -bar), extended participial attributes, the nominal style of formal texts, Funktionsverbgefüge, modal particles, subjective modal verbs, complex connectors such as indem, je nachdem and insofern als, the Futur II, word formation, and writing and speaking at B2: forum posts that argue a case, formal messages at work, presentations and discussions. About 1,000 new words build on the roughly 2,400 core words of German A1 to B1 for about 3,400 in all, and a reading list suggests novels, news and podcasts at this level. Unlocks when German B1 is complete.
author: Erudior
changelog: Reviews include the new A2 words for travel by water.

lessons.title: What they say: Konjunktiv I and indirect speech in the present
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Open any German newspaper, news website or press release and you'll find sentences like these:

- *Der Minister sagte, die Lage sei ernst.* — The minister said the situation was serious.
- *Die Firma erklärt, sie habe keine Pläne für einen Umzug.* — The company says it has no plans to move.
- *Es gebe keine Hinweise auf einen Anschlag, so die Polizei.* — There are no signs of an attack, according to the police.

*sei*, *habe* and *gebe* aren't the forms you learned for *sein*, *haben* and *geben*. They are the **[[Konjunktiv I]]**, a verb form whose main job is to report what somebody else said without the writer vouching for it. At A2 and B1 you met the Konjunktiv II (*wäre, hätte, würde*), which expresses wishes and unreal conditions. The Konjunktiv I is a different form with a different job, and at B2 you need it to read the news, to understand reports and summaries, and to write formal texts yourself.

This module is about reporting and the news. This lesson gives you the forms and the present tense of **[[indirect speech]]**; lesson 2 adds the past, the future, questions, commands and the rule for forms that look like the indicative. The theme is the press: editorial offices, sources and how journalists work.

## Direct and indirect speech

There are two ways to pass on what someone said.

**[[Direct speech]]** repeats the exact words in quotation marks. German quotation marks open low and close high: *„…“*.

- *Die Pressesprecherin sagte: „Das Rathaus bleibt am Freitag geschlossen.“* — The press spokeswoman said: "The town hall will stay closed on Friday."

Indirect speech gives the content without quotation marks, in a clause that depends on a verb of saying. In written German the verb of that clause goes into the Konjunktiv I:

- *Die Pressesprecherin sagte, das Rathaus bleibe am Freitag geschlossen.* — The press spokeswoman said the town hall would stay closed on Friday.

English shifts the tense back ("stays" → "would stay", "is" → "was"). German doesn't: it changes the mood instead. *bleibe* is not a past form; it simply marks the sentence as reported. That's why the reporting verb can be in any tense without changing the Konjunktiv I:

- *Sie sagt, das Rathaus bleibe geschlossen.*
- *Sie sagte, das Rathaus bleibe geschlossen.*
- *Sie hat gesagt, das Rathaus bleibe geschlossen.*

All three report the same present-tense statement. The Konjunktiv I present always means "at the same time as the original statement".

## Forming the Konjunktiv I

The Konjunktiv I is the most regular form in German. Take the infinitive, remove *-en* (or *-n*), and add these endings:

| | ending | kommen | haben | können | werden | wissen |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | -e | komme | habe | könne | werde | wisse |
| du | -est | kommest | habest | könnest | werdest | wissest |
| er / sie / es | -e | komme | habe | könne | werde | wisse |
| wir | -en | kommen | haben | können | werden | wissen |
| ihr | -et | kommet | habet | könnet | werdet | wisset |
| sie / Sie | -en | kommen | haben | können | werden | wissen |

Three things make it easy:

1. No vowel changes. The stem is always the stem of the infinitive. Strong verbs that change their vowel in the present (*er fährt, er gibt, er liest, er nimmt*) don't change it here: *er fahre, er gebe, er lese, er nehme*. Modal verbs keep their infinitive vowel too: *er könne, müsse, dürfe, wolle, solle, möge*.
2. The er/sie/es form ends in -e. In the indicative it ends in *-t* (*er kommt*) or has no ending (*er kann*). So *er komme* or *er könne* is instantly recognizable as Konjunktiv I.
3. Separable verbs work as usual: *Er sagt, er rufe morgen an. Sie meint, der Zug komme pünktlich an.*

The impersonal *es gibt* becomes *es gebe*, one of the most frequent forms in news German: *Es gebe noch keine Ergebnisse.* — There are no results yet (they say).

### sein: the one verb with a full set

*sein* is irregular, and it's the only verb whose Konjunktiv I differs from the indicative in every person:

| | indicative | Konjunktiv I |
|---|---|---|
| ich | bin | sei |
| du | bist | seist (also seiest) |
| er / sie / es | ist | sei |
| wir | sind | seien |
| ihr | seid | seiet |
| sie / Sie | sind | seien |

Learn *sei* and *seien* first; you'll use them constantly. Note that *ich sei* and *er sei* have no *-e*: ~~seie~~ doesn't exist.

- *Der Korrespondent berichtet, die Lage an der Grenze sei ruhig.* — The correspondent reports that the situation at the border is calm.
- *Die Verlage sagen, Papier sei zu teuer.* — The publishers say paper is too expensive.
- *Die beiden Redakteure erklären, sie seien mit der Entscheidung nicht einverstanden.* — The two editors say they don't agree with the decision.

### In practice: mainly the third person

Look at the table for *kommen* again. *ich komme, wir kommen, sie kommen* look exactly like the indicative. *du kommest* and *ihr kommet* are correct, but they sound old-fashioned and you'll rarely see them. In real texts, the Konjunktiv I you meet is almost always:

- the er/sie/es form of any verb: *er komme, sie habe, es gebe, man könne, sie werde*;
- any form of *sein*: *ich sei, sie seien*.

That covers most news reporting, because news is about third persons: the minister, the company, the police. When the Konjunktiv I would look like the indicative (*sie haben*), German replaces it with the Konjunktiv II (*sie hätten*). That replacement rule is the first topic of lesson 2.

## Why the news uses it

The Konjunktiv I says: "this is what was said; I'm passing it on, not claiming it." Compare:

- *Der Bürgermeister sagt, die Stadt hat kein Geld.* — The writer agrees, or doesn't care to distinguish.
- *Der Bürgermeister sagt, die Stadt habe kein Geld.* — The writer reports the claim neutrally.

This distance is a basic rule of objective journalism. A reporter who writes *Der Konzern sagt, die Produkte sind sicher* sounds as if they personally confirm that the products are safe. *…, die Produkte seien sicher* reports the company's statement and leaves the judgement to the reader. The Konjunktiv I is the grammar of *Sachlichkeit*: matter-of-fact, neutral reporting.

It also lets a writer continue reporting for several sentences without repeating "he said". Once a statement has been introduced, every following sentence in the Konjunktiv I still belongs to the speaker. Only a switch back to the indicative signals the writer's own voice:

> *Die Chefredakteurin verteidigte den Artikel. Die Zeitung habe alle Informationen sorgfältig geprüft. Man habe mit drei unabhängigen Quellen gesprochen. Die Kritik sei nicht berechtigt. Der Artikel erschien am Samstag auf der Titelseite.*

The editor-in-chief defended the article. The paper had checked all the information carefully, she said. They had spoken to three independent sources. The criticism was not justified. The article appeared on the front page on Saturday.

Sentences 2 to 4 are her claims (*habe, habe, sei*); the last sentence is a fact the writer states (*erschien*, indicative). English needs "she said" or a tense shift; German just changes the mood. (*habe … geprüft* is the past in indirect speech; lesson 2 covers it.)

You'll meet the Konjunktiv I in newspapers, on the radio and TV news, in reports, minutes of meetings, academic summaries and official letters. In everyday conversation, most people use the indicative or the Konjunktiv II instead; lesson 2 shows how.

## Shifting pronouns, places and times

When you report someone's words, you see them from your own point of view. Pronouns and possessives change to fit, just as in English:

- *Der Redakteur sagt: „Ich habe meinen Artikel fertig.“* → *Der Redakteur sagt, er habe seinen Artikel fertig.*
- *Die Informantin sagt zu mir: „Ich vertraue Ihnen.“* → *Die Informantin sagt, sie vertraue mir.*
- *Die Korrespondenten sagen: „Wir sind hier sicher.“* → *Die Korrespondenten sagen, sie seien dort sicher.*

Words for place and time change if the report is made somewhere else or later. If the minister spoke on Monday and the newspaper reports it on Tuesday, *heute* no longer means today:

| original words | in a later report |
|---|---|
| *heute* | *an diesem Tag, am selben Tag* |
| *gestern* | *am Tag zuvor, am Vortag* |
| *morgen* | *am nächsten Tag, am folgenden Tag* |
| *jetzt* | *zu diesem Zeitpunkt, damals* |
| *hier* | *dort* |

- *Sie sagte am Montag: „Wir veröffentlichen den Text morgen.“* → *Sie sagte am Montag, die Zeitung veröffentliche den Text am nächsten Tag.* — She said on Monday that the paper would publish the text the next day.

Don't shift by rule, though: shift by sense. If the report is made on the same day in the same place, *heute* and *hier* stay as they are. In a radio news item at noon: *Der Minister sagte heute Morgen, er komme heute noch nach Berlin.* (both *heute* are correct).

## With or without dass

Indirect speech can be introduced with *dass* or without it:

- *Sie sagt, dass die Auflage stabil sei.* — verb at the end (subordinate clause)
- *Sie sagt, die Auflage sei stabil.* — verb in position 2 (main-clause order)

Both are correct. In news texts the version without *dass* is much more common, because it's shorter and reads more easily, especially over several sentences. Never mix the two orders: ~~Sie sagt, dass die Auflage sei stabil.~~

Don't put a Konjunktiv I inside quotation marks. Direct speech keeps the speaker's exact words, in the indicative: ~~Sie sagte: „Ich sei müde.“~~ → *Sie sagte: „Ich bin müde.“*

## The newsroom

The words for this lesson come from the world of newspapers and news agencies. A newspaper's editorial team is *die Redaktion*, which is also the word for the office itself: *Er arbeitet in der Redaktion einer Lokalzeitung*. Its members are *Redakteure* and *Redakteurinnen* (editors who write and edit texts), led by the *Chefredakteur* or *Chefredakteurin*. A large paper is divided into sections called *Ressorts*: politics, business, sport, culture, local news. *Das Ressort* (pronounced as in French, re-SOHR) is also used for the area a minister or manager is responsible for.

Much of the news comes from a *Nachrichtenagentur* (news agency), which sells its reports to many papers. Papers and agencies have *Korrespondenten* and *Korrespondentinnen* abroad. On the other side, ministries, companies and clubs have a *Pressestelle* (press office) with a *Pressesprecher* or *Pressesprecherin*, whose job is to speak to journalists.

- *Die Redaktion hat die Meldung von einer Nachrichtenagentur übernommen.* — The editorial team took the report from a news agency.
- *Unsere Korrespondentin in Warschau berichtet, die Regierung plane neue Wahlen.* — Our correspondent in Warsaw reports that the government is planning new elections.
- *Der Pressesprecher sagte, das Unternehmen kommentiere keine Gerüchte.* — The spokesman said the company doesn't comment on rumours.

*Die Auflage* is the number of copies printed or sold (circulation): *Die Auflage der Zeitung sinkt seit Jahren.* An *Abonnement* (subscription, French pronunciation, a-bo-ne-MAHNG; in speech often *das Abo*) is what you take out when you *abonnieren* a paper. The *Titelseite* is the front page, and the *Leitartikel* is the editorial, the article that gives the paper's opinion on an important issue. Someone who writes or speaks opinion pieces is a *Kommentator* or *Kommentatorin*; the opinion piece itself is a *Kommentar* (A2).

Good journalism (*der Journalismus*) depends on its sources. An *Informant* or *Informantin* passes on information, often *vertraulich* (confidentially) and *anonym*. *Die Quellenlage* describes what sources are available and how reliable they are: *Die Quellenlage ist dünn* means there isn't enough evidence yet. And *die Berichterstattung* (reporting, coverage) should be *sachlich* and *objektiv*, not *einseitig* (one-sided). The nouns are *die Sachlichkeit* and *die Objektivität*.

- *Die Berichterstattung über den Streik war sehr einseitig.* — The coverage of the strike was very one-sided.
- *Wir dürfen die Informantin nicht zitieren; sie will anonym bleiben.* — We can't quote the informant; she wants to remain anonymous.
- *Ein Leitartikel darf eine Meinung haben, eine Nachricht muss sachlich sein.* — An editorial may have an opinion, a news report has to be factual.

## Text: In der Redaktionskonferenz

Monday morning at the *Hollerbacher Bote*, a small local paper. The editor-in-chief, Meral Aydın, discusses the day's stories with the editor Jonas Brandt.

> **Aydın:** Was haben wir zur Stadtbücherei?
>
> **Brandt:** Die Pressestelle der Stadt sagt, eine Sanierung sei zu teuer. Mehr wollte der Pressesprecher nicht sagen.
>
> **Aydın:** Und der Förderverein?
>
> **Brandt:** Die Vorsitzende meint, die Zahlen der Stadt seien einseitig. Außerdem habe ich eine Informantin im Rathaus. Sie sagt, es gebe schon einen Käufer für das Gebäude.
>
> **Aydın:** Ist sie zuverlässig?
>
> **Brandt:** Bisher schon. Aber sie will anonym bleiben, und die Unterlagen sind vertraulich.
>
> **Aydın:** Dann ist die Quellenlage zu dünn. Solange wir das nicht bestätigen können, kommt es nicht auf die Titelseite.
>
> **Brandt:** Verstanden. Ich schreibe einen sachlichen Bericht über die Kosten und zitiere beide Seiten.
>
> **Aydın:** Gut. Und meine Meinung dazu kommt in den Leitartikel, nicht in den Bericht.

In English:

> **Aydın:** What have we got on the city library?
>
> **Brandt:** The city's press office says a renovation is too expensive. The spokesman wouldn't say any more.
>
> **Aydın:** And the support association?
>
> **Brandt:** The chairwoman thinks the city's figures are one-sided. And I've got an informant in the town hall. She says there's already a buyer for the building.
>
> **Aydın:** Is she reliable?
>
> **Brandt:** So far, yes. But she wants to stay anonymous, and the documents are confidential.
>
> **Aydın:** Then the sources are too thin. As long as we can't confirm it, it doesn't go on the front page.
>
> **Brandt:** Understood. I'll write a factual report about the costs and quote both sides.
>
> **Aydın:** Good. And my opinion goes in the editorial, not in the report.

Notice that Brandt, a journalist talking about his sources, uses the Konjunktiv I even in speech (*sei, seien, gebe*): he's careful to show these are other people's claims. When he states facts himself, he uses the indicative (*die Unterlagen sind vertraulich*). *der Förderverein* is an association that supports an institution; *das Gebäude* is the building.

Here is his report as it appeared the next day:

> *Stadtbücherei: Stadt prüft Schließung*
>
> *Die Stadt Hollerbach prüft eine Schließung der Stadtbücherei am Mühlweg. Ein Sprecher der Stadt sagte am Montag, die Kosten für eine Sanierung seien zu hoch. Das Gebäude sei über fünfzig Jahre alt, das Dach müsse erneuert werden. Eine Entscheidung gebe es noch nicht.*
>
> *Der Förderverein der Bücherei widerspricht. Seine Vorsitzende erklärte, die Zahlen der Stadt seien einseitig. Eine Sanierung koste deutlich weniger, als die Verwaltung behaupte. Ohne die Bücherei verliere die Innenstadt einen wichtigen Treffpunkt für Schulen und Familien. Der Stadtrat berät im Oktober über die Zukunft der Bücherei.*

> *City library: city considers closure*
>
> *The city of Hollerbach is considering closing the city library on Mühlweg. A city spokesman said on Monday that the costs of a renovation were too high. The building was over fifty years old, he said, and the roof would have to be replaced. No decision had been made yet.*
>
> *The library's support association disagrees. Its chairwoman said the city's figures were one-sided. A renovation would cost considerably less than the administration claimed. Without the library, she said, the town centre would lose an important meeting place for schools and families. The city council will discuss the future of the library in October.*

Find the Konjunktiv I: *seien, sei, müsse, gebe* (the city's view), *seien, koste, behaupte, verliere* (the association's view). The informant's tip isn't in the article at all: one anonymous source wasn't enough. The first and last sentences are in the indicative (*prüft, widerspricht, berät*), because the paper states them as facts.

## Pronunciation

- *der Journalismus*: zhur-na-LIS-mus; the *J* is soft, as in French, like *s* in English "measure". The same in *der Journalist*.
- *die Redaktion*: re-dak-TSJOHN; *der Redakteur*: re-dak-TÖR, stress on the last syllable.
- *die Objektivität*: ob-jek-ti-vi-TÄT; *objektiv*: OB-jek-tif or ob-jek-TIF (both are heard).
- *sei* rhymes with *bei*; *seien* has two syllables, ZAI-en.

## Common mistakes

- Changing the vowel: ~~Er sagt, er fähre morgen.~~ → *Er sagt, er fahre morgen.* The Konjunktiv I is built on the infinitive stem. In the same way: *er gebe* (not ~~gibe~~), *sie lese*, *er nehme*.
- Adding *-e* to *sei*: ~~Sie sagt, sie seie krank.~~ → *Sie sagt, sie sei krank.*
- Confusing *seien* and *sein*: ~~Die Politiker sagen, sie sein unschuldig.~~ → *…, sie seien unschuldig.*
- Konjunktiv I inside quotation marks: ~~Er sagte: „Ich habe keine Zeit und sei müde.“~~ Direct speech is in the indicative: *Er sagte: „Ich habe keine Zeit und bin müde.“*
- Forgetting to shift the pronoun: *Anna sagt: „Ich bin Redakteurin.“* → ~~Anna sagt, ich sei Redakteurin~~ (that means *you* are the editor) → *Anna sagt, sie sei Redakteurin.*
- Main-clause order after *dass*: ~~…, dass die Zeitung habe neue Leser.~~ → *…, dass die Zeitung neue Leser habe* or *…, die Zeitung habe neue Leser.*
- Shifting tense as in English: ~~Sie sagte, das Rathaus blieb geschlossen.~~ In formal writing → *Sie sagte, das Rathaus bleibe geschlossen.*

## Key points

- Direct speech quotes exact words in *„…“*; indirect speech reports the content, in writing with the Konjunktiv I.
- Konjunktiv I = infinitive stem + *-e, -est, -e, -en, -et, -en*, with no vowel change: *er komme, habe, könne, werde, fahre, gebe, es gebe*.
- *sein*: *ich sei, du seist, er sei, wir seien, ihr seiet, sie seien*.
- In practice you mainly need the er/sie/es form and *sei/seien*; other forms look like the indicative (lesson 2).
- The Konjunktiv I present means "at the time of the statement", whatever the tense of the reporting verb.
- It marks a statement as someone else's and keeps the writer neutral; a series of Konjunktiv I sentences continues the report, and a return to the indicative is the writer's own voice.
- Shift pronouns, and place and time words where the point of view changes: *ich → er/sie, hier → dort, morgen → am nächsten Tag*.
- With *dass*: verb at the end; without *dass*: verb second. No Konjunktiv I inside quotation marks.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Indirect speech in full: the replacement rule, past, questions and commands
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 1 gave you the Konjunktiv I in the present: *er sei, sie habe, es gebe*. That's enough for a statement about the present, made by one person. But a real report needs more. People talk about the past (*he said he hadn't seen anything*), about the future (*she said she would appeal*), they ask questions and give instructions, and they come in groups (*they said they had no money*), where the Konjunktiv I looks just like the indicative.

This lesson completes the system: the **[[replacement rule]]**, the past and future in indirect speech, **[[indirect questions]]** and **[[indirect commands]]**, and how all of this sounds in everyday conversation. The theme is the courtroom, because court reports are made almost entirely of reported speech: what the defendant said, what the witness saw, what the prosecutor demanded and what the judge decided.

## The replacement rule

The Konjunktiv I exists to show that a sentence is reported. When it looks exactly like the indicative, it can't do that job:

- *Die Zeugen sagen, sie haben nichts gesehen.* — Is *haben* reported or the writer's own statement? You can't tell.

So German replaces it with the Konjunktiv II, which you know from B1:

- *Die Zeugen sagen, sie hätten nichts gesehen.* — The witnesses say they saw nothing.

The Konjunktiv II here doesn't mean "unreal" or "hypothetical". It's simply the stand-in for a Konjunktiv I that can't be seen. Where the Konjunktiv II also looks like an indicative form, which happens with weak verbs (*sie kauften* is also the simple past), the last resort is *würde* + infinitive:

| | Konjunktiv I | visible? | in indirect speech |
|---|---|---|---|
| *er (haben)* | *er habe* | yes | *er habe* |
| *sie, plural (haben)* | *sie haben* | no | → *sie hätten* |
| *ich (kommen)* | *ich komme* | no | → *ich käme* |
| *wir (können)* | *wir können* | no | → *wir könnten* |
| *sie, plural (kommen)* | *sie kommen* | no | → *sie kämen* (or *sie würden kommen*) |
| *sie, plural (zahlen)* | *sie zahlen* | no | → Konj. II *sie zahlten* = past, not visible either → *sie würden zahlen* |
| *sie, plural (sein)* | *sie seien* | yes | *sie seien* |

So the steps are: Konjunktiv I if you can see it; otherwise Konjunktiv II; if that's not visible either, *würde* + infinitive. Because *sei* and *seien* are always visible, *sein* never needs replacing.

- *Die Anwälte erklärten, ihre Mandanten wüssten nichts von dem Vertrag.* — The lawyers said their clients knew nothing about the contract. (*wissen* → *wüssten*)
- *Die Kläger meinen, sie müssten zu viel Miete zahlen.* — The plaintiffs think they have to pay too much rent. (*müssen* → *müssten*)
- *Die Nachbarn behaupten, sie würden nachts vom Lärm geweckt.* — The neighbours claim they are woken by the noise at night. (*werden* → *würden*)

In real texts you'll also see *würde* for strong verbs whose Konjunktiv II sounds old-fashioned: *sie würden helfen* is much more common than *sie hülfen*. Use *kämen, gingen, gäben, hätten, wären, könnten, müssten, wüssten* without worrying; for rarer verbs *würde* is fine.

## The past: one form for every past tense

Indirect speech has only one past: the Konjunktiv I of *haben* or *sein* + Partizip II. It reports anything the speaker said in the simple past, the perfect or the past perfect:

- *„Ich sah den Wagen.“* / *„Ich habe den Wagen gesehen.“* / *„Ich hatte den Wagen gesehen.“*
- → *Der Zeuge sagte, er habe den Wagen gesehen.* — The witness said he had seen the car.

The choice between *habe* and *sei* is the same as in the perfect:

- *Die Angeklagte sagte, sie sei an dem Abend zu Hause geblieben.* — The defendant said she had stayed at home that evening.
- *Er gab an, er habe die Frau nie getroffen.* — He stated he had never met the woman.

The replacement rule applies to the helping verb: *sie haben gesehen* → *sie hätten gesehen*; *sie seien gegangen* is visible already.

- *Die beiden Angeklagten erklärten, sie hätten von dem Geld nichts gewusst.* — The two defendants said they hadn't known anything about the money.

A past passive in indirect speech is *sei … worden*:

- *Der Verteidiger betonte, sein Mandant sei nie befragt worden.* — The defence lawyer stressed that his client had never been questioned.

## The future

For the future, use *werde* + infinitive (with *würden* in the plural):

- *Die Richterin kündigte an, sie werde das Urteil am Freitag verkünden.* — The judge announced she would deliver the verdict on Friday.
- *Die Anwälte sagten, sie würden in Berufung gehen.* — The lawyers said they would appeal.

As in direct speech, the present often stands for the future when a time word makes it clear: *Das Urteil falle am Freitag, so ein Sprecher des Gerichts.* — The verdict is due on Friday, according to a court spokesman.

## Indirect questions

An indirect question is a subordinate clause, so the verb goes to the end. Yes/no questions are introduced with *ob*, other questions with their question word. In formal reports the verb is in the Konjunktiv I (or its replacement):

- *Die Richterin fragte: „Wo waren Sie am Abend des 3. Mai?“* → *Die Richterin fragte, wo er am Abend des 3. Mai gewesen sei.*
- *„Kennen Sie den Angeklagten?“* → *Sie wollte wissen, ob die Zeugin den Angeklagten kenne.*
- *„Warum haben Sie nicht die Polizei gerufen?“* (to two witnesses) → *Der Staatsanwalt fragte die beiden, warum sie nicht die Polizei gerufen hätten.*

Typical verbs: *fragen*, *wissen wollen*, *sich erkundigen*. The question mark disappears: an indirect question is a statement about a question.

## Indirect commands and requests

You can't put an imperative into indirect speech. Instead, German uses a modal verb in the Konjunktiv I:

- *sollen* for commands and instructions: *„Setzen Sie sich!“* → *Der Richter sagte, sie solle sich setzen.*
- *mögen* for polite requests: *„Bitte sprechen Sie etwas lauter.“* → *Die Richterin bat den Zeugen, er möge etwas lauter sprechen.*

*möge* sounds formal and polite; in less formal reports *solle* is used for requests too. A common alternative is an infinitive with *zu* after verbs like *bitten*, *auffordern* (to ask, to call on) and *raten*:

- *Die Richterin forderte den Angeklagten auf, die Wahrheit zu sagen.* — The judge called on the defendant to tell the truth.
- *Seine Anwältin riet ihm, nichts mehr zu sagen.* — His lawyer advised him not to say anything else.

## Everyday speech

Everything above is the written standard: news, reports, minutes, formal letters. In conversation, the Konjunktiv I sounds bookish, and most people use one of these instead:

| register | example |
|---|---|
| formal written | *Er sagte, er sei krank und könne nicht kommen.* |
| neutral, also spoken | *Er hat gesagt, er wäre krank und könnte nicht kommen.* |
| everyday spoken | *Er hat gesagt, dass er krank ist und nicht kommen kann.* |

All three are correct German for their situation. The Konjunktiv II version (*er wäre*) is common in speech and doesn't make the statement sound unreal; the indicative after *dass* is the most informal. What you shouldn't do is use the indicative in a formal written report where the reader needs to know which statements are claims: a court report that says *Der Angeklagte sagt, er ist unschuldig* sounds as if the journalist believes it.

For your own writing at B2: use the Konjunktiv I in reports, summaries and formal texts; in e-mails to friends and in conversation, the indicative or the Konjunktiv II is natural.

## In the courtroom

Here are the people and things you meet at a trial. *Das Gericht* is the court (the institution and the building); the same word means "dish" in a menu, which context always makes clear. A trial is *der Prozess* (B1 taught it as "process") or more formally *das Verfahren*.

In a criminal trial, *der Staatsanwalt* or *die Staatsanwältin* (public prosecutor) brings *die Anklage* (the charge): *Die Staatsanwaltschaft klagt ihn wegen Betrugs an.* The person on trial is *der Angeklagte* or *die Angeklagte* (defendant), an adjective used as a noun, so it takes adjective endings: *ein Angeklagter, die Angeklagten*. Their *Anwalt* or *Anwältin* acts as *Verteidiger* or *Verteidigerin* (defence lawyer), and together they form *die Verteidigung*. Witnesses *sagen aus* (testify), and the court looks at *Beweismittel* (items of evidence).

At the end, *der Richter* or *die Richterin* gives *das Urteil* (the verdict and sentence). The defendant is *schuldig* (guilty) and is *verurteilt* (convicted, sentenced), or is *unschuldig* and *freigesprochen* (acquitted, *der Freispruch*). A sentence can be *eine Geldstrafe* (a fine) or *eine Freiheitsstrafe* (a prison sentence), which may be suspended: *zwei Jahre auf Bewährung* (two years' probation, a suspended sentence). *In Haft* means in custody. Anyone who disagrees with the verdict can *in Berufung gehen* (appeal); once that's no longer possible, the verdict is *rechtskräftig* (final). A crime committed on purpose is *vorsätzlich*.

Civil cases have their own words: you *klagen* (sue) against someone, or more formally *Klage erheben* (file a lawsuit), and the dispute is *ein Rechtsstreit*.

- *Die Richterin verurteilte den Mann zu einer Freiheitsstrafe von zwei Jahren auf Bewährung.* — The judge gave the man a two-year suspended prison sentence.
- *Mangels Beweisen wurde die Angeklagte freigesprochen.* — The defendant was acquitted for lack of evidence.
- *Die Mieter haben gegen ihren Vermieter geklagt.* — The tenants have sued their landlord.
- *Bis zum rechtskräftigen Urteil gilt jeder als unschuldig.* — Everyone is considered innocent until the verdict is final.

## Text: Ein Gerichtsbericht

This report from a local paper uses every kind of indirect speech from this lesson. Before you read the translation, find each Konjunktiv form and decide why it's there.

> *Gülle im Mühlbach: Landwirt muss Geldstrafe zahlen*
>
> *Das Amtsgericht Hollerbach hat am Dienstag einen 54-jährigen Landwirt zu einer Geldstrafe von 90 Tagessätzen zu je 50 Euro verurteilt. Die Staatsanwaltschaft hatte ihm vorgeworfen, im April mehrere tausend Liter Gülle in den Mühlbach geleitet zu haben. Hunderte Fische starben.*
>
> *Der Angeklagte bestritt die Vorwürfe. Er habe die Gülle nicht absichtlich in den Bach geleitet; ein Schlauch sei in der Nacht geplatzt. Er habe den Schaden erst am nächsten Morgen bemerkt und sofort die Feuerwehr gerufen. Seine Anwältin forderte einen Freispruch. Es gebe keinen Beweis dafür, dass ihr Mandant vorsätzlich gehandelt habe.*
>
> *Ein Nachbar sagte als Zeuge aus, er habe schon zweimal Gülle im Bach gesehen. Die Behörden hätten aber nie reagiert. Auf die Frage der Richterin, ob er den Angeklagten dabei beobachtet habe, antwortete er, das könne er nicht sagen.*
>
> *Die Staatsanwältin hielt die Geschichte vom geplatzten Schlauch für unglaubwürdig. Der Schlauch sei erst zwei Monate alt gewesen. Die Richterin folgte im Wesentlichen ihrer Argumentation: Der Landwirt habe zumindest fahrlässig gehandelt. Er solle seine Anlage in Zukunft regelmäßig prüfen lassen.*
>
> *Das Urteil ist noch nicht rechtskräftig. Die Verteidigung kündigte an, sie werde in Berufung gehen.*

> *Slurry in the Mühlbach: farmer must pay a fine*
>
> *On Tuesday, Hollerbach district court fined a 54-year-old farmer 90 daily rates of 50 euros each. The public prosecutor's office had accused him of letting several thousand litres of slurry into the Mühlbach stream in April. Hundreds of fish died.*
>
> *The defendant denied the accusations. He had not let the slurry into the stream on purpose, he said; a hose had burst during the night. He had only noticed the damage the next morning and had called the fire brigade straight away. His lawyer called for an acquittal. There was no evidence that her client had acted intentionally.*
>
> *A neighbour testified that he had seen slurry in the stream twice before. But the authorities had never reacted. When the judge asked whether he had seen the defendant doing it, he answered that he couldn't say.*
>
> *The prosecutor considered the story of the burst hose implausible. The hose had been only two months old. The judge largely followed her reasoning: the farmer had at least acted negligently. In future, he should have his equipment checked regularly.*
>
> *The verdict is not yet final. The defence announced that it would appeal.*

What the forms show: *habe … geleitet, sei … geplatzt, habe … bemerkt* (past, Konjunktiv I); *gebe, habe gehandelt* (present and past); *hätten … reagiert* (plural, replaced by Konjunktiv II); *ob er … beobachtet habe* (indirect question); *könne* (present); *solle … prüfen lassen* (indirect instruction); *werde … gehen* (future). The facts the paper states itself (the verdict, the dead fish, that the verdict isn't final) are in the indicative.

German fines are given in *Tagessätze* (daily rates): the number reflects how serious the offence is, the amount per day depends on the offender's income. *Die Gülle* is liquid manure, *fahrlässig* means negligent, *der Mandant* is a lawyer's client.

## Pronunciation

- *der Prozess*: pro-TSESS; *das Urteil*: UR-tail, stress on the first syllable, as in *verurteilen* (fer-UR-tai-len).
- *der Staatsanwalt*: SHTAATS-an-valt, long *aa*; plural *Staatsanwälte* (-vel-te).
- *die Bewährung*: be-VÄ-rung, long *ä*.
- *hätten* (short *ä*) and *hatten* (short *a*) differ only in the vowel; listen for it, because it's the difference between a reported claim and a statement of fact.

## Common mistakes

- Leaving an invisible Konjunktiv I: ~~Die Zeugen sagten, sie haben nichts gehört.~~ In a formal report → *…, sie hätten nichts gehört.*
- Using Konjunktiv II where Konjunktiv I is visible, in formal writing: *Er sagte, er hätte keine Zeit* is fine in speech, but the report standard is *er habe keine Zeit*.
- Copying the speaker's tense: ~~Sie sagte, sie sah den Unfall.~~ → *Sie sagte, sie habe den Unfall gesehen.* Every past is *habe/sei* + Partizip II.
- Wrong helping verb: ~~Er sagte, er habe nach Hause gegangen.~~ → *…, er sei nach Hause gegangen.*
- Main-clause order in an indirect question: ~~Sie fragte, ob kenne er den Mann.~~ → *Sie fragte, ob er den Mann kenne.*
- An imperative in indirect speech: ~~Er sagte, setzen Sie sich.~~ → *Er sagte, sie solle sich setzen* or *Er bat sie, sich zu setzen.*
- *möchte* for polite requests: ~~Sie bat ihn, er möchte warten.~~ In formal reports → *…, er möge warten.* (You will hear *möchte* in speech.)

## Key points

- Replacement rule: Konjunktiv I if it's visible; if it looks like the indicative, Konjunktiv II (*sie hätten, wir könnten, sie kämen*); if that isn't visible either, *würde* + infinitive (*sie würden zahlen*). *sei/seien* never need replacing.
- The past in indirect speech: *habe/sei* (or *hätten/seien*) + Partizip II, for any past tense in the original. Passive: *sei … worden*.
- The future: *werde* + infinitive, plural *würden* + infinitive.
- Indirect questions: *ob* or a question word, verb at the end, Konjunktiv I.
- Indirect commands: *solle* (instruction), *möge* (polite request), or an infinitive with *zu* after *bitten, auffordern, raten*.
- In speech, the indicative (*dass er krank ist*) or Konjunktiv II (*er wäre krank*) is normal; formal writing uses the Konjunktiv I.

lessons.title: He is said to …: subjective modal verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You've used modal verbs since A1 to talk about ability, permission, obligation and wishes: *Ich kann schwimmen. Du musst um acht da sein. Sie will Ärztin werden.* In these sentences the modal says something about the subject: what it can, must or wants to do.

The same verbs have a second use that is everywhere in the news and in gossip: they express how sure the *speaker* is, or where a piece of information comes from.

- *Der Sänger soll sehr reich sein.* — The singer is said to be very rich.
- *Sie will nichts gesehen haben.* — She claims not to have seen anything.
- *Das muss ein Fehler sein.* — That must be a mistake.
- *Er dürfte über sechzig sein.* — He's probably over sixty.

This is the **[[subjective use]]** of modal verbs. After lessons 1 and 2, it's the third way German has of keeping its distance from a claim, and a much shorter one: *Er soll zurückgetreten sein* says in four words what needs a whole clause in indirect speech. The theme is reputation, rumours and scandals: the stories where who-said-what matters most.

## Objective and subjective

Compare these pairs:

| objective (about the subject) | subjective (about the speaker's information) |
|---|---|
| *Er muss heute arbeiten.* — He has to work today. | *Er muss krank sein.* — He must be ill (I conclude). |
| *Sie soll das Geld zurückzahlen.* — She is supposed to pay the money back. | *Sie soll das Geld genommen haben.* — She is said to have taken the money. |
| *Er will Politiker werden.* — He wants to become a politician. | *Er will davon nichts gewusst haben.* — He claims to have known nothing about it. |
| *Du kannst hier parken.* — You can park here. | *Das kann nicht stimmen.* — That can't be true. |

Two signals help you tell them apart:

- A **[[perfect infinitive]]** after the modal (*genommen haben, gewusst haben, gegangen sein*) almost always means the subjective use. You can't be obliged to have done something in the past, but you can be said to have done it.
- Subjective modals are almost always in the present tense or in the Konjunktiv II (*dürfte, könnte, müsste*). The time of the event is shown by the infinitive, not by the modal: *Sie soll gelogen haben* = it's said now that she lied then.

## sollen: hearsay

Subjective *sollen* means "people say", "it's reported", "allegedly". It passes on information from other sources without saying who they are, and without vouching for it:

- *Die Schauspielerin soll heimlich geheiratet haben.* — The actress is said to have married in secret.
- *Im Hotel soll es Probleme mit dem Brandschutz geben.* — The hotel is said to have fire-safety problems.
- *Der Minister soll von dem Skandal schon seit Monaten gewusst haben.* — The minister reportedly knew about the scandal for months.

The Klatschpresse (gossip press) lives on *soll*: it can print almost any rumour as long as it's marked as hearsay. Serious journalists use it more carefully, and usually name the source: *Nach Informationen des Senders soll …* (According to the broadcaster's information …).

## wollen: a claim the speaker doubts

Subjective *wollen* reports a claim by the subject about themselves, and it signals doubt: "he says so, but …".

- *Der Angeklagte will zur Tatzeit im Kino gewesen sein.* — The defendant claims to have been at the cinema at the time of the crime.
- *Sie will das Foto nie gesehen haben.* — She claims never to have seen the photo.
- *Er will den Brief nicht bekommen haben.* — He claims not to have received the letter.

The difference: *Er soll reich sein* (others say he's rich), *Er will reich sein* (he says he's rich, or objectively: he wants to be rich; context decides). With a perfect infinitive, *wollen* is nearly always subjective.

## Degrees of certainty

Several modals express how sure the speaker is that something is true, based on evidence or reasoning. From most to least certain:

| modal | certainty | paraphrase | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *muss* | very sure, a logical conclusion | *bestimmt, sicher* | *Das Licht ist an. Sie muss zu Hause sein.* |
| *dürfte* | probable | *wahrscheinlich, vermutlich* | *Die Affäre dürfte ihm schaden.* |
| *wird (wohl)* | assumption | *wohl, wahrscheinlich* | *Er wird (wohl) im Stau stehen.* (lesson 4) |
| *kann / könnte* | possible | *vielleicht, möglicherweise* | *Das könnte eine Fälschung sein.* |
| *kann nicht* | impossible, I'm sure it's not | *auf keinen Fall* | *Das kann nicht wahr sein!* |

- *Er muss das Geld genommen haben; niemand sonst hatte den Schlüssel.* — He must have taken the money; nobody else had the key.
- *Der Rücktritt dürfte nur eine Frage der Zeit sein.* — The resignation is probably only a matter of time.
- *Das Foto könnte gefälscht sein.* — The photo could be fake.
- *Sie kann den Brief nicht geschrieben haben: Sie war zu der Zeit im Krankenhaus.* — She can't have written the letter: she was in hospital at the time.

Notes:

- *dürfte* is the Konjunktiv II of *dürfen*, but here it has nothing to do with permission. It's a careful, typical newspaper way to say "probably". The indicative *darf* has no subjective use.
- *könnte* is a little more tentative than *kann*. *Das kann sein* (that's possible) is a common reaction in conversation.
- *muss nicht* means "not necessarily": *Das muss nicht stimmen.* — That isn't necessarily true. It doesn't mean "must not".
- *müsste* (Konjunktiv II) is a confident expectation: *Der Brief müsste morgen ankommen.* — The letter should arrive tomorrow.

### mögen (recognize only)

Subjective *mögen* is rarer and sounds literary or formal. You'll see it in two uses:

- an estimate: *Sie mag etwa vierzig sein.* — She may be about forty.
- a concession before *aber*: *Das mag stimmen, aber es ist nicht die ganze Wahrheit.* — That may be true, but it's not the whole truth.

*Das mag sein* is a set phrase: "that may be so".

## The perfect infinitive

The subjective modals often refer to the past, so they need the **[[perfect infinitive]]**: Partizip II + *haben* or *sein*.

| present infinitive | perfect infinitive |
|---|---|
| *sehen* | *gesehen haben* |
| *gehen* | *gegangen sein* |
| *zurücktreten* | *zurückgetreten sein* |
| *enthüllt werden* (passive) | *enthüllt worden sein* |

In a main clause, the modal is in position 2 and the perfect infinitive goes to the end:

- *Der Politiker soll gelogen haben.*
- *Die Chefin soll schon zurückgetreten sein.*
- *Die Dokumente sollen vernichtet worden sein.* — The documents are said to have been destroyed.

In a subordinate clause, the modal goes to the very end, after the infinitive:

- *Ich habe gelesen, dass er gelogen haben soll.* — I read that he is said to have lied.
- *Ich glaube nicht, dass sie das Foto gefälscht haben kann.* — I don't think she can have faked the photo.
- *Mich ärgert, dass er von nichts gewusst haben will.* — It annoys me that he claims to have known nothing.

Subordinate clauses with subjective modals are correct but heavy, so writers usually avoid them by using the modal in a main clause.

## Other ways to say it

Each subjective modal has an equivalent with an adverb or a phrase. Use them when a modal would be ambiguous, or for variety:

| modal | alternative |
|---|---|
| *Er soll reich sein.* | *Er ist angeblich reich. Es heißt, dass er reich ist.* |
| *Sie will nichts gesehen haben.* | *Sie behauptet, nichts gesehen zu haben.* |
| *Das muss ein Irrtum sein.* | *Das ist bestimmt / sicher ein Irrtum.* |
| *Er dürfte zurücktreten.* | *Er tritt vermutlich / wahrscheinlich zurück.* |
| *Das könnte stimmen.* | *Das stimmt vielleicht / möglicherweise.* |

For nouns, use the adjectives *mutmaßlich* and *vermeintlich*, which work like *soll* inside a noun phrase:

- *der mutmaßliche Betrüger* — the suspected fraudster (probably is one, not yet proven)
- *der vermeintliche Skandal* — the supposed scandal (people thought it was one, but it probably isn't)

*mutmaßlich* leans towards "true", *vermeintlich* towards "mistaken"; *angeblich* (B1) is neutral-to-doubtful. News reports say *der mutmaßliche Täter* until a court has decided.

## Words: reputation and scandal

A public figure (*der* or *die Prominente*, an adjective used as a noun; colloquially *der Promi*) depends on *der Ruf* (reputation), *das Ansehen* (standing, prestige) and *das Image* (public image, pronounced as in English). A *Skandal* or *Affäre* can cause *einen Imageschaden*. The press can *enthüllen* (reveal) a secret, and the result is *eine Enthüllung*. People involved may *leugnen* (deny a fact), issue *ein Dementi* (an official denial), *zugeben* (admit) or *eingestehen* (admit, often to oneself: *sich einen Fehler eingestehen*). Trying to hide something is *vertuschen* (cover up).

*Betrug* is fraud, *betrügen* to cheat or deceive (also to be unfaithful to a partner), a person who does it is *ein Betrüger* or *eine Betrügerin*. *Die Fälschung* is a forgery or fake. You *verdächtigen* someone (suspect them): *Man verdächtigt ihn des Betrugs* (genitive) or more commonly *Er wird verdächtigt, …zu haben*. If the accusations are false and meant to harm, they're *Verleumdung* (slander, defamation): *jemanden verleumden*. *Unterstellen* (inseparable) means to insinuate: *Willst du mir etwa unterstellen, dass ich lüge?* The noun is *die Unterstellung*.

When the pressure grows, an organization will *sich distanzieren* (von + dative), and the person may have to *zurücktreten* (resign; *der Rücktritt*). The result for everyone: a loss of *Glaubwürdigkeit* (credibility). Someone who has lost it is *unglaubwürdig*.

- *Die Zeitung hat enthüllt, dass der Präsident Geld aus der Vereinskasse genommen haben soll.* — The paper has revealed that the president is said to have taken money from the club's funds.
- *Die Partei hat sich von ihrem Abgeordneten distanziert.* — The party has distanced itself from its MP.
- *Der Imageschaden dürfte enorm sein.* — The damage to his image is likely to be enormous.
- *Sie hat ihr Privatleben immer aus der Öffentlichkeit herausgehalten.* — She has always kept her private life out of the public eye.

## Dialogue: Hast du schon gehört?

Two colleagues, Dana and Felix, talk about a story in the local paper. Notice which modals are objective and which are subjective.

> **Dana:** Hast du das von Konrad Weidner gehört? Er soll Geld aus der Vereinskasse genommen haben.
>
> **Felix:** Weidner? Der Präsident vom FC? Das kann nicht sein. Der hat doch einen super Ruf.
>
> **Dana:** Die Zeitung hat es heute enthüllt. Es soll um fast 200.000 Euro gehen.
>
> **Felix:** Und was sagt er dazu?
>
> **Dana:** Er will von nichts gewusst haben. Sein Steuerberater müsse einen Fehler gemacht haben, sagt er.
>
> **Felix:** Das dürfte ihm kaum jemand glauben. Ohne seine Unterschrift kann niemand das Geld überwiesen haben.
>
> **Dana:** Der Verein hat sich jedenfalls schon von ihm distanziert. Und die Sponsoren sollen ziemlich sauer sein.
>
> **Felix:** Dann muss er wohl zurücktreten. Mit so einem Imageschaden kann er nicht weitermachen.
>
> **Dana:** Vielleicht. Aber bisher ist nichts bewiesen. Es könnte auch eine Verleumdung sein.

In English:

> **Dana:** Have you heard about Konrad Weidner? He's supposed to have taken money from the club's funds.
>
> **Felix:** Weidner? The president of the football club? That can't be. He's got a great reputation.
>
> **Dana:** The paper revealed it today. It's said to be almost 200,000 euros.
>
> **Felix:** And what does he say about it?
>
> **Dana:** He claims not to have known anything. His tax adviser must have made a mistake, he says.
>
> **Felix:** Hardly anybody is likely to believe that. Nobody can have transferred the money without his signature.
>
> **Dana:** Anyway, the club has already distanced itself from him. And the sponsors are said to be pretty angry.
>
> **Felix:** Then he'll probably have to resign. He can't carry on with damage to his image like that.
>
> **Dana:** Maybe. But so far nothing has been proved. It could also be slander.

Subjective: *soll … genommen haben, kann nicht sein, soll … gehen, will … gewusst haben, müsse … gemacht haben* (a subjective modal in the Konjunktiv I: Weidner's claim, reported), *dürfte, kann … überwiesen haben, sollen … sein, könnte … sein*. Objective: *muss … zurücktreten* (he will have to), *kann … nicht weitermachen* (he isn't able to). *die Vereinskasse* is a club's funds; *der Steuerberater* is a tax adviser.

## Pronunciation

- *das Image*: as in English, I-mitsh; *die Affäre*: a-FÄ-re; *das Dementi*: de-MEN-ti.
- *der Skandal*: skan-DAAL, stress on the second syllable.
- *mutmaßlich*: MUT-maas-lich, long *u* and long *a*.
- In subjective *muss*, *soll* and *will* the modal is often unstressed and the main verb stressed: *Er soll GELOGEN haben.*

## Common mistakes

- Putting the modal in the past to talk about the past: ~~Er sollte gelogen haben~~ doesn't mean "he is said to have lied". → *Er soll gelogen haben.* The perfect infinitive carries the past.
- Perfect of the modal instead of a perfect infinitive: ~~Er hat lügen sollen~~ means "he was supposed to lie" (objective). → *Er soll gelogen haben.*
- Wrong helping verb in the perfect infinitive: ~~Sie soll zurückgetreten haben.~~ → *Sie soll zurückgetreten sein.*
- Reading *muss nicht* as "must not": *Das muss nicht stimmen* = it isn't necessarily true. "Must not" is *darf nicht*.
- Using *darf* for probability: ~~Das darf stimmen.~~ → *Das dürfte stimmen.*
- Confusing *soll* and *will*: *Er soll krank sein* (others say so) vs *Er will krank sein* (he says so; doubtful).
- Mixing up *vermeintlich* and *mutmaßlich*: *der vermeintliche Täter* suggests he isn't the culprit after all.

## Key points

- Objective modals speak about the subject (*Er muss arbeiten*); subjective modals show the speaker's certainty or source (*Er muss krank sein*).
- *sollen* = it is said; *wollen* = the subject claims (doubtful).
- Certainty: *muss* (sure) > *dürfte* (probably) > *wird wohl* (assumption) > *kann/könnte* (possibly); *kann nicht* = impossible; *muss nicht* = not necessarily.
- *mögen* (recognize): *Sie mag vierzig sein. Das mag stimmen, aber …*
- For the past: modal in the present + perfect infinitive (*gesehen haben, gegangen sein*): *Er soll gelogen haben.*
- Alternatives: *angeblich, es heißt* (sollen), *behaupten* (wollen), *bestimmt* (muss), *vermutlich* (dürfte), *vielleicht* (könnte); before nouns *mutmaßlich* and *vermeintlich*.

lessons.title: Will have done: Futur II and assumptions about the past
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 3 showed how German expresses certainty and guesses with modal verbs: *Sie muss den Termin vergessen haben. Er dürfte schon zu Hause sein.* This lesson adds one more tool for the same job, and a tense you'll need when you talk about plans with a deadline: the **[[Futur II]]**.

- *Bis 2041 werden wir die Wohnung abbezahlt haben.* — By 2041 we will have paid off the flat.
- *Sie wird den Bus verpasst haben.* — She'll have missed the bus (I suppose).

The first sentence is about the future; the second is about the past. The same form does both, and in everyday German the second use is the more common one. You'll learn when the Futur II is natural, when Germans replace it with the perfect, and how it behaves in subordinate clauses. The theme is money over a lifetime: saving, investing, loans and planning for retirement.

## The form

The Futur II is *werden* + perfect infinitive (Partizip II + *haben* or *sein*, from lesson 3):

| | werden | … | Partizip II | haben / sein |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | werde | den Kredit bis dahin | getilgt | haben |
| du | wirst | das Geld schon | ausgegeben | haben |
| er / sie / es | wird | den Brief wohl | bekommen | haben |
| wir | werden | bis Mai alles | bezahlt | haben |
| ihr | werdet | bis dahin in Rente | gegangen | sein |
| sie / Sie | werden | gestern | angekommen | sein |

*haben* or *sein* is chosen exactly as in the perfect: *sie wird gegangen sein*, *er wird verloren haben*. *werden* is in position 2 and the perfect infinitive goes to the end, in the order Partizip II + *haben/sein*.

## Use 1: finished by a point in the future

The Futur II describes something that will be complete before a point in the future. It nearly always comes with a time phrase: *bis* (by), *bis dahin* (by then), *in zehn Jahren*, *wenn* …

- *Bis Ende des Jahres werde ich 5.000 Euro gespart haben.* — By the end of the year I will have saved 5,000 euros.
- *In zwanzig Jahren wird die Inflation einen großen Teil dieses Geldes aufgefressen haben.* — In twenty years, inflation will have eaten up a large part of this money.
- *Wenn du in Rente gehst, wirst du über vierzig Jahre lang eingezahlt haben.* — When you retire, you'll have paid in for over forty years.

In conversation, German usually prefers the perfect with a future time phrase. It means the same and is less heavy:

- *Bis Ende des Jahres habe ich 5.000 Euro gespart.*
- *Bis 2041 haben wir die Wohnung abbezahlt.*

The time phrase makes the future meaning clear. The Futur II is used in writing, in plans and forecasts, and when the speaker wants to stress that something will be finished.

## Use 2: an assumption about the past

This is the use you'll hear most. *Er wird … haben/sein* expresses a confident guess about something that has already happened. It often comes with *wohl*, *sicher*, *bestimmt* or *schon*:

- *Frau Berg ist nicht im Büro. Sie wird wohl noch beim Termin in der Bank sein.* (Futur I: assumption about now)
- *Das Geld ist nicht da. Die Überweisung wird sich verzögert haben.* (Futur II: assumption about the past) — The transfer will have been delayed.
- *Die Aktie ist gestern stark gefallen. Die Firma wird schlechte Zahlen gemeldet haben.* — The share fell sharply yesterday. The company will have reported bad figures.
- *Keine Sorge, du wirst den Kontoauszug bestimmt nur verlegt haben.* — Don't worry, you'll just have mislaid the bank statement.

So the Futur I and II make a pair for assumptions:

| about the present | about the past |
|---|---|
| *Er wird im Stau stehen.* — He's probably stuck in traffic. | *Er wird im Stau gestanden haben.* — He was probably stuck in traffic. |
| *Sie wird krank sein.* — She's probably ill. | *Sie wird krank gewesen sein.* — She was probably ill. |

The Futur II assumption is close to the subjective modals: *Sie wird den Termin vergessen haben* ≈ *Sie dürfte den Termin vergessen haben* ≈ *Sie hat den Termin wohl vergessen*. The last version, perfect + *wohl*, is the everyday one, and you'll often hear it instead of the Futur II.

How do you know which use you have? Look at the context. A future time point (*bis 2041, in fünf Jahren*) points to use 1; a past situation or particles like *wohl* point to use 2.

## In subordinate clauses

In a subordinate clause, *werden* goes to the very end, after the perfect infinitive:

- *Ich hoffe, dass wir die Wohnung bis 2041 abbezahlt haben werden.* — I hope that we will have paid off the flat by 2041.
- *Sie ist sicher, dass er die Rechnung vergessen haben wird.* — She's sure that he will have forgotten the bill.
- *Wir rechnen damit, dass die Zinsen bis dahin gestiegen sein werden.* — We expect interest rates to have risen by then.

The verb cluster at the end has three parts: Partizip II, *haben/sein*, then *werden*. Read it backwards to understand it: *werden* (future) + *haben* + *abbezahlt* = "will have paid off".

In indirect speech (lesson 2), the Futur II takes the Konjunktiv I of *werden*: *Die Beraterin sagte, er werde bis dahin genug angelegt haben.* — The adviser said he would have invested enough by then.

You may also see a passive Futur II in formal texts. Just recognize it: *Bis 2030 wird das Darlehen getilgt worden sein.* — By 2030 the loan will have been repaid.

## Money over a lifetime

The vocabulary of this lesson comes from personal finance. Germany's pension system is often described as having three pillars: the state pension (*die gesetzliche Rente*), the company pension (*die Betriebsrente*) and private provision. Together they make up your *Altersvorsorge* (retirement provision). If you *vorsorgen* (make provision) in time, the gap between your salary and your pension will be smaller.

Ways to invest your money (*die Geldanlage*; the verb is *Geld anlegen*):

- *das Sparkonto*: safe, but at a low *Zinssatz* (interest rate), *die Inflation* reduces your *Kaufkraft* (purchasing power).
- *die Aktie* (share): you become an *Aktionär* or *Aktionärin* (shareholder) and may receive *eine Dividende* each year. Shares are traded *an der Börse* (on the stock exchange).
- *der Fonds* (fund; the *-s* is silent, as in French: *fõ*): many shares or other *Wertpapiere* (securities) in one product, which spreads the risk.
- *die Anleihe* (bond): you lend money to a state or company.
- *die Immobilie* (property): most buyers need *Eigenkapital* (their own funds, a deposit) and *ein Darlehen* (a loan) from the bank, which they *tilgen* (repay) in monthly *Raten* (instalments) until it's *abbezahlt* (paid off).

What you get back on an investment is *die Rendite* (return, yield). A high return usually means the investment is *riskant*. *Das Vermögen* is everything you own (assets, wealth). *Die Finanzen* (plural only) are your finances; *das Budget* (pronounced as in French, bü-DZHÉ) is how much you can spend. *Die Rücklage* is money set aside for emergencies, and *die Absicherung* is protection against risks: a *Lebensversicherung* (life insurance) is one way to *absichern* your family. Every month the bank sends a *Kontoauszug* (bank statement), and *eine Anlageberatung* (investment advice) helps you choose. If you spend more than you have, you *verschulden sich* (get into debt).

Remember that *der Zins* (B1) is usually used in the plural for "interest" on money: *Die Zinsen sind gestiegen.* — Interest rates have gone up.

## Dialogue: Bei der Anlageberatung

Svenja and Tarek Kaya, both in their early forties, talk to a financial adviser, Frau Lenz.

> **Frau Lenz:** Sie möchten also mehr für Ihre Altersvorsorge tun. Wie sieht Ihre Situation im Moment aus?
>
> **Tarek:** Wir haben vor sechs Jahren eine Wohnung gekauft. Das Darlehen tilgen wir mit einer Rate von 1.100 Euro im Monat.
>
> **Frau Lenz:** Und wann werden Sie es abbezahlt haben?
>
> **Svenja:** Wenn alles gut geht, werden wir die Wohnung bis 2041 abbezahlt haben. Dann bin ich 59.
>
> **Frau Lenz:** Gut. Haben Sie außerdem Rücklagen?
>
> **Tarek:** Etwa drei Monatsgehälter auf dem Sparkonto. Aber bei diesem Zinssatz frisst die Inflation das langsam auf.
>
> **Frau Lenz:** Das stimmt. Mit einem breit gestreuten Fonds können Sie langfristig eine bessere Rendite erzielen. Natürlich ist das riskanter als ein Sparkonto.
>
> **Svenja:** Mein Vater hat in den Neunzigern Aktien gekauft und viel Geld verloren.
>
> **Frau Lenz:** Er wird damals auf ein paar Technologiefirmen gesetzt haben, oder? Das war vor dem Jahr 2000 typisch. Ein Fonds verteilt das Risiko auf Hunderte von Firmen.
>
> **Tarek:** Und wie viel könnten wir bis zur Rente zusammenbekommen?
>
> **Frau Lenz:** Wenn Sie zwanzig Jahre lang jeden Monat 300 Euro anlegen, werden Sie insgesamt 72.000 Euro eingezahlt haben. Was daraus wird, hängt von der Börse ab. Versprechen kann ich Ihnen nichts.

In English:

> **Frau Lenz:** So you'd like to do more for your retirement. What does your situation look like at the moment?
>
> **Tarek:** We bought a flat six years ago. We're paying off the loan at 1,100 euros a month.
>
> **Frau Lenz:** And when will you have paid it off?
>
> **Svenja:** If all goes well, we'll have paid off the flat by 2041. I'll be 59 then.
>
> **Frau Lenz:** Good. Do you also have savings set aside?
>
> **Tarek:** About three months' salary in a savings account. But at this interest rate, inflation is slowly eating it up.
>
> **Frau Lenz:** That's true. With a broadly diversified fund you can get a better return in the long term. Of course, that's riskier than a savings account.
>
> **Svenja:** My father bought shares in the nineties and lost a lot of money.
>
> **Frau Lenz:** He'll have bet on a few technology companies at the time, won't he? That was typical before 2000. A fund spreads the risk over hundreds of companies.
>
> **Tarek:** And how much could we put together by the time we retire?
>
> **Frau Lenz:** If you invest 300 euros every month for twenty years, you'll have paid in 72,000 euros in total. What becomes of it depends on the stock market. I can't promise you anything.

Three Futur II forms, two uses: *werden … abbezahlt haben* and *werden … eingezahlt haben* are completed future events (use 1); *wird … gesetzt haben* is Frau Lenz's guess about the past (use 2). *breit gestreut* means widely spread (diversified), *erzielen* to achieve, *auf etwas setzen* to bet on something, *zusammenbekommen* to put together, raise.

## Pronunciation

- *der Fonds*: fõ, one syllable with a nasal vowel, as in French; the plural is written the same and said fõs.
- *die Aktie*: AK-tsje, two syllables; *der Aktionär*: ak-tsjo-NÄR.
- *die Rendite*: ren-DII-te; *die Immobilie*: i-mo-BII-lje.
- *das Darlehen*: DAR-le-en, stress on the first syllable, the *h* is silent.

## Common mistakes

- Wrong order at the end: ~~Bis 2041 werden wir die Wohnung haben abbezahlt.~~ → *… die Wohnung abbezahlt haben.* Partizip II first, then *haben/sein*.
- Wrong helping verb: ~~Sie wird schon nach Hause gegangen haben.~~ → *… gegangen sein.*
- In a subordinate clause, *werden* not at the end: ~~…, dass er wird es vergessen haben.~~ → *…, dass er es vergessen haben wird.*
- Reading every Futur II as future: *Er wird es gewusst haben* usually means "he probably knew it", not "he will have known it".
- Overusing it in speech: *Bis Montag werde ich den Bericht geschrieben haben* is correct but heavy in a chat; *Bis Montag habe ich den Bericht geschrieben* is more natural.
- The singular for interest: everyday German says *Die Zinsen sind gestiegen*, in the plural. The singular *der Zins* is mostly technical (*der Leitzins*, the central bank's base rate).

## Key points

- Futur II = *werden* + Partizip II + *haben/sein*: *Wir werden die Wohnung abbezahlt haben. Er wird gegangen sein.*
- Use 1: finished before a point in the future, usually with *bis*, *in … Jahren*, *wenn*. In speech the perfect + time phrase is more common: *Bis 2041 haben wir sie abbezahlt.*
- Use 2: an assumption about the past, often with *wohl, sicher, bestimmt*: *Sie wird den Bus verpasst haben.* Everyday alternative: *Sie hat wohl den Bus verpasst.*
- Futur I assumes about the present (*Er wird im Büro sein*), Futur II about the past (*Er wird schon gegangen sein*).
- Subordinate clause: *…, dass er es vergessen haben wird.* Indirect speech: *…, er werde es bis dahin geschafft haben.*

lessons.title: According to …: reporting verbs and the media landscape
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now put any statement into indirect speech. But a good report does more than repeat: it tells the reader *how* something was said. Did the minister simply say it, or did she stress it, admit it, deny it or promise it? And where does the information come from? This lesson is about the tools for that:

- **[[reporting verbs]]** with different shades of meaning: *betonen, einräumen, bestreiten, versichern, ankündigen, verkünden, bekräftigen, warnen*;
- ways to name the source: *laut, zufolge, gemäß, nach Angaben, wie … mitteilte, so …*;
- when a report uses the Konjunktiv I and when the indicative is normal;
- the difference between neutral and evaluative reporting.

The theme is broadcasting and the media: TV and radio, podcasts and streaming, and the people who make and watch them.

## Reporting verbs and what they add

Many reporting verbs were introduced at B1. Here they are together, with the attitude each one adds:

| verb | meaning | what it tells the reader |
|---|---|---|
| *sagen, erklären, mitteilen* | say, state, announce | neutral |
| *betonen* | stress, emphasize | the speaker found this important |
| *einräumen* | concede, admit | the speaker didn't want to say it |
| *zugeben* | admit (lesson 3) | the speaker admits a fault |
| *bestreiten* | deny, dispute | the speaker says it's not true |
| *versichern* | assure | the speaker promises it's true |
| *bekräftigen* | reaffirm, reiterate | the speaker repeats a position firmly |
| *ankündigen* | announce (in advance) | something will happen |
| *verkünden* | announce, proclaim | a decision or result is made public |
| *warnen vor* + dative | warn of, against | a danger |
| *behaupten* | claim | the writer doubts it |

Most of them take indirect speech with or without *dass*:

- *Die Moderatorin betonte, die Sendung sei nicht abgesetzt.* — The presenter stressed that the show had not been cancelled.
- *Der Sender räumte ein, dass Fehler gemacht worden seien.* — The broadcaster admitted that mistakes had been made.
- *Die Intendantin versicherte, es werde keine Entlassungen geben.* — The director-general gave assurances that there would be no redundancies.
- *Die Regierung bekräftigte, sie halte an dem Plan fest.* — The government reaffirmed that it was sticking to the plan.

Several also take an infinitive with *zu* (same subject) or a simple object:

- *Er bestritt, die E-Mail geschrieben zu haben.* — He denied having written the e-mail.
- *Sie kündigte ihren Rücktritt an.* — She announced her resignation.
- *Die Jury verkündete das Ergebnis um Mitternacht.* — The jury announced the result at midnight.
- *Experten warnen vor zu viel Medienkonsum bei Kindern.* — Experts warn against too much media consumption among children.

*ankündigen* is separable (*kündigte … an, hat angekündigt*); *verkünden* and *bekräftigen* are inseparable (*verkündete, hat verkündet*). *ankündigen* looks forward (something planned), *verkünden* makes something official, often solemnly: *das Urteil verkünden, den Wahlsieg verkünden*.

## Naming the source: laut, zufolge, gemäß, nach

German has several short ways to say "according to".

*laut* stands before the noun. With a plain noun, it has no visible case; with an article it takes the dative, or in formal writing the genitive:

- *laut Polizei, laut Gesetz, laut Umfrage*
- *laut dem Bericht* / *laut des Berichts* (both accepted; the dative is more common in speech)
- *laut Angaben des Senders* — according to the broadcaster

*zufolge* takes the dative and stands *after* the noun: it's a **[[postposition]]**.

- *dem Bericht zufolge* — according to the report
- *Augenzeugen zufolge* — according to eyewitnesses
- *einer neuen Studie zufolge* — according to a new study

*gemäß* (+ dative, before or after the noun) is formal and usually means "in accordance with" a rule or agreement rather than "according to" a speaker: *gemäß der Vereinbarung, dem Vertrag gemäß, gemäß Artikel 5*. Don't use it for what a person said.

*nach* + dative works in fixed phrases: *nach Angaben der Polizei* (according to police information), *nach Informationen des Spiegels*, *nach eigenen Angaben* (by its own account). With opinions, *nach* goes after the noun: *meiner Meinung nach*.

### wie … mitteilte and so …

Two more patterns are typical of news:

- A clause with *wie*, which names the source and then states the content in the indicative: *Wie ein Sprecher des Senders mitteilte, wird die Talkshow im Sommer eingestellt.* — As a spokesman for the broadcaster announced, the talk show will be discontinued in the summer.
- *so* + source at the end, after a comma, with no verb: *Die Quote sei stabil, so die Programmdirektorin.* — The ratings were stable, according to the programme director.

## Konjunktiv I or indicative?

In lesson 1 you learned that the Konjunktiv I marks reported speech. When the source is already named inside the same sentence, writers often don't need it:

- After *laut, zufolge, nach Angaben*: the indicative is normal. *Laut Polizei wurde niemand verletzt.* (The Konjunktiv I, *sei … verletzt worden*, also occurs.)
- After *wie … mitteilte*: the indicative is the standard choice (*Wie der Sender mitteilte, ist …*). The Konjunktiv I is sometimes seen there, but it's redundant, because *wie* already names the source.
- After a reporting verb + *dass*: both are common; the Konjunktiv I is more neutral and more formal.
- After verbs that present the content as a fact (*bestätigen* confirm, *zeigen*, *beweisen*), and often after *einräumen* and *zugeben*: the indicative is natural, because the speaker admits something that is true. *Der Sender räumte ein, dass die Quoten sinken.*
- In a series of sentences continuing a report (lesson 1): the Konjunktiv I, because nothing else shows that the sentences are still the speaker's.

## Neutral and evaluative reporting

The choice of verb can make a report neutral or slant it. Compare two versions of the same news:

> *Version A: Die Intendantin erklärte, der Sender müsse sparen. Sie sagte, die Nachrichten seien davon nicht betroffen.*
>
> *Version B: Die Intendantin behauptete, der Sender müsse sparen. Sie versuchte zu beschwichtigen: Die Nachrichten seien angeblich nicht betroffen.*

Version A is neutral: *erklären* and *sagen* pass the statement on. Version B suggests that the writer doesn't believe her: *behaupten* (claim), *beschwichtigen* (to play down, to placate) and *angeblich* (allegedly) all express doubt. That's fine in a *Kommentar* (opinion piece), but not in a news report. Watch for these signals when you read, and choose neutral verbs when you write a report or a summary at B2.

## The media landscape

Germany's *Medienlandschaft* has two kinds of broadcasters. The public-service broadcasters (*der öffentlich-rechtliche Rundfunk*: ARD with its regional stations, ZDF and Deutschlandradio) are financed mainly by the *Rundfunkbeitrag*, a monthly fee paid per household, whether or not you watch or listen. Private broadcasters are financed by advertising. The *Rundfunkbeitrag* and what the public broadcasters should offer are a regular topic of political debate.

*Der Rundfunk* (B1) covers both radio and TV; *der Hörfunk* is the formal word for radio broadcasting, and a single station is *ein Radiosender*. Every broadcaster has *eine Mediathek*, an online library where you can stream programmes after they have been *ausgestrahlt* (broadcast; *die Ausstrahlung*). *Die Sendezeit* is airtime or a programme's time slot. *Die Einschaltquote* (ratings) measures how many people watch; *die Reichweite* (reach) how many people a medium reaches in total.

Typical formats: *die Nachrichtensendung* (news programme), presented by a *Nachrichtensprecher* or *Nachrichtensprecherin* (newsreader); *die Livesendung* (live broadcast); *die Talkshow*, which a *Moderator* or *Moderatorin* (presenter, host) *moderiert*; *die Reportage* (an on-the-spot report or feature, French pronunciation re-por-TAA-zhe) and *die Dokumentation* (documentary, often *die Doku*). Audio formats reach *Zuhörer* and *Zuhörerinnen* (listeners), TV formats *Zuschauer* and *Zuschauerinnen* (viewers). *Der Podcast* has become a major *Medium* (plural *die Medien*), and *Influencer* and *Influencerinnen* reach millions of young people without a broadcaster at all. A state that controls what may be broadcast is said to *zensieren* (censor) the media.

- *Die Dokumentation wird am Sonntag um 20.15 Uhr ausgestrahlt und ist danach in der Mediathek abrufbar.* — The documentary will be broadcast on Sunday at 8.15 pm and can be watched in the online library afterwards.
- *Die Einschaltquoten der Talkshow sind seit Jahren rückläufig.* — The talk show's ratings have been falling for years.
- *Viele Jugendliche streamen lieber, als lineares Fernsehen zu schauen.* — Many young people prefer streaming to watching scheduled TV.
- *Die Ankündigung des Senders sorgte für Kritik.* — The broadcaster's announcement caused criticism.

## Text: Ein Sender baut um

This news report from the media section of a newspaper uses many of the reporting tools from this lesson.

> *Mehr Podcasts, weniger Talkshow*
>
> *Der Regionalsender WRS baut sein Programm um. Wie Intendantin Karin Holm am Mittwoch ankündigte, soll eine der beiden Talkshows am Abend ab Januar wegfallen. Stattdessen wolle man mehr Geld in Reportagen, Dokumentationen und Podcasts investieren. Holm betonte, die Nachrichtensendungen seien von den Kürzungen nicht betroffen. Die Livesendung um 19 Uhr bleibe auf ihrem Sendeplatz.*
>
> *Der Sender reagiert damit auf den veränderten Medienkonsum. Laut einer Studie des Senders sehen Zuschauerinnen und Zuschauer unter 40 kaum noch lineares Fernsehen; die meisten nutzen vor allem die Mediathek. Holm räumte ein, dass die Einschaltquoten der Talkshow seit Jahren sinken. Zugleich bestritt sie, dass die Reform mit dem Streit um den Rundfunkbeitrag zusammenhänge.*
>
> *Kritik kam vom Personalrat des Senders. Dessen Vorsitzender warnte vor einem Abbau beim Journalismus. Der WRS dürfe seine Reichweite im Hörfunk nicht aufs Spiel setzen, so der Vorsitzende.*

> *More podcasts, less talk show*
>
> *The regional broadcaster WRS is restructuring its programmes. As director-general Karin Holm announced on Wednesday, one of the two evening talk shows is to be dropped from January. Instead, she said, the station wants to invest more money in reports, documentaries and podcasts. Holm stressed that the news programmes were not affected by the cuts. The live programme at 7 pm would keep its slot.*
>
> *The broadcaster is reacting to changing media consumption. According to a study by the broadcaster, viewers under 40 hardly watch scheduled TV any more; most of them mainly use the online library. Holm admitted that the talk show's ratings have been falling for years. At the same time, she denied that the reform had anything to do with the dispute over the licence fee.*
>
> *Criticism came from the station's staff council. Its chairman warned against cuts to journalism. WRS must not put its radio audience at risk, the chairman said.*

Look at how each statement is introduced: *wie … ankündigte* + indicative (*soll … wegfallen*: here *soll* is objective, "is to"); *wolle man* (Konjunktiv I continuing the report); *betonte* + Konjunktiv I; *laut* + indicative; *räumte ein, dass* + indicative (an admitted fact); *bestritt, dass* + Konjunktiv I (her denial, not the paper's view); *warnte vor* + noun; *so der Vorsitzende* after Konjunktiv I. *Die Intendantin* is the director-general of a public broadcaster, *lineares Fernsehen* is TV watched at broadcast times, *der Personalrat* is the staff council in a public institution, and *etwas aufs Spiel setzen* means to put something at risk.

## Pronunciation

- *die Reportage* and *die Mediathek*: re-por-TAA-zhe, me-di-a-TEEK.
- *der Moderator*: mo-de-RAA-tor; plural *Moderatoren*: mo-de-ra-TOO-ren (the stress moves).
- *die Einschaltquote*: AIN-shalt-kvo-te; *qu* is *kv*.
- *der Podcast*, *die Talkshow*, *streamen*, *der Influencer*: roughly as in English, but with a German *r*.

## Common mistakes

- *laut* after the noun: ~~der Polizei laut~~ → *laut Polizei*. And *zufolge* before it: ~~zufolge dem Bericht~~ → *dem Bericht zufolge*.
- Using *gemäß* for a person's statement: ~~gemäß dem Minister~~ → *laut dem Minister, nach Angaben des Ministers*.
- A redundant Konjunktiv I after *wie … mitteilte*: *Wie der Sender mitteilte, sei die Sendung abgesetzt* is often seen, but the standard choice is the indicative → *Wie der Sender mitteilte, ist die Sendung abgesetzt.*
- *warnen vor* with the accusative: ~~Sie warnte vor den Medienkonsum~~ → *vor dem Medienkonsum* (dative).
- *ankündigen* not separated: ~~Der Sender ankündigte eine neue Sendung~~ → *Der Sender kündigte eine neue Sendung an.*
- *behaupten* in a neutral report: it signals doubt. For a neutral report → *sagen, erklären*.
- *bestreiten* with *nicht*: ~~Er bestritt, das Geld nicht genommen zu haben~~ means he denied *not* taking it. → *Er bestritt, das Geld genommen zu haben.*

## Key points

- Reporting verbs add attitude: *betonen* (stress), *einräumen* (concede), *bestreiten* (deny), *versichern* (assure), *bekräftigen* (reaffirm), *ankündigen* (announce in advance), *verkünden* (make public), *warnen vor* + dative, *behaupten* (claim, doubtful).
- They take indirect speech (with or without *dass*), often a *zu*-infinitive, or a noun.
- Sources: *laut Polizei / laut dem Bericht*; *dem Bericht zufolge* (after the noun, dative); *nach Angaben der Polizei*; *gemäß* only for rules; *wie … mitteilte*; *…, so die Polizei*.
- With *laut, zufolge, nach Angaben* and *wie …* the indicative is normal; after reporting verbs the Konjunktiv I is the neutral choice; after *einräumen, zugeben, bestätigen* the indicative is common.
- Neutral reporting uses neutral verbs; *behaupten, angeblich, beschwichtigen* show the writer's doubt and belong in opinion pieces.
