- A noun can have attributes on both sides: participle attributes and adjectives in front, genitives and prepositional phrases after.
- Read long phrases noun first, then the participle, then the words in between, then the right side.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Verbal style and nominal style
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Compare two ways of saying the same thing:

- *Weil viele Lehrkräfte fehlen, fällt oft Unterricht aus.* — Because many teachers are missing, lessons are often cancelled.
- *Wegen des Lehrkräftemangels kommt es häufig zu Unterrichtsausfällen.* — Owing to the teacher shortage, there are frequent cancellations of lessons.

The first sentence builds the meaning around verbs (*fehlen, ausfallen*): this is **[[verbal style]]** (*Verbalstil*). The second turns the actions into nouns (*der Mangel, der Ausfall*) and links them with prepositions: this is **[[nominal style]]** (*Nominalstil*). Spoken German is mostly verbal. Reports, applications, academic papers, official letters and news headlines lean towards nominal style, because it is short and impersonal and puts the facts in front.

At B2 you need to do two things: understand nominal style when you read it, by turning it back into clauses in your head, and use a moderate amount of it in formal writing. This lesson shows you how to build nouns from verbs, how to turn subordinate clauses into prepositional phrases and back, and where the subject and object of the action go. Together with the participle attributes of lessons 11 and 12, this is the third tool of dense texts.

The theme is the German education system: school types, compulsory schooling, support for weaker pupils and the long debate about fairness in education.

## Nouns from verbs

German has four main ways of making a noun from a verb. This process is called **[[nominalization]]**.

| type | how | examples |
|---|---|---|
| *-ung* | stem + *-ung*; always feminine | *fördern → die Förderung, verbessern → die Verbesserung, prüfen → die Prüfung, versetzen → die Versetzung* |
| infinitive | the infinitive with a capital letter; always neuter | *lernen → das Lernen, lesen → das Lesen, sitzenbleiben → das Sitzenbleiben* |
| stem noun, often with a vowel change | a short noun from the stem; usually masculine | *abschließen → der Abschluss, abbrechen → der Abbruch, beginnen → der Beginn, ankommen → die Ankunft, teilnehmen → die Teilnahme* |
| *-e* | stem + *-e*; feminine | *suchen → die Suche, helfen → die Hilfe, reisen → die Reise* |

The **[[nominalized infinitive]]** (*das Lernen*) is the safe choice when no other noun exists, or when you mean the activity itself, ongoing: *das Lernen in Gruppen* (learning in groups), *beim Schreiben* (while writing). The *-ung* noun often means the single act or its result: *die Prüfung* (the exam), *die Übersetzung* (the translation).

The stem nouns have to be learned one by one, but many follow the vowel of the past forms: *schließen – schloss – der Schluss / Abschluss*, *brechen – brach – der Bruch / Abbruch*, *ziehen – zog – der Zug / Umzug*, *greifen – griff – der Griff / Eingriff*.

## From clause to phrase

A subordinate clause becomes a prepositional phrase with the noun. Each conjunction has its preposition:

| verbal style (clause) | nominal style (phrase) | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *wenn / als man ankommt* | *bei der Ankunft* | time, condition |
| *weil es regnete* | *wegen des Regens / aufgrund des Regens* | cause |
| *obwohl er krank war* | *trotz seiner Krankheit* | concession |
| *um die Schulen zu verbessern / damit die Schulen besser werden* | *zur Verbesserung der Schulen* | purpose |
| *nachdem sie die Schule abgeschlossen hatte* | *nach dem Schulabschluss* | time after |
| *bevor das Schuljahr beginnt* | *vor Beginn des Schuljahres* | time before |
| *während er studierte* | *während seines Studiums* | time during |
| *seit sie umgezogen ist* | *seit ihrem Umzug* | since |
| *indem man Lehrkräfte einstellt* | *durch die Einstellung von Lehrkräften* | means |
| *falls Unterricht ausfällt* | *im Fall eines Unterrichtsausfalls / bei Unterrichtsausfall* | condition |
| *ohne dass die Eltern zustimmen* | *ohne Zustimmung der Eltern* | without |

Purpose with *zu* + *-ung* noun (*zur Verbesserung, zur Förderung, zur Vorbereitung*) is one of the most common patterns in formal German: *Das Land stellt 50 Millionen Euro zur Förderung benachteiligter Schulen bereit.* (The state is providing 50 million euros to support disadvantaged schools.)

## Where do the subject and the object go?

In a clause, the subject and the object have their cases. In a nominal phrase, they usually become a **[[genitive attribute]]** after the noun.

The object of the verb becomes a genitive.

- *Man reformiert das Schulsystem.* → *die Reform des Schulsystems* (the reform of the school system)
- *Man fördert die Kinder.* → *die Förderung der Kinder*

The subject of an intransitive verb also becomes a genitive.

- *Die Schülerinnen kommen an.* → *die Ankunft der Schülerinnen*
- *Die Schulabbrüche nehmen zu.* → *die Zunahme der Schulabbrüche*

When there's both a subject and an object, the object takes the genitive and the doer comes in with *durch* (or, less formally, *von*):

- *Die Schulen fördern begabte Kinder.* → *die Förderung begabter Kinder durch die Schulen*

A pronoun becomes a possessive:

- *Sie ist angekommen.* → *ihre Ankunft* — *Wir haben uns beworben.* → *unsere Bewerbung*

No article? Use von + dative. A genitive needs an article or an adjective to show it. Without one, *von* takes over:

- *Man stellt Lehrkräfte ein.* → *die Einstellung von Lehrkräften* (not ~~die Einstellung Lehrkräfte~~)
- but with an adjective: *die Einstellung zusätzlicher Lehrkräfte*

Prepositional objects keep their preposition:

- *sich auf die Prüfung vorbereiten* → *die Vorbereitung auf die Prüfung*
- *an einem Kurs teilnehmen* → *die Teilnahme an einem Kurs*
- *über die Reform diskutieren* → *die Diskussion über die Reform*

Adverbs become adjectives:

- *Die Regierung hat die Schulen schnell reformiert.* → *die schnelle Reform der Schulen durch die Regierung*
- *Die Kinder lernen früh.* → *das frühe Lernen der Kinder*

### Nominal style and the verbs that remain

Turning verbs into nouns leaves the sentence with few real verbs. The ones that remain are often weak, general verbs: *erfolgen* (to take place), *kommen zu* (to happen), *führen zu* (to lead to), *sorgen für*, or the Funktionsverbgefüge of lesson 9 (*zur Verfügung stellen, in Kraft treten*):

- *Die Anmeldung erfolgt online.* — Registration is done online. (= *Man meldet sich online an.*)
- *Der Lehrkräftemangel führt zu Unterrichtsausfall.* — The shortage of teachers leads to cancelled lessons.

## When is nominal style right?

Nominal style is right where texts must be short, precise and impersonal:

- headlines: *Schulreform: Einführung der Ganztagsschule ab 2027*
- CVs and lists: *Organisation des Abschlussballs, Betreuung neuer Schülerinnen und Schüler*
- reports and official letters: *Nach Prüfung Ihres Antrags …* (After examining your application …)
- academic writing: *Die Untersuchung der Lernmotivation erfolgte mithilfe eines Fragebogens.*

It becomes a problem when it's piled up. This sentence is grammatically correct but almost unreadable:

- *Zur Sicherstellung der Durchführung der Maßnahmen zur Verbesserung der Bildungschancen ist eine Erhöhung der Mittel erforderlich.*

Four nouns in *-ung* in a chain of genitives. Undo two of them and it's clear:

- *Damit die Maßnahmen für bessere Bildungschancen durchgeführt werden können, braucht es mehr Geld.* — So that the measures for better educational opportunities can be carried out, more money is needed.

A good B2 compromise in an e-mail or essay: one or two nominal phrases per sentence, a real verb in every sentence, and no chains of more than two genitives.

## The education system: the words

Education in Germany is the responsibility of the sixteen federal states (*Bildung ist Ländersache*): each state has its own *Kultusministerium* (ministry of education and cultural affairs), its own *Lehrpläne* (curricula), and a slightly different *Schulsystem*. *Das Bildungswesen* is the whole education sector; *das Bildungssystem* is the way it's organized; *die Bildungspolitik* is education policy.

- *Die Schulpflicht* (compulsory schooling) starts at about six. All *schulpflichtigen* children must go to school; homeschooling is generally not allowed in Germany.
- After four years (six in Berlin and Brandenburg) of primary school, children move on to the *Sekundarstufe* (secondary level) and to a *Schulform* (type of school). The traditional three are the *Hauptschule*, *Realschule* and *Gymnasium*; many states have merged the *Hauptschule* with other types.
- *Die Ganztagsschule* (all-day school) has spread a lot. From 2026, primary school children gain a legal right to all-day care, introduced one year group at a time.
- A pupil who fails a year may have to *sitzenbleiben* (repeat the year; *ist sitzengeblieben*) instead of getting *die Versetzung* (moving up). Critics say it does more harm than good.
- *Der Leistungsdruck* (pressure to perform) and *Prüfungsangst* (exam anxiety) are big topics, and so is *Nachhilfe*: private tutoring, which many families pay for. Schools offer *Förderunterricht* (extra support lessons) as well.
- *Die Inklusion* means that children with and without disabilities learn together. *Die Hochbegabung* (giftedness) needs support too: *Förderung* means support, funding or encouragement.
- *Die Bildungsgerechtigkeit* (fairness in education) is the central debate: in Germany, the *Bildungsabschluss* (qualification) a child reaches still depends strongly on the parents' education and income. *Benachteiligte* children have worse *Bildungschancen*. *Frühkindliche Bildung* (early-childhood education) in nurseries is seen as one way to change this.
- *Die Schulleitung* is the head teacher and management of a school; *der Abschlussjahrgang* is the final-year group. *Der Schulabbruch* is dropping out of school. *Die Schulbildung* is the schooling someone has had, and *der Bildungsweg* their path through education: *auf dem zweiten Bildungsweg* means getting a qualification later in life, through evening classes for example.
- *Die Lernmotivation* is the motivation to learn; *das Bildungsniveau* the level of education; *die Schulreform* a reform of schools.

## Text: Zwei Versionen

The same news told twice: first by a head teacher at a parents' evening, then in the school's annual report. Read both and compare.

> Am Elternabend (gesprochen):
>
> Liebe Eltern, ich habe gute Nachrichten. Weil wir im letzten Jahr drei neue Lehrkräfte einstellen konnten, ist viel weniger Unterricht ausgefallen. Und weil wir den Förderunterricht ausgebaut haben, sind nur noch acht Kinder sitzengeblieben. Vor zwei Jahren waren es noch zwanzig! Ab Februar bieten wir außerdem Kurse an, damit sich die Abschlussklassen besser auf die Prüfungen vorbereiten können. Wer mitmachen möchte, meldet sich einfach im Sekretariat an.
>
> Im Jahresbericht (geschrieben):
>
> Durch die Einstellung von drei zusätzlichen Lehrkräften konnte der Unterrichtsausfall im vergangenen Schuljahr deutlich reduziert werden. Infolge des Ausbaus des Förderunterrichts ging die Zahl der Nichtversetzungen von zwanzig auf acht zurück. Zur besseren Vorbereitung des Abschlussjahrgangs auf die Prüfungen werden ab Februar zusätzliche Kurse angeboten. Die Anmeldung erfolgt über das Sekretariat.

In English (the content is the same; the second version sounds like this):

> At the parents' evening: Dear parents, I've got good news. Because we were able to hire three new teachers last year, far fewer lessons were cancelled. And because we've expanded the support lessons, only eight children had to repeat a year. Two years ago it was twenty! From February we're also offering courses so the final classes can prepare better for the exams. Anyone who wants to take part just signs up at the office.
>
> In the annual report: Through the recruitment of three additional teachers, lesson cancellation was significantly reduced in the past school year. As a result of the expansion of support lessons, the number of pupils not moved up fell from twenty to eight. For the better preparation of the final-year group for the exams, additional courses will be offered from February. Registration is via the school office.

What changed: *weil … einstellen konnten* → *durch die Einstellung von*; *weil wir … ausgebaut haben* → *infolge des Ausbaus*; *damit … sich vorbereiten können* → *zur besseren Vorbereitung … auf*; *meldet sich an* → *die Anmeldung erfolgt*. The written version also uses the passive (*reduziert werden, angeboten*) and drops "we": the school disappears behind the facts.

Words to note from the text: *der Elternabend* (parents' evening), *ausbauen* (to expand; *der Ausbau*), *das Sekretariat* (school office), *infolge* (as a result of, + genitive), *die Nichtversetzung* (not being moved up a year), *der Unterrichtsausfall* (cancelled lessons).

## Pronunciation

- *das Kultusministerium*: KUL-tus-mi-nis-TEH-ri-um, main stress on *Kul-* (as in most compounds), a secondary stress on *-te-*.
- *das Bildungsniveau*: French *niveau*, said ni-VOH, stressed on its last syllable (the compound as a whole is stressed on *Bil-*).
- *die Inklusion*: in-klu-ZJOHN; *-sion* is said like *-zjohn*, as in *die Diskussion*.
- *die Sekundarstufe*: ze-kun-DAAR-shtoo-fe.

## Common mistakes

- Genitive without an article: ~~die Einstellung Lehrkräfte~~ → *die Einstellung von Lehrkräften* (or *zusätzlicher Lehrkräfte*, with an adjective).
- Keeping the accusative: ~~die Förderung die Kinder~~ → *die Förderung der Kinder*.
- Losing the preposition of a prepositional object: ~~die Vorbereitung der Prüfung~~ → *die Vorbereitung auf die Prüfung*.
- Small letters: nominalized infinitives are nouns and take a capital: *beim Lernen*, *das Sitzenbleiben*.
- Wrong gender: every *-ung* noun is feminine (*die Versetzung*), every nominalized infinitive is neuter (*das Lesen*).
- Nominalizing everything. A text with no real verbs reads like a form. Keep at least one active verb per sentence.

## Key points

- Verbal style builds sentences around verbs and is typical of speech; nominal style turns actions into nouns and is typical of formal writing.
- Nouns from verbs: *-ung* (feminine), nominalized infinitive (neuter), stem nouns (*der Abschluss, die Ankunft*) and *-e* nouns (*die Suche*).
- Clauses become prepositional phrases: *wenn → bei*, *weil → wegen/aufgrund*, *obwohl → trotz*, *um … zu → zu(r)*, *nachdem → nach*, *bevor → vor*, *indem → durch*.
- The object (or the subject of an intransitive verb) becomes a genitive; the doer comes with *durch*; pronouns become possessives; no article → *von*; prepositional objects keep their preposition.
- Use it in moderation: no long genitive chains, and keep a real verb in each sentence.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Notwithstanding, by means of: formal prepositions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 13 turned clauses into nouns, and nouns need prepositions to link them: *wegen des Regens, trotz der Kritik, zur Verbesserung*. Formal German has a whole set of extra prepositions for this, most of them with the genitive. You won't use them much in conversation, but you'll find them in every hospital letter, contract, instruction leaflet and news report, and the Goethe B2 reading texts are full of them.

In B1 you learned *wegen, trotz, während, statt, innerhalb, außerhalb*, and maybe some of the official ones from the B1 honors lessons: *aufgrund, infolge, angesichts, hinsichtlich, anlässlich*. This lesson adds the next layer:

- *ungeachtet* (notwithstanding), *seitens* (on the part of), *zwecks* (for the purpose of), *mittels* (by means of), *zugunsten* (in favour of)
- *inmitten* (in the middle of), *unweit* (not far from), *oberhalb* / *unterhalb* (above / below)
- *einschließlich* (including), *abzüglich* (minus, less)
- and one with the dative: *entgegen* (contrary to)

The theme is health and medicine: illnesses, infections, hospitals and treatment. Hospital and insurance letters are the place where you'll most often need these prepositions.

## The genitive prepositions in a table

| preposition | meaning | everyday alternative | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *ungeachtet* | notwithstanding, regardless of | *trotz* | *Ungeachtet der Risiken entschied er sich für die Operation.* |
| *seitens* | on the part of, from | *von* | *Seitens der Klinik gab es keine Einwände.* |
| *zwecks* | for the purpose of | *für, um … zu* | *Der Patient wurde zwecks Untersuchung stationär aufgenommen.* |
| *mittels* | by means of | *mit, mithilfe* | *Der Erreger wurde mittels eines Bluttests nachgewiesen.* |
| *zugunsten* | in favour of, for the benefit of | *für* | *Die Spenden gehen zugunsten der Kinderklinik.* |
| *inmitten* | in the middle of, amid | *mitten in* | *Inmitten der Pandemie wurde das Krankenhaus erweitert.* |
| *unweit* | not far from | *nicht weit von* | *Die Praxis liegt unweit des Bahnhofs.* |
| *oberhalb* | above | *über* | *Die Schmerzen sitzen oberhalb des Knies.* |
| *unterhalb* | below | *unter* | *Der Wert liegt unterhalb der Grenze.* |
| *einschließlich* | including | *mit, inklusive* | *Die Kosten einschließlich der Medikamente trägt die Krankenkasse.* |
| *abzüglich* | minus, less (money) | *minus, ohne* | *Sie erhalten den Betrag abzüglich der Zuzahlung zurück.* |

A few notes on meaning:

- *ungeachtet* is a formal *trotz*: something doesn't stop the action. It can also follow its noun in very formal style: *aller Warnungen ungeachtet* (all warnings notwithstanding).
- *seitens* names the side that does something, often an institution: *seitens der Ärzte, seitens der Regierung*. Many people write *vonseiten* (or *von Seiten*) + genitive instead.
- *zwecks* is office German, typical of forms and letters, and often used without an article: *zwecks Terminabsprache* (to arrange an appointment). In a normal sentence, *um … zu* or *zur* + noun sounds better.
- *mittels* is about the tool or method, very common in medicine and technology: *mittels Ultraschall, mittels einer Spritze*.
- *zugunsten* can also be written *zu Gunsten*. Its opposite is *zulasten* / *zu Lasten* (at the expense of).
- *einschließlich* (including) and *abzüglich* (minus) appear with prices and amounts. The partner of *abzüglich* is *zuzüglich* (plus): *50 Euro zuzüglich Versand*.

## entgegen: contrary to, with the dative

*entgegen* means "contrary to, against" (an expectation, an advice, a rule). It takes the dative, and it can stand before or after its noun:

- *Entgegen dem Rat ihrer Ärztin ging sie wieder arbeiten.* — Contrary to her doctor's advice, she went back to work.
- *Dem Rat ihrer Ärztin entgegen ging sie wieder arbeiten.* (same meaning, more literary)
- *Entgegen allen Erwartungen erholte er sich schnell.* — Contrary to all expectations, he recovered quickly.

Because it sounds like the other formal prepositions, many native speakers use it with the genitive (~~entgegen des Rates~~). Dictionaries and style guides treat that as a mistake; use the dative.

## When the genitive doesn't show

A genitive is only visible if there is an article or an adjective to carry the ending. Without one, two things can happen.

A singular noun without an article often stands alone, and nobody can see the case. That's normal with *zwecks*, *mittels*, *einschließlich* and *abzüglich*:

- *zwecks Untersuchung, mittels Ultraschall, einschließlich Frühstück, abzüglich Rabatt*

A plural noun without an article switches to the dative, just as with *wegen* in B1:

- *mittels Röntgenstrahlen* (by means of X-rays; counted as dative, though here the dative and genitive plural look the same)
- *einschließlich Getränken* (including drinks; here the dative *-n* shows)

With an adjective, the genitive is back: *mittels moderner Geräte* (by means of modern equipment), *einschließlich aller Nebenkosten* (including all extra costs).

With place prepositions that have no article, use *von*: *oberhalb von 2.000 Metern* (above 2,000 metres), *unweit von Hamburg* (not far from Hamburg). Before a place name without an article, *von* is the normal choice.

## Reviewing the B1 prepositions

These five came in B1 and appear constantly in formal texts. Here they are in health contexts:

- *aufgrund* (because of, due to): *Aufgrund einer akuten Infektion musste die Operation verschoben werden.*
- *infolge* (as a result of): *Infolge der Pandemie fielen viele Eingriffe aus.*
- *angesichts* (in view of): *Angesichts der vielen Erkrankungen schließt die Kita.*
- *hinsichtlich* (with regard to): *Hinsichtlich der Wirksamkeit gibt es noch keine sicheren Daten.*
- *anlässlich* (on the occasion of): *Anlässlich des Weltgesundheitstags informiert die Klinik über Prävention.*

## Register: which one to use?

These prepositions sound formal, and some of them (*zwecks*, *seitens*) sound like an official form. In an e-mail to a friend, use the everyday alternative:

| formal letter | e-mail to a friend |
|---|---|
| *Zwecks Terminvereinbarung bitten wir um Rückruf.* | *Ruf doch bitte an, damit wir einen Termin ausmachen können.* |
| *Seitens der Krankenkasse liegt noch keine Zusage vor.* | *Die Krankenkasse hat noch nicht zugesagt.* |
| *Ungeachtet der Schmerzen lief sie weiter.* | *Obwohl es wehtat, lief sie weiter.* |

In your own formal writing at B2 (a complaint, a letter to an insurer), *aufgrund*, *hinsichtlich*, *einschließlich* and *entgegen* are useful. Use *zwecks* and *seitens* sparingly: they can make you sound like a 1970s civil servant.

## The words: health and medicine

You know the basics from B1 (*die Diagnose, die Behandlung, die Therapie, die Nebenwirkung, chronisch*). These words take you further.

Illness and infection. *Die Erkrankung* is the formal word for an illness; *erkranken* (to fall ill; *ist erkrankt*) is its verb: *Sie ist an Grippe erkrankt.* *Die Vorerkrankung* is a pre-existing condition. An illness can be *akut* (acute) or chronic. *Der Erreger* (pathogen) can be *ein Virus* (plural *die Viren*) or *eine Bakterie* (plural *die Bakterien*; in the singular people also say *das Bakterium*). An infection (*die Infektion*) that passes from person to person is *ansteckend* (contagious). A worldwide outbreak is *eine Pandemie*. Your *Immunsystem* (immune system) and your *Abwehrkräfte* (the body's defences, plural only) fight it off.

Diagnosis and treatment. Doctors *diagnostizieren* an illness. Treatment is *ambulant* (outpatient: you go home the same day) or *stationär* (inpatient: you stay in hospital). An operation or procedure is *der Eingriff*; for a big one you need *eine Narkose* (anaesthesia). The most serious cases go to *die Intensivstation* (intensive care unit). *Rezeptpflichtige* medicines are available only with a prescription.

Results. *Die Wirksamkeit* is how well a treatment works; a *wirksames* medicine works. *Die Heilung* is the cure; an illness is *heilbar* (curable) or *unheilbar* (incurable). *Die Genesung* is the recovery: *Wir wünschen Ihnen eine schnelle Genesung!* *Die Prävention* (prevention) is about stopping illness before it starts.

## Text: Ein Brief aus der Klinik

A letter that a patient receives before a planned operation. Hospitals write in exactly this style.

> Ihr stationärer Aufenthalt am 14. März
>
> Sehr geehrte Frau Demir,
>
> wir bestätigen Ihre Aufnahme zwecks eines geplanten Eingriffs am rechten Knie. Bitte melden Sie sich am Aufnahmetag um 7:30 Uhr an der Patientenanmeldung im Hauptgebäude, unweit des Haupteingangs.
>
> Der Eingriff erfolgt in Vollnarkose. Bitte kommen Sie nüchtern, das heißt: ab Mitternacht nichts mehr essen. Bringen Sie alle Befunde einschließlich der Röntgenbilder sowie eine Liste Ihrer Medikamente mit. Sollten Sie kurz vor dem Termin an einer akuten Infektion erkranken, informieren Sie uns bitte umgehend, da der Eingriff in diesem Fall aus Sicherheitsgründen verschoben werden muss.
>
> Seitens Ihrer Krankenkasse liegt die Kostenzusage bereits vor. Für den stationären Aufenthalt fällt lediglich die gesetzliche Zuzahlung von 10 Euro pro Tag an. Diese wird Ihnen bei der Entlassung in Rechnung gestellt.
>
> Wir weisen darauf hin, dass entgegen einer weit verbreiteten Annahme auch nach kleinen Eingriffen eine Begleitperson Sie abholen muss. Sie dürfen 24 Stunden lang nicht selbst Auto fahren.
>
> Wir wünschen Ihnen schon jetzt eine gute Genesung.
>
> Mit freundlichen Grüßen
> Ihr Team der Orthopädie

In English:

> Your hospital stay on 14 March
>
> Dear Ms Demir,
>
> We confirm your admission for a planned procedure on your right knee. Please report at 7:30 a.m. on the day of admission to the patient registration desk in the main building, not far from the main entrance.
>
> The procedure will be carried out under general anaesthesia. Please come with an empty stomach, which means: nothing to eat after midnight. Bring all medical reports including the X-rays, and a list of your medicines. If you should come down with an acute infection shortly before the appointment, please let us know immediately, as in that case the procedure must be postponed for safety reasons.
>
> Your health insurance fund has already confirmed it will cover the costs. For the hospital stay you only have to pay the statutory co-payment of 10 euros per day. This will be invoiced to you on discharge.
>
> Please note that, contrary to a widespread belief, someone must collect you even after minor procedures. You must not drive yourself for 24 hours.
>
> We wish you a good recovery in advance.
>
> Kind regards,
> Your orthopaedics team

Words to note from the text: *die Aufnahme* (here: admission to hospital), *die Vollnarkose* (general anaesthesia), *nüchtern* (with an empty stomach; also "sober"), *der Befund* (medical findings, report), *umgehend* (immediately, formal), *die Kostenzusage* (confirmation that costs are covered), *die Zuzahlung* (co-payment), *die Entlassung* (here: discharge from hospital), *die Begleitperson* (person accompanying you).

The 10 euros per day is the real co-payment for adults with statutory insurance in Germany, charged for up to 28 days a year.

## Pronunciation

- *die Narkose*: nar-KOH-ze, a long *o* and a voiced *s*.
- *das Virus*: VEE-rus, with a *v* said like English *v* (from Latin). Plural *Viren*: VEE-ren.
- *die Bakterie*: bak-TEH-rje, three syllables, like *die Familie* (fa-MEE-lje).
- *stationär*: shta-tsjo-NÄR; *ambulant*: am-bu-LANT.
- *die Intensivstation*: in-ten-ZEEF-shta-tsjohn.

## Common mistakes

- *entgegen* with the genitive: ~~entgegen des ärztlichen Rates~~ → *entgegen dem ärztlichen Rat*.
- A visible dative after a genitive preposition when an article is there: ~~mittels einem Test~~ → *mittels eines Tests*. The dative is only for plurals without an article.
- Too much office German: ~~Zwecks Erholung fahre ich ans Meer~~ in a postcard sounds comic. Write *Ich fahre ans Meer, um mich zu erholen.*
- Confusing *einschließlich* (including) and *ausschließlich* (exclusively, only; also "excluding" in prices).
- *erkranken* takes *sein*: ~~Sie hat an Grippe erkrankt~~ → *Sie ist an Grippe erkrankt.*
- *das Virus*, not ~~der Virus~~, in writing (*der Virus* is common in speech and accepted by Duden for everyday use, but *das* is the standard form).

## Key points

- Formal genitive prepositions: *ungeachtet, seitens, zwecks, mittels, zugunsten, inmitten, unweit, oberhalb, unterhalb, einschließlich, abzüglich*.
- *entgegen* takes the dative and can stand before or after the noun: *entgegen dem Rat, dem Rat entgegen*.
- Without an article, a singular noun often stands bare (*zwecks Untersuchung*); a plural switches to the dative (*mittels Röntgenstrahlen*); with an adjective the genitive returns.
- Place prepositions with names or numbers: *unweit von Hamburg, oberhalb von 2.000 Metern*.
- These are written and formal. In speech use *trotz, von, um … zu, mit, für, nicht weit von*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Whose, whoever, which: relative clauses at B2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You've used relative clauses since A2 and learned them in every case in B1, including *dessen* and *deren* for "whose", which you only had to recognize. In this module you've also seen their compact cousins, the participle attributes. This lesson finishes the picture:

- *dessen* and *deren* used actively, after prepositions (*mit dessen Hilfe*, *in deren Haus*) and with adjectives (*deren älteste Tochter*);
- **[[free relative clauses]]** with *wer* and *was* that start the sentence (*Wer zu spät kommt, den bestraft das Leben*);
- *welcher* as a formal relative pronoun and the form *derer*, both to recognize;
- how to choose between a relative clause and a participle attribute.

The theme is demography and family: an ageing society, falling and rising birth rates, new family forms and the question of how work and family fit together.

## dessen and deren: the rule in one line

*dessen* and *deren* mean "whose" (or "of which"). They agree with the owner, the noun before the comma, and never change for the noun that follows:

| owner (antecedent) | "whose" |
|---|---|
| masculine or neuter singular | *dessen* |
| feminine singular or any plural | *deren* |

- *Der Nachbar, dessen Kinder bei uns spielen, …* (owner: *der Nachbar*)
- *Die Kollegin, deren Mann Elternzeit nimmt, …* (owner: *die Kollegin*)
- *Die Familien, deren Einkommen niedrig ist, …* (owner: *die Familien*)
- *Das Dorf, dessen Bevölkerung schrumpft, …* (owner: *das Dorf*)

The noun after *dessen/deren* has no article: ~~deren die Kinder~~. *dessen* and *deren* take the place of the article, as *sein* and *ihr* would in a main clause: *Ihr Mann nimmt Elternzeit* → *…, deren Mann Elternzeit nimmt*.

### After a preposition

A preposition goes in front of *dessen/deren*, and it decides the case of the noun that follows, not of *dessen/deren*, which never change:

- *Das ist die Stiftung, mit deren Hilfe das Mehrgenerationenhaus gebaut wurde.* — That's the foundation with whose help the multigenerational house was built.
- *Der Verein, in dessen Räumen die Kinderbetreuung stattfindet, sucht Freiwillige.* — The association in whose rooms the childcare takes place is looking for volunteers.
- *Meine Freundin, bei deren Eltern ich während des Studiums gewohnt habe, …* — My friend, at whose parents' house I lived while I was a student, …

### With an adjective: strong endings

An adjective after *dessen/deren* takes the strong ending (the one it would have with no article at all), because *dessen/deren* don't show the case of the following noun:

| case | example |
|---|---|
| nominative | *die Frau, deren ältester Sohn in Kanada lebt* / *deren älteste Tochter* / *deren jüngstes Kind* |
| accusative | *der Mann, dessen neuen Partner ich kennengelernt habe* |
| dative | *die Familie, mit deren jüngster Tochter ich befreundet bin* |

Compare: *mit ihrer jüngsten Tochter* (after *ihrer*, weak) but *mit deren jüngster Tochter* (after *deren*, strong). If that feels strange, you're in good company; even native speakers hesitate here, so it's worth learning the rule.

## Free relative clauses: wer … der, was … das

A **[[free relative clause]]** has no noun before it: it starts with *wer* (whoever, the person who) or *was* (whatever, the thing that) and works as a part of the main clause, often its subject or object. You met them in proverbs in B1. Now you'll build them.

The main clause usually picks up the free relative clause with a form of *der* or *das* at its start. That word takes the case the main clause needs:

- *Wer zu spät kommt, den bestraft das Leben.* — Whoever comes too late is punished by life. (*wer*: subject of *kommt*; *den*: object of *bestraft*)
- *Wem die Kinderbetreuung zu teuer ist, der kann einen Zuschuss beantragen.* — Anyone who finds childcare too expensive can apply for a subsidy. (*wem*: dative with *zu teuer sein*; *der*: subject of *kann*)
- *Wen das Thema interessiert, dem empfehle ich diesen Bericht.* — Whoever is interested in the topic, I recommend this report to them.
- *Was Sie heute sparen, das fehlt Ihnen im Alter nicht.* — What you save today, you won't be short of in old age.

When both cases are the same, the pick-up word is usually left out:

- *Wer Elterngeld beantragen will, (der) muss einen schriftlichen Antrag stellen.* (both nominative)
- *Was er sagt, (das) stimmt.* (both nominative)

When they differ, the pick-up word must be there: ~~Wer zu spät kommt, bestraft das Leben~~ would mean "Whoever comes late punishes life".

With a verb that takes a preposition, the pick-up word is a *da(r)*-word:

- *Was in der Studie steht, darüber wird viel diskutiert.* — What's in the study is much discussed.
- *Wovon viele träumen, davon sprechen nur wenige offen.* — What many dream of, few talk about openly.

## welcher: the formal relative *(receptive)*

In formal and older texts, *welcher, welche, welches* (with the endings of *dieser*) can replace *der, die, das* as a relative pronoun:

- *Die Kommission, welche den Bericht erstellt hat, empfiehlt eine Reform des Generationenvertrags.*

Today it's mainly used to avoid two identical words in a row: *die Frau, die die Studie leitet* → *die Frau, welche die Studie leitet*. It has no genitive (no ~~welches~~ for "whose"), so you can't use it for *dessen/deren*. You only need to recognize it.

## derer: "of those who" *(receptive)*

*derer* looks like a relative pronoun, but it's the genitive plural of the demonstrative *die* (those), and it appears before a relative clause:

- *Die Zahl derer, die allein leben, steigt.* — The number of those who live alone is rising.
- *Wir sprechen im Namen derer, die keine Stimme haben.* — We speak on behalf of those who have no voice.

The relative pronoun "whose" for plurals is always *deren*: *die Familien, deren Kinder …*, not ~~derer Kinder~~. Learn *derer* as a reading word: it means "of those (who)".

## Relative clause or participle attribute?

Lessons 11 and 12 showed that many relative clauses can be packed in front of the noun. Which one should you choose?

| relative clause | participle attribute |
|---|---|
| *die Menschen, die allein leben* | *die allein lebenden Menschen* |
| *die Zahl der Kinder, die im letzten Jahr geboren wurden* | *die Zahl der im letzten Jahr geborenen Kinder* |
| *ein Programm, das vom Bund gefördert wird* | *ein vom Bund gefördertes Programm* |

- In speech, and whenever the content is long, use a relative clause.
- In writing, a short attribute (two or three words) saves space and keeps the sentence moving.
- Some things only a relative clause can do: a relative pronoun that isn't the subject (*die Stadt, in der ich wohne*), *dessen/deren*, modal verbs other than "must/can", and any tense contrast you need to make clear.
- Mixing both is fine and often elegant: *Die vom Bund geförderten Mehrgenerationenhäuser, deren Zahl seit 2006 stark gewachsen ist, bringen Alt und Jung zusammen.*

## The words: demography and family forms

*Die Demografie* is the study of population and how it changes; the adjective is *demografisch*: *der demografische Wandel* (demographic change) is one of the most common phrases in German politics. *Der Wandel* is a deep, slow change, more than *die Änderung*.

An ageing society. *Die Lebenserwartung* (life expectancy) in Germany is around 80 years and has risen for decades, while *die Geburtenrate* (birth rate) has been well below two children per woman for decades. The result is *die Alterung* (ageing) of the population, which critics call *Überalterung* (an excessively old population). *Der Geburtenrückgang* (fall in births) is partly balanced by *die Zuwanderung* (immigration). Many rural regions, especially in eastern Germany, have lost people through *Abwanderung* (people moving away): their towns *schrumpfen* (shrink; *sind geschrumpft*), while big cities grow. *Das Bevölkerungswachstum* (population growth) in the world as a whole is slowing down.

Pensions and care. The German pension system rests on *der Generationenvertrag* (the "contract between the generations"): people in work pay for today's pensioners. If the number of workers *zurückgeht* (falls; *ist zurückgegangen*), the system comes under pressure, and *Altersarmut* (poverty in old age) becomes a risk. More old people also means more who are *pflegebedürftig* (in need of care; *die Pflegebedürftigkeit*).

Family forms. The *Kleinfamilie* (parents plus one or two children) has been the norm for decades; the *Großfamilie* (several generations, many relatives) is rarer. Families with three or more children are *kinderreich*; couples without children are *kinderlos*. There are many *Lebensformen* (ways of living): marriage, *die Partnerschaft* (partnership), the unmarried *Lebensgemeinschaft* (couple living together), *Alleinerziehende* (single parents), *Regenbogenfamilien* (families with same-sex parents) and *Mehrgenerationenhäuser*, where several generations live or meet under one roof. When a marriage fails, couples *sich scheiden lassen* (get divorced): *Sie haben sich letztes Jahr scheiden lassen.* *Die Familienplanung* is deciding if and when to have children.

Work and family. *Die Vereinbarkeit von Familie und Beruf* (reconciling family and work) depends on *Kinderbetreuung* (childcare) and on *Elternzeit* (parental leave: up to three years per parent with job protection). During part of it, parents receive *Elterngeld* (parental allowance), which replaces about two thirds of the lost income for up to 14 months if both parents take part.

*der Alleinerziehende* and *die Alleinerziehende* are adjectival nouns, like *der Angestellte* from B1: *ein Alleinerziehender, eine Alleinerziehende, die Alleinerziehenden, viele Alleinerziehende*.

## Text: Ein Vortrag an der Volkshochschule

The opening of a talk at an adult education centre about demographic change.

> Guten Abend, meine Damen und Herren. Wer heute durch ein Dorf in der Uckermark oder im Erzgebirge fährt, dem fallen zuerst die leeren Häuser auf. Viele junge Menschen, deren Eltern dort ihr ganzes Leben verbracht haben, sind in die Städte gezogen. Zurück bleibt eine Generation, deren Kinder und Enkel oft Hunderte Kilometer entfernt wohnen.
>
> Was wir dort sehen, ist kein lokales Problem. Es ist ein Blick in die Zukunft des ganzen Landes. Die Lebenserwartung steigt, die Geburtenrate bleibt niedrig, und die geburtenstarken Jahrgänge der Sechzigerjahre gehen jetzt in Rente.
>
> Was bedeutet das für den Generationenvertrag, auf dem unser Rentensystem beruht? Wer heute zwanzig ist, wird im Alter wahrscheinlich länger arbeiten müssen. Und die Zahl derer, die gepflegt werden müssen, wird bis 2050 deutlich steigen.
>
> Aber ich möchte heute Abend nicht nur über Probleme sprechen. Ich möchte Ihnen auch ein Projekt vorstellen, mit dessen Hilfe ein kleines Dorf in Brandenburg wieder lebendig geworden ist: ein Mehrgenerationenhaus, in dessen Café sich jeden Tag Rentnerinnen, junge Eltern und Schulkinder treffen. Wen das neugierig macht, den lade ich ein, nach dem Vortrag noch zu bleiben.

In English:

> Good evening, ladies and gentlemen. Anyone who drives through a village in the Uckermark or the Ore Mountains today notices the empty houses first. Many young people whose parents spent their whole lives there have moved to the cities. Left behind is a generation whose children and grandchildren often live hundreds of kilometres away.
>
> What we see there is not a local problem. It's a look into the future of the whole country. Life expectancy is rising, the birth rate stays low, and the baby-boom year groups of the sixties are now retiring.
>
> What does that mean for the contract between the generations on which our pension system rests? Anyone who is twenty today will probably have to work longer in old age. And the number of those who need care will rise significantly by 2050.
>
> But I don't want to talk only about problems this evening. I would also like to present a project with whose help a small village in Brandenburg has come back to life: a multigenerational house in whose café pensioners, young parents and schoolchildren meet every day. If that makes you curious, I invite you to stay on after the talk.

Words to note from the text: *auffallen* (to be noticed, strike someone: *mir fällt auf*), *die Uckermark* and *das Erzgebirge* (rural regions in Brandenburg and Saxony), *geburtenstark* (with many births), *der Jahrgang* (year group, people born in one year), *in Rente gehen* (to retire), *beruhen auf* (to rest on), *lebendig* (lively, alive), *neugierig* (curious).

## Pronunciation

- *die Demografie*: de-mo-gra-FEE, stress on the last syllable, like all nouns in *-ie* from Greek (*die Biologie, die Pandemie*).
- *der Generationenvertrag*: ge-ne-ra-TSJOH-nen-fer-trahk; the *v* in *Vertrag* is an *f*.
- *dessen* has a short *e* and a sharp *ss*: DESS-en; *deren* has a long *e*: DEH-ren.

## Common mistakes

- Agreeing with the wrong noun: ~~die Frau, dessen Sohn~~ → *die Frau, deren Sohn*. Look back to the owner, not forward to the thing owned.
- Adding an article: ~~der Mann, dessen der Sohn~~ → *der Mann, dessen Sohn*.
- Weak endings after *dessen/deren*: ~~mit deren jüngsten Tochter~~ → *mit deren jüngster Tochter*.
- Leaving out the pick-up word when the cases differ: ~~Wer das liest, gefällt der Bericht~~ → *Wer das liest, dem gefällt der Bericht.*
- *derer* for "whose": ~~die Familien, derer Kinder~~ → *die Familien, deren Kinder*.
- *sich scheiden lassen* is reflexive and needs *lassen*: ~~Sie haben geschieden~~ → *Sie haben sich scheiden lassen.* (*Sie sind geschieden* describes the state: they are divorced.)

## Key points

- *dessen* (masculine/neuter owner) and *deren* (feminine or plural owner) agree with the owner, take no article after them, and never change their form.
- After a preposition, the preposition gives the case to the following noun: *mit deren Hilfe, in dessen Café*.
- Adjectives after *dessen/deren* take strong endings: *deren ältester Sohn, mit deren jüngster Tochter*.
- Free relative clauses: *wer/was …, der/das …*; the pick-up word takes the main clause's case and can only be dropped when both cases match.
- *welcher* is a formal relative pronoun; *derer* means "of those (who)". Recognize both.
- Choose relative clauses for speech and long content, short participle attributes for compact writing.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Die Würde des Menschen: reading the Grundgesetz
lessons.body:
## Why read the Grundgesetz?

*Das Grundgesetz* (the Basic Law) has been Germany's constitution since 1949. Its first nineteen articles are the *Grundrechte* (basic rights), and they are some of the most quoted sentences in the German language: in court rulings, political debates, school textbooks and the citizenship test.

The Grundgesetz is also a perfect B2 reading text. Its sentences are short and dense, it uses the structures of this module (nominal style, participle attributes, *sein* + *zu*), and it has its own legal conventions: the present tense used as a rule, a precise way of citing articles, and a few old-fashioned forms. As an official German text it isn't protected by copyright (§ 5 of the German Copyright Act exempts laws), so we can quote it directly.

This honors lesson shows you how legal German works, how to cite and paraphrase an article, and the words you need to talk about basic rights.

## The present tense as a rule

In everyday German, the present tense describes what is the case. In a law, it describes what must be the case. This **[[normative present]]** is the main feature of legal German:

- *Die Wohnung ist unverletzlich.* (Art. 13 Abs. 1) — The home may not be violated. (Literally: the home is inviolable.)
- *Eine Zensur findet nicht statt.* (Art. 5 Abs. 1) — Censorship does not take place, meaning: it is not allowed.
- *Politisch Verfolgte genießen Asylrecht.* (Art. 16a Abs. 1) — People who are politically persecuted have a right to asylum.

English laws often use "shall" for this. German doesn't need a modal verb: the plain present is a command. *Eine Zensur findet nicht statt* doesn't claim that there is never any censorship anywhere; it forbids it.

The passive works the same way: *Die ungestörte Religionsausübung wird gewährleistet* (Art. 4 Abs. 2) — People can practise their religion undisturbed; the state must make sure of it.

## haben + zu and sein + zu: duties and requirements

Where a law wants to say who must do what, it often uses *haben* + *zu* (active: someone has to do something) or *sein* + *zu* (passive: something has to be done), which you know from lesson 7:

- *Über die Zulässigkeit und Fortdauer einer Freiheitsentziehung hat nur der Richter zu entscheiden.* (Art. 104 Abs. 2) — Only a judge may decide whether, and for how long, someone may be deprived of their liberty.
- *Jeder wegen des Verdachtes einer strafbaren Handlung vorläufig Festgenommene ist spätestens am Tage nach der Festnahme dem Richter vorzuführen, …* (Art. 104 Abs. 3) — Anyone arrested on suspicion of a crime must be brought before a judge by the day after the arrest at the latest, …

Look at the second sentence with the tools of this module. *Jeder … vorläufig Festgenommene* is an extended participle attribute with an adjectival noun: *jeder Festgenommene* (everyone who has been arrested), extended by *wegen des Verdachtes einer strafbaren Handlung vorläufig*. Then *ist … vorzuführen* = *muss vorgeführt werden*.

The modal verbs appear too, especially *dürfen* in the negative for prohibitions: *Niemand darf wegen seiner Behinderung benachteiligt werden.* (Art. 3 Abs. 3) — Nobody may be put at a disadvantage because of a disability.

## Nominal style and old forms

Legal German packs actions into nouns: *die Freiheitsentziehung* (deprivation of liberty), *die Religionsausübung* (practice of religion), *die Gesetzgebung* (legislation), *die Rechtsprechung* (administration of justice). Unpack them as you learned in lesson 13: *die Freiheitsentziehung* = *jemandem die Freiheit entziehen*.

The text of 1949 also keeps a few forms that sound old today, especially the dative *-e* on masculine and neuter nouns:

- *Alle Staatsgewalt geht vom Volke aus.* (Art. 20 Abs. 2) — All power of the state comes from the people. (today: *vom Volk*)
- *In keinem Falle darf ein Grundrecht in seinem Wesensgehalt angetastet werden.* (Art. 19 Abs. 2) — A basic right may never be infringed in its essential content. (today: *in keinem Fall*)
- *Ehe und Familie stehen unter dem besonderen Schutze der staatlichen Ordnung.* (Art. 6 Abs. 1) — Marriage and family are specially protected by the state. (today: *Schutz*)

Recognize these; don't copy them into your own writing.

## Citing articles: Artikel, Absatz, Satz

A German law is divided into articles (*Artikel*, abbreviated *Art.*; in ordinary laws often *Paragraf*, *§*), each article into paragraphs (*Absatz*, *Abs.*), and each paragraph into sentences (*Satz*, *S.*). The law itself is abbreviated: *GG* for Grundgesetz.

| written | said |
|---|---|
| *Art. 1 Abs. 1 GG* | *Artikel eins, Absatz eins Grundgesetz* |
| *Art. 5 Abs. 1 S. 3 GG* | *Artikel fünf, Absatz eins, Satz drei Grundgesetz* |
| *Art. 16a GG* | *Artikel sechzehn a Grundgesetz* |

Prepositions for citing: *nach Art. 8 GG*, *gemäß Art. 8 GG* (formal), *laut Artikel 8*, *in Artikel 8 heißt es: …*, *Artikel 8 garantiert / schützt / regelt …*.

## Paraphrasing: from the article to your own words

When you write about the Grundgesetz (in an essay, a presentation, the B2 exam), you'll usually paraphrase. Three useful steps:

1. Name the article and the verb of guarantee: *Artikel 8 garantiert …*
2. Turn the normative present into a modal verb or *dürfen*: *Alle Deutschen dürfen sich … versammeln.*
3. Unpack nominal style into clauses where it helps.

Original: *Alle Deutschen haben das Recht, sich ohne Anmeldung oder Erlaubnis friedlich und ohne Waffen zu versammeln.* (Art. 8 Abs. 1)

Paraphrase: *Artikel 8 des Grundgesetzes schützt die Versammlungsfreiheit: Deutsche dürfen sich friedlich und unbewaffnet versammeln, ohne vorher um Erlaubnis zu fragen.* — Article 8 protects freedom of assembly: Germans may assemble peacefully and unarmed without asking for permission first.

Paragraph 2 of the same article allows laws to regulate assemblies in the open air, which is why outdoor demonstrations normally have to be registered with the authorities in advance (spontaneous ones are an exception); permission, though, is never needed.

Notice *Alle Deutschen*: some basic rights belong to everyone (*Jeder hat das Recht …*, *Alle Menschen …*), others only to German citizens (*Alle Deutschen …*). Lawyers call them *Jedermannsrechte* and *Deutschenrechte*.

## The words: constitution and basic rights

Article 1 is the most famous sentence of the Grundgesetz:

> *Die Würde des Menschen ist unantastbar. Sie zu achten und zu schützen ist Verpflichtung aller staatlichen Gewalt.* (Art. 1 Abs. 1)
>
> Human dignity may not be violated. Respecting and protecting it is the duty of all state power.

*Die Würde* is dignity; *unantastbar* means that it may not be touched at all (*antasten*: to touch, to infringe). The next paragraph of Article 1 commits Germany to *die Menschenrechte* (human rights).

- *Die Gleichheit* (equality): *Alle Menschen sind vor dem Gesetz gleich.* (Art. 3 Abs. 1)
- *Die Religionsfreiheit* (freedom of religion): Art. 4 calls the freedom of faith and conscience *unverletzlich* (inviolable); the noun is *die Unverletzlichkeit*, used for the home too: *die Unverletzlichkeit der Wohnung* (Art. 13).
- *Die Versammlungsfreiheit* (freedom of assembly): Art. 8.
- *Das Asylrecht* (the right of asylum): Art. 16a.
- *gewährleisten* (to guarantee, ensure; *hat gewährleistet*): the state *gewährleistet* rights; the noun *die Gewährleistung* is also the legal word for a product warranty.
- *verankert* (anchored, laid down): *Das Recht ist im Grundgesetz verankert.*

The structure of the state:

- *Die Gewaltenteilung* (separation of powers): *Gesetzgebung* (legislative), *vollziehende Gewalt* (executive) and *Rechtsprechung* (judiciary), named in Art. 20 Abs. 2.
- *Der Rechtsstaat*: a state under the rule of law, where the government itself is bound by law (Art. 20 Abs. 3).
- *Das Bundesverfassungsgericht* (Federal Constitutional Court) in Karlsruhe decides whether a law is *verfassungswidrig* (unconstitutional). Any person who believes the state has violated one of their basic rights can, after going through the other courts, file a *Verfassungsbeschwerde* (constitutional complaint).

Some principles can never be changed. Art. 79 Abs. 3, often called the *Ewigkeitsklausel* (eternity clause), says that an amendment touching *die in den Artikeln 1 und 20 niedergelegten Grundsätze* (the principles laid down in Articles 1 and 20) is *unzulässig* (inadmissible). That's an extended participle attribute from lesson 11, protecting the core of the constitution.

## Text: Drei Fragen an eine Verfassungsrechtlerin

A short interview from a student magazine (original text; the interviewee is fictional).

> Frau Professorin Brandt, warum ist Artikel 1 so berühmt?
>
> Weil er die Antwort auf die Verbrechen des Nationalsozialismus ist. Die Väter und Mütter des Grundgesetzes wollten 1949 klarstellen, dass der Staat für den Menschen da ist und nicht umgekehrt. Deshalb steht die Würde ganz am Anfang, noch vor allen anderen Grundrechten.
>
> Was bedeutet „unantastbar“ in der Praxis?
>
> Die meisten Grundrechte dürfen durch Gesetz eingeschränkt werden, etwa die Versammlungsfreiheit, wenn eine Demonstration gefährlich wird. Bei der Würde ist das anders: Sie darf mit keinem anderen Interesse abgewogen werden. Das Bundesverfassungsgericht hat zum Beispiel ein Gesetz für verfassungswidrig erklärt, das den Abschuss entführter Passagierflugzeuge erlaubte.
>
> Und was sollten Studierende im ersten Semester unbedingt lesen?
>
> Die ersten zwanzig Artikel. Das dauert eine halbe Stunde, und danach versteht man die meisten politischen Debatten in Deutschland besser.

In English:

> Professor Brandt, why is Article 1 so famous?
>
> Because it's the answer to the crimes of National Socialism. In 1949 the fathers and mothers of the Grundgesetz wanted to make clear that the state exists for people and not the other way round. That's why dignity comes right at the beginning, even before all the other basic rights.
>
> What does "inviolable" mean in practice?
>
> Most basic rights may be restricted by law, for example freedom of assembly when a demonstration becomes dangerous. Dignity is different: it may not be weighed against any other interest. The Federal Constitutional Court, for example, declared unconstitutional a law that allowed hijacked passenger planes to be shot down.
>
> And what should first-semester students definitely read?
>
> The first twenty articles. That takes half an hour, and afterwards you understand most political debates in Germany better.

Words to note from the text: *der Verfassungsrechtler, die Verfassungsrechtlerin* (constitutional lawyer), *umgekehrt* (the other way round), *einschränken* (to restrict), *abwägen* (to weigh up), *der Abschuss* (shooting down), *entführen* (to hijack, kidnap). The ruling mentioned is real: in 2006 the court struck down the part of the Aviation Security Act (*Luftsicherheitsgesetz*) that allowed this.

## Common mistakes

- Reading the normative present as a description: *Eine Zensur findet nicht statt* is a ban, not a report.
- Copying the old dative *-e* into your own texts: write *vom Volk*, *in keinem Fall*.
- Mixing up *Artikel* and *Absatz*: *Art. 1 Abs. 1* is the first paragraph of the first article. Ordinary laws use *§* (*Paragraf*) instead of *Artikel*.
- Saying ~~das Grundgesetz sagt~~ in formal writing. Better: *Das Grundgesetz garantiert / bestimmt / schützt …* or *In Artikel 3 heißt es: …*.
- Treating every right as a right of everyone: check whether the article says *jeder* or *alle Deutschen*.

## Key points

- Legal German uses the present tense as a rule: *Die Wohnung ist unverletzlich* = it must not be violated.
- Duties appear as *haben* + *zu* (*hat … zu entscheiden*) and *sein* + *zu* (*ist … vorzuführen*); prohibitions as *darf nicht* / *niemand darf*.
- Nominal style, participle attributes and old dative *-e* forms (*vom Volke*) are typical; unpack them when you paraphrase.
- Cite as *Art. 5 Abs. 1 S. 3 GG*; say *Artikel fünf, Absatz eins, Satz drei*.
- Paraphrase with *garantieren, schützen, gewährleisten* and modal verbs.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Book and film reviews: writing a Rezension
lessons.body:
## What a Rezension is

*Die Rezension* (review) of a book, film, play or exhibition is one of the most popular text types in German newspapers. It appears in *das Feuilleton*, the arts and culture section, written by professional *Kritikerinnen und Kritiker*, and it fills online shops and blogs, written by readers like you. Reviews are a common kind of reading text at B2, and giving your opinion about a book or film is something you'll often do when speaking and writing.

A good review does three things: it tells you what the work is about without spoiling it, it judges it with reasons, and it recommends it (or not) to a particular audience. This honors lesson gives you the language for all three: evaluative adjectives and the words that make them stronger or weaker, participle attributes for compact descriptions, and the Konjunktiv II for recommendations and polite criticism.

## Judging: evaluative adjectives

Reviews live on adjectives. Here are the most useful ones, from praise to criticism.

| positive | neutral or mixed | negative |
|---|---|---|
| *gelungen* (successful, well done) | *solide* (solid) | *misslungen* (failed, unsuccessful) |
| *fesselnd, packend* (gripping) | *unterhaltsam* (entertaining) | *langatmig* (long-winded, slow) |
| *lesenswert, sehenswert* (worth reading/seeing) | *vorhersehbar* (predictable) | *langweilig* |
| *überzeugend* (convincing) | *routiniert* (competent, but no surprises) | *oberflächlich* (superficial) |
| *bewegend* (moving) | *ungewöhnlich* (unusual) | *kitschig* (sentimental, kitschy) |

Many of these are participles: *fesselnd* (from *fesseln*, to tie up, to captivate), *packend* (from *packen*, to grip), *bewegend*, *überzeugend*. *Gelungen* and *misslungen* are past participles of *gelingen* and *misslingen*: *Die Verfilmung ist gelungen* = the film adaptation has worked out well.

## Stronger, weaker: intensifiers

The adjective alone is rarely enough. German critics adjust it with an **[[intensifier]]**, a word that makes it stronger or weaker. Getting these right is what makes a review sound natural:

| intensifier | effect | example |
|---|---|---|
| *äußerst, höchst, überaus* | extremely, highly (formal) | *ein äußerst spannender Roman*, *höchst unterhaltsam* |
| *ausgesprochen* | really, decidedly | *ausgesprochen witzig* |
| *durchaus* | definitely, quite (often with a "but" to follow) | *Der Film ist durchaus gelungen, aber zu lang.* |
| *ziemlich, recht* | fairly, rather | *ziemlich vorhersehbar*, *recht unterhaltsam* |
| *eher* | rather, more … than not | *eher enttäuschend* |
| *etwas* | a bit (mostly with negative adjectives) | *etwas langatmig* |
| *wenig* | not very | *wenig überzeugend* |
| *alles andere als* | anything but | *alles andere als langweilig* |

Two notes:

- *ziemlich* and *recht* sound positive with positive adjectives (*recht gelungen*) but often damn with faint praise: *ziemlich gut* can mean "OK, not great".
- *durchaus* concedes something before a criticism. *Das Buch hat durchaus starke Momente, …* tells the reader a "but" is coming.

*höchst* only goes with adjectives that can be graded and sound educated: *höchst interessant, höchst problematisch*, but not ~~höchst gut~~.

## Describing compactly: participle attributes

A review has little space, so critics use the participle attributes of lessons 11 and 12 to describe characters and scenes:

- *Die von Lena Hartmann gespielte Kommissarin* — the detective played by Lena Hartmann
- *der in den Neunzigerjahren in Leipzig spielende Roman* — the novel set in Leipzig in the nineties (*spielen*: to be set)
- *eine bis zum Schluss offen bleibende Frage* — a question that stays open until the end
- *der kaum zu ertragende Höhepunkt* — the almost unbearable climax (gerundive with *kaum*)

Combined with an intensifier: *die äußerst überzeugend gespielte Hauptfigur* (the extremely convincingly acted main character).

## Recommending: the Konjunktiv II

Recommendations and polite criticism are often made in the Konjunktiv II, which softens them and sounds less like an order:

- *Der Roman wäre allen zu empfehlen, die …* — The novel could be recommended to anyone who … (*wäre zu empfehlen* = *sein* + *zu* in the Konjunktiv II)
- *Etwas mehr Tempo hätte dem Film gutgetan.* — A bit more pace would have done the film good.
- *Hier hätte man sich mehr Mut gewünscht.* — One would have wished for more courage here.
- *Ohne die Nebenhandlung wäre das Buch hundert Seiten kürzer und deutlich besser.* — Without the subplot the book would be a hundred pages shorter and much better.

The plain recommendation in the indicative is fine too, and very common at the end of a review: *Absolut lesenswert!* — *Unbedingt ansehen!* — *Ein Film für einen langen Sonntagabend.*

## How to structure a review

1. Introduction: title, author or director, genre, year, the hook (why this work, why now). *Mit „…“ legt X ihren dritten Roman vor.*
2. Content: a short summary in the present tense, without the ending. *Der Roman erzählt von …*, *Im Mittelpunkt steht …*, *Die Handlung spielt in …*
3. Evaluation: two or three points with reasons and examples: the story, the characters, the language or the camera, *die Besetzung* (the cast), *die Inszenierung* (the staging or direction).
4. Conclusion and recommendation: for whom, and how strongly. *Wer …, sollte …*, *Fazit: …*

For plays, *die Uraufführung* is the very first performance of a new play; *inszenieren* (to stage, direct) is what the director does. A film made from a novel is *die Verfilmung*. And reviewing is *rezensieren*: *Sie rezensiert jede Woche ein neues Buch.*

## Text: Eine Filmkritik

A review from a culture blog. The film and the novel are invented.

> Stille Wasser (Regie: Paul Engel, 118 Minuten)
>
> Mit „Stille Wasser“ kommt die Verfilmung eines der meistgelesenen Romane der letzten Jahre ins Kino. Die Geschichte spielt in einem kleinen Fischerdorf an der Ostsee, in das die junge Ärztin Nora nach dem Tod ihrer Mutter zurückkehrt. Dort stößt sie auf ein seit Jahrzehnten gehütetes Familiengeheimnis.
>
> Die Besetzung ist durchaus gelungen. Vor allem die von Mira Sander gespielte Nora überzeugt: Sie zeigt mit wenigen Blicken mehr als viele Dialoge. Auch die Bilder der im Nebel liegenden Küste sind äußerst stimmungsvoll.
>
> Leider kann die Inszenierung mit der Vorlage nicht ganz mithalten. Was im Roman packend erzählt wird, wirkt im Film oft etwas langatmig. Die Nebenhandlung um den Bürgermeister ist alles andere als notwendig, und ein strafferer Schnitt hätte dem Film gutgetan.
>
> Fazit: eine solide, stellenweise bewegende Verfilmung, die aber an den Roman nicht heranreicht. Wer das Buch kennt, wird eher enttäuscht sein; allen anderen wäre der Film für einen ruhigen Abend durchaus zu empfehlen. Lesenswerter bleibt jedoch das Original.

In English:

> Still Waters (directed by Paul Engel, 118 minutes)
>
> With "Still Waters", the film adaptation of one of the most-read novels of recent years comes to cinemas. The story is set in a small fishing village on the Baltic coast, to which the young doctor Nora returns after her mother's death. There she comes across a family secret that has been kept for decades.
>
> The cast is definitely a success. Above all Nora, played by Mira Sander, is convincing: she shows more with a few looks than many dialogues do. The images of the coast lying in the mist are extremely atmospheric too.
>
> Unfortunately, the direction can't quite keep up with the original. What the novel tells grippingly often feels a bit long-winded in the film. The subplot about the mayor is anything but necessary, and tighter editing would have done the film good.
>
> Conclusion: a solid, at times moving adaptation which doesn't, however, match the novel. Anyone who knows the book will rather be disappointed; to everyone else the film could definitely be recommended for a quiet evening. The original remains more worth reading, though.

Words to note from the text: *die Regie* (direction; *Regie: …* = directed by), *stoßen auf* (to come across), *hüten* (to guard, keep), *stimmungsvoll* (atmospheric), *die Vorlage* (the original, source text), *mithalten* (to keep up), *die Nebenhandlung* (subplot), *straff* (tight), *der Schnitt* (editing), *stellenweise* (in places), *heranreichen an* (to match, come up to).

## Common mistakes

- Telling the ending: a review summarizes the setup, not the solution.
- Past tense in the summary: German reviews summarize plots in the present: *Nora kehrt zurück*, not ~~Nora kehrte zurück~~.
- *etwas* with positive adjectives: ~~etwas spannend~~ sounds odd. Use *recht spannend* or *ziemlich spannend*.
- Using *höchst* with simple adjectives: ~~höchst gut~~ → *sehr gut*.
- *gelungen* vs *gelingen*: the adjective is *gelungen* (*eine gelungene Verfilmung*); the verb is *gelingen* (*Der Film ist ihm gelungen*). The negative adjective is *misslungen*.
- Only adjectives, no reasons: every judgment needs a *weil* or an example.

## Key points

- A review informs (present-tense summary, no spoilers), judges with reasons, and recommends for a particular audience.
- Key adjectives: *gelungen / misslungen, fesselnd, packend, langatmig, lesenswert*.
- Intensifiers fine-tune the judgment: *äußerst, durchaus, ziemlich, eher, etwas, wenig, alles andere als*.
- Participle attributes describe compactly: *die von X gespielte Figur*.
- Konjunktiv II for recommendations and soft criticism: *wäre zu empfehlen, hätte gutgetan*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Doch, ja, halt, eben, mal: modal particles
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 3 was about dense written German: participle attributes, nominal style, formal prepositions. This module turns to the other end of the language: talking, arguing, conceding, persuading. And nothing makes spoken German sound more natural, or a learner sound more like a textbook, than a small set of words that grammar books long ignored: *ja, doch, mal, halt, eben, schon, denn, wohl, etwa, eigentlich, ruhig, bloß, nur*.

Compare:

- *Komm rein.* — Come in. (correct, but can sound like an order)
- *Komm doch rein!* — Do come in! (friendly, inviting)
- *Komm doch mal rein!* — Why don't you come in for a bit? (relaxed, warm)

The three sentences say the same thing. What changes is the speaker's attitude: how sure they are, what they assume you already know, whether they are urging, softening or giving up. These little words are called **[[modal particles]]** (German: *Modalpartikeln* or *Abtönungspartikeln*, from *abtönen*, "to tone down, shade"). You met a few of them at A2 and B1 (*ja, doch, wohl, halt*). This lesson gives you the whole set, how they behave in a sentence, and how to tell them apart from the same words used as adverbs or conjunctions.

The theme is conversation, humour and manners: small talk, irony, jokes, body language and the famous German directness.

## What makes a word a modal particle

A modal particle doesn't change whether a sentence is true. *Das ist ja teuer* and *Das ist teuer* describe the same price. The particle adds a comment from the speaker: "as we can both see". Five features help you recognize one:

1. It is unstressed. *Das ist ja teuer* (no stress on *ja*). If you stress the word, it is usually something else (see the section on stress below).
2. It can be left out without making the sentence wrong or changing its facts.
3. It never stands in position 1. ~~Ja ist das teuer.~~ The particle lives in the middle of the sentence, after the conjugated verb.
4. It can't be negated, asked about or used as an answer on its own. In *Ist das teuer? — Ja.* the answer *ja* is the word "yes", not the particle.
5. It depends on the sentence type. *denn* appears in questions, *mal* in requests, *ja* in statements. Each particle has its favourite sentence types.

There is usually no word-for-word English translation. English does the same work with tone of voice, tag questions (*isn't it?*), or words like *just, really, after all, come on, by the way*. So learn each particle as a function, not as a translation.

## Where particles go

Particles sit in the middle of the sentence (between the conjugated verb and the rest of the predicate). A simple rule that works most of the time: after the pronouns, before the new information.

- *Ich habe es dir doch gestern gesagt.* — I told you yesterday, didn't I? (pronouns *es dir* first, then *doch*, then the rest)
- *Hast du denn schon mit ihr gesprochen?* — So, have you already spoken to her?
- *Das ist ja eine gute Idee!* — Oh, that's a good idea!
- *Er kommt wohl nicht mehr.* — He's probably not coming any more.

The particle comes before *nicht* and before the part of the sentence that carries the main stress. Moving it to the end, or to the start, is wrong: ~~Das ist eine gute Idee ja.~~ ~~Doch habe ich es dir gesagt.~~ (*Doch* at the start is possible, but then it is the adverb "however, yet", not the particle: see below.)

## The particles one by one

### ja: as we both know

In statements, *ja* marks something as known or obvious to both speakers. English might say "as you know", "after all", or nothing at all.

- *Du kennst ja meinen Bruder, der hat einen sehr trockenen Humor.* — You know my brother, he has a very dry sense of humour.
- *Wir müssen nicht lange diskutieren, das Ergebnis ist ja klar.* — We don't need to discuss for long; the result is obvious.

In exclamations, *ja* marks surprise at something you have just noticed:

- *Das ist ja witzig!* — Oh, that's funny!
- *Du bist ja ganz nass!* — You're soaking wet!

### doch: but surely, come on

*doch* has three main uses.

Contradiction or reminder: the speaker expects agreement, or thinks the listener has forgotten or is ignoring something.

- *Das war doch nur ein Witz!* — It was only a joke! (Don't take it seriously.)
- *Du weißt doch, dass ich keinen Sarkasmus mag.* — You know I don't like sarcasm (so why are you doing this?).

Urging in imperatives and suggestions: it makes a request friendlier and more insistent.

- *Setz dich doch!* — Do sit down!
- *Erzähl doch mal, wie war die Reise?* — Go on, tell me, how was the trip?

Wishes with the Konjunktiv II (you met these at B1):

- *Wenn er doch nur ein bisschen taktvoller wäre!* — If only he were a bit more tactful!

### mal: just, for a moment

*mal* (from *einmal*) softens requests and suggestions. It makes them sound casual, as if the request is small.

- *Kannst du mal kurz das Fenster aufmachen?* — Could you just open the window for a moment?
- *Schau mal, da drüben!* — Look, over there!
- *Ich muss mal telefonieren.* — I just need to make a phone call.

### halt and eben: that's just how it is

Both express resignation: the situation is a fact, there's no point arguing. *halt* is more common in the south and in Austria and Switzerland, *eben* more common in the north; both are understood everywhere, and many speakers combine them (*eben halt*).

- *Er ist halt so, man kann ihn nicht ändern.* — That's just the way he is; you can't change him.
- *Wenn der Zug nicht kommt, nehmen wir eben den Bus.* — If the train doesn't come, we'll just take the bus.
- *Smalltalk ist eben nicht jedermanns Sache.* — Small talk simply isn't everyone's thing.

### schon: it'll be fine, granted

*schon* as a particle reassures, or concedes something before a *but*.

- *Keine Sorge, das wird schon klappen.* — Don't worry, it'll work out.
- *Das ist schon richtig, aber so direkt musst du es nicht sagen.* — That's true enough, but you don't need to say it so bluntly.

In imperatives it shows impatience: *Komm schon!* — Come on!

### denn: so, then (in questions)

In questions, *denn* shows real interest and makes the question sound friendly and connected to the situation. Questions without it can sound abrupt. With a critical tone it can also show surprise or reproach.

- *Wie geht es dir denn?* — So how are you?
- *Was ist denn hier los?* — What's going on here, then?
- *Warum hast du ihn denn unterbrochen?* — Why on earth did you interrupt him?

*denn* as a particle only appears in questions. In a statement, *denn* is the conjunction "because" (in position 0).

### wohl: probably, I suppose

*wohl* marks an assumption: the speaker isn't sure. You have met it with *werden* (*Er wird wohl krank sein*), but it works with any verb.

- *Sie ist wohl schon nach Hause gegangen.* — She's probably gone home already.
- *Das war wohl ironisch gemeint.* — I suppose that was meant ironically.

### etwa: surely not … ?

In a yes/no question, *etwa* shows that the speaker is surprised and expects, or hopes for, the answer "no".

- *Hast du etwa mein ganzes Eis gegessen?* — You haven't eaten all my ice cream, have you?
- *Ist das etwa schon zu Ende?* — Is that really over already?

Compare *Bist du müde?* (neutral question), *Bist du denn müde?* (friendly interest) and *Bist du etwa müde?* (surprised: surely you're not tired already?).

### eigentlich: by the way, actually

In questions, *eigentlich* opens a new topic or asks about something basic, often casually, like English "by the way" or "actually".

- *Was machst du eigentlich beruflich?* — What do you actually do for a living?
- *Wie spät ist es eigentlich?* — What time is it, by the way?

In statements it is the adverb "actually, in fact", often introducing a contrast: *Eigentlich wollte ich nur kurz plaudern, aber dann haben wir zwei Stunden geredet.*

### ruhig: go ahead

In imperatives and with *können*, *ruhig* gives permission or encouragement: there's no problem.

- *Frag ruhig, wenn du etwas nicht verstehst.* — Feel free to ask if you don't understand something.
- *Sie können mich ruhig unterbrechen.* — Do feel free to interrupt me.

### bloß and nur: warnings and wishes

In imperatives, *bloß* and *nur* turn a command into a warning (often with a little threat). In wishes and in questions to yourself, they express a strong desire or helplessness.

- *Erzähl das bloß nicht meinem Chef!* — Whatever you do, don't tell my boss!
- *Mach nur keine Anspielungen auf sein Alter!* — Just don't make any allusions to his age!
- *Wenn ich bloß schlagfertiger wäre!* — If only I were quicker with a comeback!
- *Wo habe ich nur meine Brille hingelegt?* — Where on earth did I put my glasses?

## Combinations

Particles often come in pairs. The most common combinations, and the order in which they appear, are worth learning as chunks:

| Combination | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *doch mal* | friendly urging | *Ruf doch mal an!* — Why don't you give me a call? |
| *ja wohl* | indignation, "surely" | *Das ist ja wohl nicht dein Ernst!* — You can't be serious! |
| *denn eigentlich* | curious question | *Was willst du denn eigentlich?* — So what do you actually want? |
| *doch nur / doch bloß* | wish | *Hätte ich doch nur nichts gesagt!* — If only I hadn't said anything! |
| *eben mal* | casual "just", quickly | *Ich schau eben mal nach.* — I'll just have a quick look. |

As a rough guide, *ja* comes before *doch*, and both before *mal*. Native speakers rarely use more than two or three particles in one sentence.

## Particle or something else?

Almost every particle also has a "normal" meaning. The test is stress and position: the normal word can usually stand in position 1, be stressed, or answer a question.

| Word | As a particle | As something else |
|---|---|---|
| *ja* | *Das ist ja toll!* | *Ja.* — yes (answer) |
| *doch* | *Komm doch mit!* | *Doch!* — yes (to a negative question); *Er wollte kommen, doch er war krank.* — but (conjunction) |
| *denn* | *Was ist denn los?* | *…, denn ich war krank.* — because |
| *mal* | *Hör mal!* | *drei mal vier* — three times four |
| *eben* | *Das ist eben so.* | *Er ist eben gegangen.* — just now; *eine ebene Fläche* — a flat surface |
| *schon* | *Das klappt schon.* | *Bist du schon fertig?* — already |
| *etwa* | *Hast du etwa gelogen?* | *etwa zwanzig Leute* — about, approximately |
| *ruhig* | *Frag ruhig!* | *Sei ruhig!* — be quiet |
| *bloß* | *Sag bloß nichts!* | *bloß ein Witz* — merely, only |
| *wohl* | *Er ist wohl krank.* | *Ich fühle mich wohl.* — well, comfortable |

Some sentences are ambiguous on paper and only clear when spoken. *Er ist eben gegangen* can mean "He has just (now) left" (adverb, stressed *EBEN*) or "Well, he left, that's how it is" (particle, unstressed).

## Stress changes everything

When a particle-like word is stressed, the meaning shifts. Three common cases:

- *Das ist DOCH richtig.* — It IS right after all. (stressed *doch*: insisting against doubt)
- *Komm JA nicht zu spät!* — Don't you dare be late! (stressed *ja* in an imperative: a warning)
- *Das habe ich SCHON verstanden, aber …* — I DID understand that, but … (stressed *schon*: concession)

## Talking about conversation

The words in this lesson describe how people talk to each other. A few notes:

- *der Humor* (no plural in normal use) and *humorvoll* (humorous, with a sense of humour); *witzig* is "funny, witty", *der Witz* a joke. *Einen Witz erzählen* is to tell a joke, and *die Pointe* is its punchline: *Er hat die Pointe vergessen.*
- *die Ironie* says the opposite of what is meant, often gently; *der Sarkasmus* is sharper and meant to hurt. The adjectives are *ironisch* and *sarkastisch*: *Das war ironisch gemeint, nicht böse.*
- *die Anspielung* is a hint or allusion, and *anspielen auf* + accusative is "to allude to": *Worauf spielst du an?* — What are you getting at?
- *Jemanden auf den Arm nehmen* (literally "take someone on your arm", like a small child) means "to pull someone's leg": *Du nimmst mich doch auf den Arm!*
- *plaudern* is relaxed chatting; *der Smalltalk* (also written *Small Talk*) is polite talk about safe topics. An empty polite phrase is *eine Floskel*: *"Wie geht's?" ist oft nur eine Floskel.*
- *schlagfertig* describes someone who always has a quick, witty reply ready; the noun is *die Schlagfertigkeit*.
- Body language: *die Körpersprache, die Geste* (gesture), *der Blickkontakt* (eye contact), *nicken* (to nod), *zwinkern* (to wink), *lächeln* (to smile), *schmunzeln* (to smile to yourself, to grin quietly in amusement), *der Tonfall* (tone of voice).
- *unterbrechen* is inseparable: *Er unterbricht mich ständig. Sie hat mich unterbrochen.* The noun is *die Unterbrechung*.

### Direct or rude?

German speakers are often described as direct (*die Direktheit*): many say what they think and don't wrap criticism in compliments. In many situations this isn't considered *unhöflich* (rude) but honest. *Höflichkeit* (politeness) in German often shows up less in praise and more in form: *Sie* vs *du*, titles, greetings, punctuality. Modal particles are one of the main tools for softening: *Kannst du mal …?* is much friendlier than *Kannst du …?*. Someone who is *taktvoll* knows what not to say; someone who is *taktlos* doesn't.

## Dialogue: Auf der Firmenfeier

Two colleagues, Jana and Felix, meet at a company party. Listen for the particles.

```dialogue lang=de-DE
# Auf der Firmenfeier
Jana: Na, Felix, du bist ja auch hier! Ich dachte, du hasst Smalltalk.
= Well, Felix, you're here too! I thought you hated small talk.
Felix: Tu ich auch. Aber der Chef hat halt gesagt, wir sollen alle kommen.
= I do. But the boss just said we should all come.
Jana: Ach, komm. So schlimm ist es doch nicht. Hast du denn schon was gegessen?
= Oh, come on. It's not that bad. So have you eaten anything yet?
Felix: Nein. Ich stehe seit zehn Minuten neben Herrn Brandt, und er erzählt einen Witz nach dem anderen.
= No. I've been standing next to Mr Brandt for ten minutes and he's telling one joke after another.
Jana: Und? Sind sie wenigstens witzig?
= And? Are they at least funny?
Felix: Na ja. Er vergisst immer die Pointe. Und ich nicke eben und lächle.
= Well. He always forgets the punchline. And I just nod and smile.
Jana: Du bist aber auch taktvoll! Ich hätte ihn wohl längst unterbrochen.
= You really are tactful! I'd probably have interrupted him long ago.
Felix: Du? Du bist doch die Höflichkeit in Person.
= You? You're politeness itself.
Jana: Das war jetzt ironisch, oder?
= That was ironic, wasn't it?
Felix: Ein bisschen. Sag mal, was machst du eigentlich am Wochenende?
= A little. Tell me, what are you actually doing at the weekend?
Jana: Nichts Besonderes. Warum? Willst du mich etwa einladen?
= Nothing special. Why? You're not going to invite me, are you?
Felix: Vielleicht. Aber erzähl das bloß nicht Herrn Brandt, sonst kommt er mit.
```
