lessons.title: Language and identity: register and variation
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A B2 speaker doesn't just know German; they know which German to use. The same person writes *Wir bitten um Ihr Verständnis* in a notice to customers, says *Tut mir leid* to a colleague, and texts *sorry, sorry!!* to a friend. Each is right in its place and wrong in the others. This lesson puts those **[[registers]]** side by side, looks closely at the spoken German you hear every day but rarely see in textbooks, and at two areas where German is changing in front of you: English loanwords and **[[gender-inclusive language]]**.

These are also topics Germans themselves argue about, so the lesson's text is a radio discussion, and you'll practise reporting people's views on language in Konjunktiv I (lessons 01–02). The words are about language itself: multilingualism, identity, borrowing and change.

## Three registers side by side

German, like English, has a range from formal written to casual spoken, but the differences are larger and more visible in grammar:

| formal written | neutral | colloquial |
|---|---|---|
| *Wir bitten, die Verspätung zu entschuldigen.* | *Entschuldigen Sie bitte die Verspätung.* | *Sorry, bin spät dran.* |
| *Eine Teilnahme ist leider nicht möglich.* | *Ich kann leider nicht teilnehmen.* | *Ich schaff's leider nicht.* |
| *Aufgrund des Streiks entfällt der Unterricht.* | *Wegen des Streiks fällt der Unterricht aus.* | *Wegen dem Streik ist heute kein Unterricht.* |
| *Haben Sie Fragen, so wenden Sie sich an …* | *Wenn Sie Fragen haben, fragen Sie …* | *Wenn was ist, ruf an.* |

The formal column uses the tools of this course: nominal style, the passive, formal prepositions with the genitive (lesson 14), verb-first conditionals (*Haben Sie Fragen, so …*). The colloquial column drops sounds and words, uses *wegen* + dative and *was* for *etwas*, and is full of particles (lesson 16). The neutral middle is what you should use with strangers, at work and in most of the exam.

*die Umgangssprache* is everyday spoken language (*umgangssprachlich*: colloquial), *die Schriftsprache* the written standard, and *die Jugendsprache* the slang of young people, which changes so fast that dictionaries of it are out of date when they're printed. *die Ausdrucksweise* is a person's way of expressing themselves: *Achte bitte auf deine Ausdrucksweise!* (Mind your language!)

## Features of spoken German

These features are normal in speech, even among educated speakers, but don't belong in formal writing. You need to understand all of them and may use them in casual conversation.

### weil (and obwohl) with main-clause order

In speech, *weil* is very often followed by main-clause word order, usually with a small pause:

- *Ich komm heute nicht, weil – ich hab echt keine Zeit.* (written: *weil ich wirklich keine Zeit habe*)
- *Wir nehmen das Auto, obwohl – eigentlich wär der Zug schneller.*

Linguists point out that this *weil* often gives a reason for saying something rather than a cause, and that it works more like *denn*. In writing, and in the exam, *weil* always sends the verb to the end.

### Ellipsis: leaving words out

Spoken German drops what the listener can supply, especially a pronoun in position 1:

- *Kommst du mit? – Geht nicht, muss noch arbeiten.* (= *Das geht nicht, ich muss …*)
- *Weiß ich nicht.* · *Hab ich schon gemacht.* · *Kenn ich.* (= *Das weiß ich nicht* …)
- *Noch Fragen? – Nee, alles klar.*

Endings and sounds go too: *ich hab, ich komm, gibt's, haste* (*hast du*), *'ne* (*eine*), *'nen* (*einen*), *nee* (*nein*).

### Tag questions

English builds **[[tag questions]]** from the verb (isn't it, don't you). German has no such system. Instead one word goes at the end, and it depends on the region:

| tag | where | example |
|---|---|---|
| *oder?* | everywhere | *Das war doch gut, oder?* |
| *ne?* / *nich?* | north and centre | *Du kommst morgen, ne?* |
| *gell?* / *gelle?* | south, Austria | *Das ist schön, gell?* |
| *wa?* | Berlin | *Ganz schön kalt, wa?* |
| *nicht wahr?* | formal, a little old-fashioned | *Sie sind Frau Dr. Lenz, nicht wahr?* |

### Ausklammerung in speech

Lesson 27 introduced Ausklammerung, phrases after the final verbs. In speech it is very common, for afterthoughts and to keep the middle of the sentence short: *Ich hab sie getroffen gestern, beim Bäcker.* · *Wir haben lange gesprochen über das Problem.* In writing, put those phrases back inside: *Ich habe sie gestern beim Bäcker getroffen.*

## Anglicisms

*der Anglizismus* is an English word used in German. German has borrowed from other languages for centuries: from Latin (*das Fenster* from *fenestra*, *die Mauer* from *murus*), from French (*das Büro, die Etage*), and since the 20th century mostly from English. A loanword (*das Lehnwort*) has adapted so completely that nobody hears it as foreign; a *Fremdwort* still looks and sounds foreign (*der Computer, das Meeting*).

### Which gender?

Borrowed nouns need a gender, and there are a few tendencies, not fixed rules:

- the gender of a German word with a similar meaning: *das Meeting* (*das Treffen*), *die E-Mail* (*die Nachricht, die Post*), *der Workshop* (*der Kurs*), *die Deadline* (*die Frist*);
- the form of the word: *-ing* nouns are usually neuter (*das Marketing, das Training*), *-er* nouns masculine (*der Computer, der Server*), *-ness* nouns feminine (*die Fitness*);
- some have two, at least for a while: *der/das Laptop*, *der/das Blog*.

Some English-looking words aren't English at all. *das Handy* (mobile phone), *der Beamer* (projector), *das Homeoffice* (working from home) and *der Oldtimer* (vintage car) are German creations, which an English speaker wouldn't recognize in that sense.

### Conjugating English verbs

English verbs become weak German verbs with *-en*: *chatten, posten, liken, managen, downloaden*. The present is regular (*ich chatte, sie postet*). The participle is where it gets interesting:

- one-part verbs take *ge-…-t* like any weak verb: *hat gechattet, hat gepostet, hat gelikt* (also written *geliked*), *hat gemanagt*;
- verbs that look like a particle + verb split like a separable verb, or don't: *hat downgeloadet* and *hat gedownloadet*, *hat upgedatet* and *hat geupdatet* are both in use. There is no form everybody agrees on, which is one reason careful writers prefer *herunterladen* (*hat heruntergeladen*) and *aktualisieren* (*hat aktualisiert*).

Opinions differ on how many Anglicisms are too many. A useful test for your own writing: does a German word exist that your reader will understand just as well? In a formal letter, write *Frist* rather than *Deadline* and *Besprechung* rather than *Meeting*; at a start-up, the English word may be the normal one.

## Gender-inclusive language

The traditional way to refer to a mixed group in German is the masculine plural: *die Lehrer, die Studenten, alle Mitarbeiter*. This is called the **[[generic masculine]]**. Many people find that it makes women and non-binary people invisible, and so several other forms are now used. The verb *gendern* (*ich gendere, hat gegendert*) means using such forms, and *geschlechtergerecht* means gender-fair. Here they are, described as current usage:

| form | example | where you'll see it |
|---|---|---|
| *Doppelnennung* (naming both) | *Lehrerinnen und Lehrer, liebe Kolleginnen und Kollegen* | speeches, letters, official texts; widely accepted |
| slash | *Lehrer/-innen, Mitarbeiter/-innen* | forms, job ads |
| participle or adjective as a noun | *die Studierenden, die Lehrenden, die Mitarbeitenden* | universities, administration |
| neutral nouns | *die Lehrkraft, das Kollegium, die Belegschaft, das Team* | everywhere |
| *Gendersternchen* (asterisk) and similar signs | *Lehrer\*innen, Lehrer:innen, Lehrer_innen* | universities, some media and companies |

The asterisk, the colon and the underscore are spoken with a short break, a glottal stop, before *-innen*: *Lehrer – innen*. They are the most debated forms. The Council for German Orthography (*Rat für deutsche Rechtschreibung*) has not made them part of official spelling, and several German states don't allow them in schools or in their own administration, while many universities, companies and media use them. Some people reject gendering altogether. In the exam and at work, the Doppelnennung and neutral forms are always safe: *Liebe Kolleginnen und Kollegen*, *alle Mitarbeitenden*, *die Lehrkräfte*.

The *(m/w/d)* in job ads (lesson 28) belongs here too: since the end of 2018, German law has recognized a third gender entry, *divers*, and job ads address it.

## Text: a radio discussion

From the radio programme *Sprachlabor*.

> Moderatorin: Herzlich willkommen zum „Sprachlabor“. Unser Thema heute: Verliert das Deutsche seine Identität? Frau Professorin Demir, Sie sind Sprachwissenschaftlerin. Sind Anglizismen eine Gefahr?
>
> Prof. Demir: Nein. Das Deutsche hat immer Wörter aus anderen Sprachen übernommen, früher aus dem Lateinischen und dem Französischen, heute eben aus dem Englischen. Lehnwörter wie „Fenster“ hält niemand mehr für fremd. Eine Sprache wandelt sich, solange sie gesprochen wird.
>
> Herr Lorenz: Da muss ich widersprechen. Wenn in einer Besprechung nur noch von Deadlines und Feedback die Rede ist, verstehen manche älteren Kollegen nicht mehr, worum es geht. Sprache soll doch der Verständigung dienen.
>
> Prof. Demir: Das ist aber kein Problem der Anglizismen, sondern eine Frage der Ausdrucksweise. Fachsprache schließt immer Leute aus, ob auf Englisch oder auf Deutsch.
>
> Moderatorin: Leonie, du bist siebzehn. Wie redet ihr in der Schule?
>
> Leonie: Kommt drauf an. Mit meinen Freunden red ich ganz anders als mit Lehrern, ist ja klar. Und zu Hause sprechen wir Türkisch, das ist meine Herkunftssprache. Ich finde, zweisprachig aufzuwachsen ist ein Riesenvorteil, oder?
>
> Herr Lorenz: Absolut. Aber dann muss die Sprachförderung an den Schulen besser werden, und zwar in beiden Sprachen.
>
> Moderatorin: Und das Gendern? Leonie, machst du das?
>
> Leonie: Im Chat schon, mit Sternchen. In Klausuren nicht, weil – bei uns darf man das nicht.
>
> Herr Lorenz: Ich schreibe „Schülerinnen und Schüler“. Das ist geschlechtergerecht, und jeder kann es lesen.
>
> Prof. Demir: Für mich als Wissenschaftlerin ist interessant, dass die Sprachgemeinschaft das gerade selbst aushandelt. Ob sich das Sternchen durchsetzt, wird sich zeigen.

In English:

> Presenter: A warm welcome to "Sprachlabor". Our topic today: is German losing its identity? Professor Demir, you are a linguist. Are Anglicisms a danger?
>
> Prof. Demir: No. German has always taken words from other languages, from Latin and French in the past, from English today. Nobody considers loanwords like "Fenster" foreign any more. A language changes as long as it is spoken.
>
> Mr Lorenz: I have to disagree there. When a meeting is all about deadlines and feedback, some older colleagues no longer understand what it's about. Surely language is supposed to help people understand each other.
>
> Prof. Demir: But that's not a problem of Anglicisms, it's a question of how people express themselves. Specialist language always excludes people, whether in English or in German.
>
> Presenter: Leonie, you're seventeen. How do you all talk at school?
>
> Leonie: Depends. I talk totally differently with my friends than with teachers, obviously. And at home we speak Turkish, that's my heritage language. I think growing up bilingual is a huge advantage, isn't it?
>
> Mr Lorenz: Absolutely. But then language support in schools has to get better, in both languages.
>
> Presenter: And gender-inclusive language? Leonie, do you use it?
>
> Leonie: In chats, yes, with the asterisk. Not in exams, because – we're not allowed to at our school.
>
> Mr Lorenz: I write "Schülerinnen und Schüler". It's gender-fair, and everyone can read it.
>
> Prof. Demir: As a scholar, what interests me is that the language community is negotiating this itself right now. Whether the asterisk will catch on remains to be seen.

Notice the registers: the professor speaks in full, written-like sentences; Leonie uses ellipsis (*Kommt drauf an*, *ist ja klar*), *red ich*, the tag *oder?* and *weil* with main-clause order. Words to note: *widersprechen* (to contradict), *von etwas ist die Rede* (something is being talked about), *aushandeln* (to negotiate), *sich durchsetzen* (to catch on, prevail), *der Riesenvorteil* (huge advantage).

## Reporting views on language

When you summarize a discussion like this one in writing, you report each speaker's view in Konjunktiv I (lessons 01–02), with a reporting verb that shows their attitude (lesson 05):

- *Die Sprachwissenschaftlerin betonte, das Deutsche habe schon immer Wörter aus anderen Sprachen übernommen; Sprachwandel sei normal.*
- *Herr Lorenz widersprach: Sprache solle der Verständigung dienen.*
- *Leonie meinte, zweisprachig aufzuwachsen sei ein großer Vorteil.*
- *Prof. Demir wies darauf hin, dass Fachsprache immer Menschen ausschließe.*

Remember the replacement rule: where the Konjunktiv I looks like the indicative, use the Konjunktiv II: *Sie sagten, sie hätten keine Zeit* (not *sie haben*).

## More words about language

- *die Mehrsprachigkeit* (multilingualism), *mehrsprachig* (multilingual), *zweisprachig* (bilingual): *Viele Kinder in Deutschland wachsen mehrsprachig auf.*
- *die Erstsprache* (first language), *die Zweitsprache* (second language) and *die Herkunftssprache* (heritage language, the language of the family's origin) are more precise than *Muttersprache*, which suggests a single language learned from the mother. *die Fremdsprache* (A2) is a language learned as foreign.
- *die Amtssprache* is an official language: *Deutsch ist Amtssprache in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz.* At national level it is also official in Liechtenstein, Luxembourg and Belgium, and regionally in South Tyrol in Italy; lesson 93 looks at the varieties. *die Sprachpolitik* is language policy.
- *beherrschen* is to have full command of a language: *Sie beherrscht drei Sprachen fließend.* *akzentfrei* means without an accent: *Er spricht akzentfrei Deutsch.*
- *die Verständigung* is communication, reaching understanding; *sich verständigen* is to make oneself understood: *Wir haben uns auf Englisch verständigt.*
- *die Identität* and *die Zugehörigkeit* (belonging): *Sprache ist ein Teil der Identität.* · *ein Gefühl der Zugehörigkeit*. *die Sprachgemeinschaft* is the community of speakers.
- *der Sprachwandel* is language change; *sich wandeln* is to change gradually (more formal than *sich ändern*).
- *die Redewendung* is an idiom (*jemandem auf den Wecker gehen*, to get on someone's nerves); *das Sprichwort* is a proverb (*Übung macht den Meister*, practice makes perfect).
- *sprachlich* (linguistic) and *der Sprachkurs* (language course), *die Sprachförderung* (language support).

## Pronunciation

- *der Anglizismus*: ang-gli-TSIS-mus. Plural *die Anglizismen*.
- *die Identität*: i-den-ti-TÄT, stress at the end.
- *beherrschen*: be-HER-schen; the *be-* is unstressed.
- English loanwords keep roughly their English sound but German stress patterns in compounds: *das Meeting* (MEE-ting), *der Meetingraum* (MEE-ting-raum).
- The gender gap: *Lehrer\*innen* is said with a short stop before *innen*, like the break in *be-enden*.

## Common mistakes

- *weil* with main-clause order in writing: ~~…, weil ich habe keine Zeit.~~ → *…, weil ich keine Zeit habe.*
- Colloquial forms in a formal text: ~~Ich schaff's leider nicht~~ → *Ich kann leider nicht teilnehmen*; ~~wegen dem Streik~~ → *wegen des Streiks*.
- Guessing English genders from English: there is no "it". *die E-Mail*, *das Meeting*, *der Workshop*.
- English participles: ~~hat gechatted~~ → *hat gechattet*.
- Assuming the generic masculine is always fine. In a letter to a group, *Liebe Kolleginnen und Kollegen* is the safe choice.
- *Handy* or *Beamer* in English: these are German words; in English it's a mobile (phone) and a projector.

## Key points

- Choose the register for the reader: formal written (nominal style, passive, genitive), neutral (normal sentences, *Sie*), colloquial (ellipsis, contractions, particles).
- Spoken German: *weil* and *obwohl* often take main-clause order; pronouns in position 1 are dropped (*Weiß ich nicht*); tag questions *oder?, ne?, gell?*; Ausklammerung. None of this belongs in formal writing.
- Anglicisms: the gender often follows a German word with the same meaning (*das Meeting, die E-Mail*); English verbs are weak (*hat gechattet*); some "English" words are German creations (*das Handy*).
- Gender-inclusive forms: Doppelnennung, slash, participles (*die Studierenden*), neutral nouns, asterisk and colon. Usage is debated; Doppelnennung and neutral forms are always safe.
- Report views on language with reporting verbs and Konjunktiv I.

lessons.title: The Goethe-Zertifikat B2 and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last core lesson of German B2. It describes what B2 means, explains the best-known exam at this level, the Goethe-Zertifikat B2, with a strategy for every part, and reviews the grammar of the whole course with a table that points back to the lessons. Its questions mix exam knowledge with review from all six modules.

You don't need to take an exam to have reached B2. But B2 is the level that many universities, employers and professional bodies in German-speaking countries ask for, so it's worth knowing how the exam works. Requirements, fees and rules change, so always check with the institution that asks for the certificate and with the exam centre.

## What B2 means

B2 is the fourth of the six levels of the **[[CEFR]]** (the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages) and the upper of the two "independent user" levels. The framework describes each level with **[[can-do statements]]**. In plain words, at B2 you:

- follow the main ideas of complex texts and talks on concrete and abstract topics, including discussions in your own field;
- talk with native speakers fluently and spontaneously enough that neither side has to make a special effort;
- write clear, detailed texts on a wide range of subjects, and argue a point of view with its advantages and disadvantages.

Compared with B1, the change is less about new situations and more about depth and control. At B1 you could tell what happened and say what you think. At B2 you can report what others said without taking sides (Konjunktiv I), weigh arguments (*zwar … aber, wenngleich, dem lässt sich entgegenhalten*), read dense written German (participle attributes, nominal style, the passive in all its forms), and choose the register that fits the reader. Fast dialect speech, very specialized texts and literary style are still hard; that is the job of C1.

## The Goethe-Zertifikat B2

The exam for adults is modular: four separate *Module*, which you can take together on one day or one at a time.

| module | time | parts and items | what you do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lesen | 65 minutes | 5 parts, 30 items | match statements to four people; put sentences into gaps in a text (two are extra); multiple choice on an article; match headings or statements to opinion texts; match headings to the paragraphs of a regulation |
| Hören | about 40 minutes | 4 parts, 30 items | five short texts heard once (two items each); a radio interview heard twice; a discussion heard once ("who says what?"); a short lecture heard twice |
| Schreiben | 75 minutes | 2 parts | a forum post giving and justifying your opinion (about 150 words, four content points); a message to a superior (about 100 words, four points in a sensible order) |
| Sprechen | about 15 minutes in pairs, plus 15 minutes preparation | 2 parts | a talk of about four minutes on a topic, then questions from your partner and the examiners; a discussion with your partner of about five minutes on a controversial question |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: The four modules of the Goethe-Zertifikat B2
  accDescr: Lesen, 65 minutes, five parts with 30 items. Hören, about 40 minutes, four parts with 30 items. Schreiben, 75 minutes, a forum post of about 150 words and a message of about 100 words. Sprechen, about 15 minutes in pairs plus 15 minutes of preparation, a talk and a discussion. Each module is scored out of 100 and passed with 60.
  L["Lesen: 65 min, 5 parts, 30 items"] --- H["Hören: about 40 min, 4 parts, 30 items"]
  H --- S["Schreiben: 75 min, forum post and message"]
  S --- P["Sprechen: about 15 min in pairs, talk and discussion"]
```

Each module is scored out of 100 points and passed with 60. In Lesen and Hören each of the 30 items is worth the same (the raw score is multiplied by about 3.33). The grades:

| points | grade (*Notenstufe*) |
|---|---|
| 90–100 | sehr gut |
| 80–89 | gut |
| 70–79 | befriedigend |
| 60–69 | ausreichend |

Because the modules are separate, you can repeat only the one you didn't pass. Whether results from different dates can be combined on one certificate depends on the rules in force and the exam centre: ask before you register.

The Goethe-Institut publishes free official practice material, including a complete model test (*Modellsatz*) with answers and the audio:

- [Model test for adults (PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/pro/relaunch/prf/materialien/B2/b2_modellsatz_erwachsene.pdf)
- [Listening audio and speaking example for the model test (video)](https://goethemp4s.akamaized.net/resources/files/mp477/b2_modellsatz_rahmen_erwachsene-v16.mp4)
- [Interactive online practice](https://bfu.goethe.de/b2_mod_2MX6/index.php)
- [Official exam rules (Durchführungsbestimmungen, PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/resources/files/pdf325/durchfuehrungsbestimmungen_b2.pdf)

Other exams test the same level with different tasks, for example telc Deutsch B2 and the ÖSD Zertifikat B2.

## Strategies for each module

### Lesen

- Teil 1 (statements and four people): read the statements first, then each person's text. Underline the words that carry the meaning, and expect paraphrase: the text won't use the statement's words. With nine statements and four people, a person can be the answer more than once.
- Teil 2 (sentences into gaps): this is a **[[cohesion]]** task. Look at both sides of each gap: pronouns (*sie, dies, dabei*), connectors (*jedoch, außerdem*) and repeated nouns tell you which sentence fits. Two sentences are *überzählig* (extra), so don't force them in.
- Teil 3 (multiple choice): the questions follow the order of the text. Wrong options often repeat words from the text with a changed meaning: check negation, *nicht nur … sondern auch*, and who said what.
- Teil 4 (opinion texts): decide for each text whether the writer is for, against or in between, then match. Modal particles and hedges (*eigentlich, durchaus, zwar … aber*, lessons 16–19) carry the attitude.
- Teil 5 (a regulation): typical of company rules or terms and conditions, full of passive, *sein + zu* and nominal style (lessons 06–09, 13). Read the headings, then skim each paragraph for its topic.
- Time: 65 minutes for 30 items is about two minutes each. Write the answers on the *Antwortbogen* (answer sheet) as you go.

### Hören

- Use the reading time before each part to read the questions and predict what you'll hear.
- Teil 1 and Teil 3 are heard only once. Answer immediately, then move on; don't lose the next item worrying about the last.
- Teil 2 (interview, twice): the first time, answer what you can; the second time, check. The expert often corrects the interviewer: listen for *Das würde ich so nicht sagen* and *Im Gegenteil*.
- Teil 3 (discussion): for each statement, decide who says it: the presenter or one of the guests. Note each speaker's position in two words.
- Teil 4 (lecture, twice): signposts (*Erstens, Im Gegensatz dazu, Zusammenfassend*) show the structure; the honors lesson 25h2 practises this.

### Schreiben

- Teil 1, the forum post (lesson 19): about 150 words in about 50 minutes. Cover all four *Inhaltspunkte*, give your opinion with reasons and an example, and mention another view. Link the points; don't answer them as a list.
- Teil 2, the message (lesson 26): about 100 words in about 25 minutes. Choose a sensible order, use the Konjunktiv II for requests, and don't forget the Betreff, the Anrede and the Gruß.
- *Zeiteinteilung* (time management) matters: plan for five minutes, write, and keep five minutes to check endings, verb position and commas. Writing far more than the word count doesn't earn points and makes mistakes more likely.

### Sprechen

- During the 15 minutes of preparation you get notes for both parts. For the talk (Teil 1), plan a structure: introduction, two or three points with examples, your opinion, a conclusion (lesson 25). Write key words, not sentences.
- In the talk, signpost: *Ich möchte über … sprechen. Zunächst … Ein weiterer Punkt ist … Zum Schluss …*
- After your partner's talk, you ask a question. Listen while they speak and note one point you can ask about.
- In the discussion (Teil 2, lesson 20): give your opinion, react to your partner's arguments, agree and disagree politely, and try to reach a compromise. It is a conversation, not two monologues.

## How writing and speaking are marked

In broad terms, examiners judge four things in writing, and a fifth in speaking:

- whether you did the task: all content points, the right text type, the right register;
- **[[coherence]]** (*die Kohärenz*): whether the text is logically built and linked, with connectors and references (*kohärent*);
- vocabulary (*die Wortwahl*): range and accuracy, words that fit the topic and register;
- grammar: range and accuracy; a B2 text should use subordinate clauses, the passive and the Konjunktiv where they fit;
- in speaking, also pronunciation and intonation.

The *Bewertungskriterien* (assessment criteria) reward a text that works for its reader. A text with a few small mistakes and a clear *Textaufbau* (structure) scores better than one with no mistakes that misses a content point.

## A reading text in the style of Lesen Teil 5

Here are three paragraphs from an original set of rules. In the exam you would match each paragraph to one of several headings.

> § 3 Die Räume stehen den Mitgliedern montags bis freitags von 7 bis 22 Uhr zur Verfügung. Wer außerhalb dieser Zeiten arbeiten möchte, hat dies mindestens zwei Tage vorher bei der Verwaltung zu beantragen.
>
> § 4 Besprechungsräume sind über das Buchungssystem zu reservieren. Wird ein gebuchter Raum nicht innerhalb von 15 Minuten nach Beginn genutzt, kann er von anderen Mitgliedern belegt werden.
>
> § 5 Für Schäden, die durch unsachgemäße Nutzung der Geräte entstehen, haftet das Mitglied. Defekte sind unverzüglich der Verwaltung zu melden.

In English:

> § 3 The rooms are available to members Monday to Friday from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. Anyone who wishes to work outside these hours must apply to the management at least two days in advance.
>
> § 4 Meeting rooms must be reserved through the booking system. If a booked room is not used within 15 minutes of the start, other members may take it.
>
> § 5 The member is liable for damage caused by improper use of the equipment. Defects must be reported to the management immediately.

Possible headings: *Öffnungszeiten und Sonderzeiten* (§ 3), *Buchung von Räumen* (§ 4), *Haftung und Reparaturen* (§ 5), plus distractors like *Kosten der Mitgliedschaft* that fit none. Notice the grammar: *zur Verfügung stehen* (a Funktionsverbgefüge, lesson 09), *hat … zu beantragen* and *sind … zu reservieren* (passive alternatives, lesson 07), a verb-first conditional (*Wird ein gebuchter Raum nicht … genutzt, …*), and the passive with a modal (*kann … belegt werden*). *haften für* is to be liable for, *unverzüglich* means immediately, without delay.

## A discussion in the style of Sprechen Teil 2

Two candidates discuss the question: *Sollten Unternehmen ihren Beschäftigten die Viertagewoche anbieten?*

> Anna: Ich bin eindeutig dafür. Studien zeigen, dass ausgeruhte Beschäftigte produktiver sind, und für Firmen ist das ein gutes Argument im Wettbewerb um Fachkräfte.
>
> Malik: Da hast du sicher recht, was Büros angeht. Aber denk mal an ein Krankenhaus oder einen Busbetrieb. Dort müsste man mehr Leute einstellen, und die gibt es ja gar nicht.
>
> Anna: Das ist ein wichtiger Einwand. Vielleicht müsste man das je nach Branche unterschiedlich regeln.
>
> Malik: Genau. Wäre es nicht sinnvoller, die Firmen selbst entscheiden zu lassen, statt es für alle vorzuschreiben?
>
> Anna: Damit könnte ich leben, sofern die Beschäftigten mitreden dürfen.
>
> Malik: Einverstanden. Dann sind wir uns einig: freiwillig, je nach Branche, und mit Beteiligung der Beschäftigten.

In English:

> Anna: I'm clearly in favour. Studies show that rested employees are more productive, and for companies it's a good argument in the competition for skilled workers.
>
> Malik: You're certainly right as far as offices are concerned. But think of a hospital or a bus company. There you'd have to hire more people, and they simply aren't there.
>
> Anna: That's an important objection. Maybe it would have to be regulated differently depending on the sector.
>
> Malik: Exactly. Wouldn't it make more sense to let the companies decide for themselves, instead of prescribing it for everyone?
>
> Anna: I could live with that, provided the employees have a say.
>
> Malik: Agreed. Then we agree: voluntary, depending on the sector, and with the employees involved.

Both speakers state a position with a reason, concede a point (*Da hast du sicher recht, was … angeht. Das ist ein wichtiger Einwand.*), propose with the Konjunktiv II (*Wäre es nicht sinnvoller, …?*), use connectors from this course (*je nach, sofern, statt … zu*) and end with a compromise. That is what examiners want to hear. *die Viertagewoche* is the four-day week; *mitreden* is to have a say.

## Review of the course

| lessons | topic | example |
|---|---|---|
| 01–02 | Konjunktiv I and indirect speech, the replacement rule | *Sie sagte, sie habe keine Zeit; die Kollegen hätten keine Zeit.* |
| 03 | subjective modal verbs | *Er soll reich sein. Sie will nichts gesehen haben.* |
| 04 | Futur II | *Sie wird den Bus verpasst haben.* |
| 05 | reporting verbs, *laut, zufolge* | *Laut Polizei … · Dem Bericht zufolge …* |
| 06 | Zustandspassiv | *Die Brücke ist gesperrt.* |
| 07 | passive alternatives | *Das Formular ist bis Freitag abzugeben. Das lässt sich reparieren.* |
| 08 | the passive in every tense | *Das Werk war schon geschlossen worden.* |
| 09 | Funktionsverbgefüge | *eine Entscheidung treffen, in Betracht ziehen* |
| 10 | verb prefixes | *UMfahren* (to knock down) vs *umFAHren* (to drive around) |
| 11–12 | participle attributes and the gerundive | *die seit Jahren steigenden Mieten · das zu lösende Problem* |
| 13 | nominal and verbal style | *bei der Ankunft = wenn man ankommt* |
| 14 | formal prepositions | *ungeachtet der Kritik, mittels eines Tests* |
| 15 | dessen/deren, wer … der | *die Firma, deren Chef … · Wer zu spät kommt, …* |
| 16 | modal particles | *Das ist ja interessant. Komm doch mal vorbei.* |
| 17 | *indem, sofern, je nachdem* | *Man spart Geld, indem man …* |
| 18 | concession and comparison | *Wenngleich … · Er tut so, als hätte er nichts gehört.* |
| 19–20 | argumentation and discussion | *Zwar …, aber … · Wäre es nicht sinnvoller, …?* |
| 21–22 | word formation | *die Erkenntnis, benutzerfreundlich, fehleranfällig* |
| 23 | infinitive clauses in the perfect and passive | *Er behauptet, die Rakete gesehen zu haben.* |
| 24 | describing trends and data | *um 3 Prozent steigen · auf 3 Prozent steigen* |
| 25 | presentations and Mittelfeld order | *Ich komme nun zu … · Er hat es ihr gestern gegeben.* |
| 26 | formal messages at work | *Wäre es möglich, …? Ich würde Sie bitten, …* |
| 27 | verb clusters and the double infinitive | *…, dass er hätte kommen sollen.* |
| 28 | applications | *Seit 2021 arbeite ich als … · Leitung eines Teams* |
| 29 | register and variation | *weil + main-clause order in speech; Kolleginnen und Kollegen* |

If one of these still feels uncertain, go back to that lesson's quiz and its vocabulary before the exam. The course's question bank lets you practise by topic.

## What comes next: C1

C1 is the level of "proficient users": you understand long, demanding texts and implicit meaning, express yourself fluently without searching for words, and use the language flexibly for work and study. In German-speaking countries, C1 is the usual requirement for studying in German. Besides the Goethe-Zertifikat C1, universities in Germany accept tests such as TestDaF and the DSH. The best preparation is quantity: read newspapers and novels, listen to podcasts and radio, and write regularly. The reading list of this course suggests where to start.

## Exam and study language

The exam papers are in German, so learn the words they use: *der Prüfungsteil* (part of the exam), *die Lesezeit* (reading time before a listening part), *die Vorbereitungszeit* (preparation time), *der Lückentext* (gapped text), *die Mehrfachauswahl* (multiple choice), *das Leseverstehen* and *das Hörverstehen* (reading and listening comprehension), *der Inhaltspunkt* (content point), *der Forumsbeitrag* (forum post), *der Sprachgebrauch* (use of language), *das Kriterium* (criterion; plural *die Kriterien*), *das Prüfungsergebnis* (result), *die Niveaustufe* (CEFR level), *der Schwerpunkt* (focus, main emphasis) and *schwerpunktmäßig* (mainly, with a focus on).

## Pronunciation

- *das Kriterium*: kri-TEE-ri-um, plural *die Kriterien* (kri-TEE-ri-en).
- *die Kohärenz*: ko-hä-RENTS; *kohärent*: ko-hä-RENT.
- *das Niveau* is French: ni-VO, stress at the end. *die Niveaustufe*: ni-VO-shtoo-fe.
- *überzählig*: Ü-ber-tsä-lig, stress on the first syllable.

## Common mistakes

- Treating the content points as a checklist: answer each point, but in a connected text with connectors.
- Ignoring the word count: much less than 150/100 words usually means a content point is too thin; much more means more mistakes.
- Monologues in the discussion. React to what your partner says: *Da hast du recht, aber … · Was hältst du davon, wenn …?*
- Forcing the extra sentences into Lesen Teil 2. Two of them don't belong anywhere.
- Waiting for the exact words in Hören. The answers are almost always paraphrased.
- *das Kriterium* in the plural: ~~die Kriteriums~~ → *die Kriterien*.

## Key points

- B2: complex texts on concrete and abstract topics, fluent conversation with native speakers, clear detailed texts that argue a view.
- Goethe-Zertifikat B2: Lesen 65 min (5 parts, 30 items), Hören about 40 min (4 parts, 30 items), Schreiben 75 min (forum post about 150 words, message about 100 words), Sprechen about 15 min in pairs plus 15 min preparation (talk and discussion).
- Each module out of 100, pass with 60; grades at 90, 80, 70 and 60; modules can be taken and repeated separately.
- Strategies: read questions first, expect paraphrase, watch for extra items, plan your writing time, and in speaking, react to your partner.
- Writing and speaking are judged on task completion, coherence, vocabulary and grammar (and pronunciation in speaking).
- The review table points to the lessons; free official practice sets are on the Goethe-Institut website.

lessons.title: Arbeitsrecht: contracts, works councils and collective agreements
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

An employment contract is one of the most important documents you'll ever sign in German, and it is written in a style of its own: rules in the passive, obligations with *sein + zu* and *haben + zu*, and conditions without *wenn*. This honors lesson teaches you to read that style, using an original contract as the example, and introduces the main institutions of German labour law: notice and dismissal protection, sick pay, holiday entitlement, the minimum wage, works councils and collective agreements.

It builds on the passive alternatives of lesson 07, the passive in all tenses (lesson 08) and the formal register of lessons 26 and 29. Austrian and Swiss law differ in many details, so the facts here are about Germany, as of 2026. This is a language lesson, not legal advice: for a real contract, ask a works council, a union or a lawyer.

## The language of rules

Legal texts describe what must, may or will happen in general, not what someone is doing now. Four structures do most of the work.

### The present tense as rule

The present indicative states a rule: *Die Probezeit beträgt sechs Monate.* (The probation period is six months.) *Der Arbeitnehmer erhält ein Bruttogehalt von 3.800 Euro.* There's no *soll* or *muss*: the present is the law.

### The passive

The passive leaves out who does something, because the rule applies whoever it is, or because it is obvious:

- *Das Gehalt wird jeweils am Monatsende gezahlt.* — The salary is paid at the end of each month.
- *Überstunden werden durch Freizeit ausgeglichen.* — Overtime is compensated with time off.
- *Die Arbeitszeit wird elektronisch erfasst.* — Working time is recorded electronically.

### sein + zu and haben + zu

Lesson 07 introduced *sein + zu* + infinitive as a passive with *müssen* or *können*. In contracts it almost always means "must be done":

- *Die Kündigung ist schriftlich zu erklären.* = *Die Kündigung muss schriftlich erklärt werden.* — Notice must be given in writing.
- *Urlaub ist rechtzeitig zu beantragen.* — Leave must be applied for in good time.

*haben + zu* is its active partner: the subject has the obligation.

- *Der Arbeitnehmer hat seine Arbeitsunfähigkeit unverzüglich mitzuteilen.* = *… muss … mitteilen.* — The employee must report his inability to work without delay.
- *Der Arbeitgeber hat die Arbeitszeit zu erfassen.* — The employer must record working hours.

With a negation, be careful: *ist nicht zu …* means "must not" or "cannot", not "doesn't have to": *Die Daten sind nicht an Dritte weiterzugeben* (the data must not be passed on to third parties).

### Conditions without wenn

Instead of *wenn*, legal German often starts a conditional clause with the finite verb. The main clause that follows usually starts with *so* or *dann*, or directly with its verb:

- *Wird der Vertrag nicht bis zum 30. Juni gekündigt, verlängert er sich um ein Jahr.* = *Wenn der Vertrag nicht … gekündigt wird, …* — If the contract isn't terminated by 30 June, it is extended by a year.
- *Ist der Arbeitnehmer arbeitsunfähig erkrankt, so hat er dies unverzüglich mitzuteilen.* — If the employee is ill and unable to work, he must report it immediately.
- *Sollte eine Bestimmung dieses Vertrags unwirksam sein, bleiben die übrigen Bestimmungen wirksam.* — Should a provision of this contract be invalid, the remaining provisions remain valid.

This is the **[[verb-first conditional]]**. You'll recognize it by the finite verb in first position in a statement, followed by a comma and a second verb. *Sollte* in first position is especially common: it makes the condition sound less likely, like English "should".

| with wenn | verb-first |
|---|---|
| *Wenn das Arbeitsverhältnis endet, …* | *Endet das Arbeitsverhältnis, …* |
| *Wenn Überstunden angeordnet werden, …* | *Werden Überstunden angeordnet, …* |
| *Wenn der Arbeitnehmer krank sein sollte, …* | *Sollte der Arbeitnehmer krank sein, …* |

The everyday word *falls* (B1) does the same job in a normal subordinate clause: *Falls der Arbeitnehmer krank ist, …*

## Text: from an employment contract

An original contract, as a mid-sized company might use it. The employee is called *der Arbeitnehmer* throughout, the traditional generic masculine of legal texts; many contracts now add a note that it refers to all genders, or write *die Arbeitnehmerin / der Arbeitnehmer*.

> § 2 Probezeit
>
> Die ersten sechs Monate gelten als Probezeit. Während der Probezeit kann das Arbeitsverhältnis von beiden Seiten mit einer Frist von zwei Wochen gekündigt werden.
>
> § 5 Vergütung
>
> Der Arbeitnehmer erhält ein monatliches Bruttogehalt von 3.800 Euro. Das Gehalt wird jeweils zum Monatsende auf ein vom Arbeitnehmer zu benennendes Konto überwiesen.
>
> § 6 Urlaub
>
> Der Arbeitnehmer hat Anspruch auf 28 Arbeitstage Urlaub im Kalenderjahr. Der Urlaub ist rechtzeitig zu beantragen und mit dem Vorgesetzten abzustimmen.
>
> § 7 Arbeitsverhinderung
>
> Ist der Arbeitnehmer infolge Krankheit arbeitsunfähig, so hat er dies dem Arbeitgeber unverzüglich mitzuteilen. Dauert die Arbeitsunfähigkeit länger als drei Kalendertage, ist sie durch eine ärztliche Bescheinigung nachzuweisen.
>
> § 9 Kündigung
>
> Nach Ablauf der Probezeit gelten die gesetzlichen Kündigungsfristen. Die Kündigung bedarf der Schriftform; eine Kündigung per E-Mail ist unwirksam. Das Recht zur fristlosen Kündigung aus wichtigem Grund bleibt unberührt.
>
> § 12 Schlussbestimmungen
>
> Sollte eine Bestimmung dieses Vertrags unwirksam sein, wird die Wirksamkeit der übrigen Bestimmungen davon nicht berührt.

In English:

> § 2 Probation
>
> The first six months count as a probation period. During probation, either side may terminate the employment with two weeks' notice.
>
> § 5 Pay
>
> The employee receives a monthly gross salary of 3,800 euros. The salary is transferred at the end of each month to an account to be named by the employee.
>
> § 6 Holiday
>
> The employee is entitled to 28 working days of holiday per calendar year. Holiday must be applied for in good time and agreed with the superior.
>
> § 7 Absence
>
> If the employee is unable to work as a result of illness, he must notify the employer without delay. If the inability to work lasts longer than three calendar days, it must be proven with a doctor's certificate.
>
> § 9 Termination
>
> After the probation period, the statutory notice periods apply. Notice must be given in writing; notice by e-mail is invalid. The right to terminate without notice for good cause remains unaffected.
>
> § 12 Final provisions
>
> Should a provision of this contract be invalid, the validity of the remaining provisions is not affected.

Look at the structures: the present as rule (*gelten, erhält*), the passive (*gekündigt werden, wird … überwiesen*), *sein + zu* (*ist … zu beantragen*, *ist … nachzuweisen*), *haben + zu* (*hat … mitzuteilen*), a gerundive (*ein vom Arbeitnehmer zu benennendes Konto*, lesson 12), and verb-first conditionals in §§ 7 and 12. Words to note: *das Arbeitsverhältnis* (employment relationship), *die Vergütung* (pay, remuneration), *der Anspruch auf* (entitlement to), *die Schriftform* (written form), *etwas bedarf der Schriftform* (requires written form, with the genitive), *unwirksam* (invalid, void), *unberührt bleiben* (to remain unaffected), *infolge* + genitive (as a result of; here without an article: *infolge Krankheit*).

## The main rules of German labour law

The contract only makes sense against the law behind it. In outline:

- Notice and dismissal. Every notice of termination must be in writing on paper with a signature; an e-mail or a text message is not enough. The basic notice period is four weeks (to the 15th or the end of a month), and it gets longer for the employer the longer someone has worked there. *Der Kündigungsschutz* (protection against dismissal) under the Dismissal Protection Act applies after six months in a business with more than ten employees: the employer then needs a reason linked to the person, their conduct or the needs of the business.
- Warning and dismissal without notice. Before dismissing someone for their conduct, an employer usually has to give a formal warning first: *die Abmahnung*, from *abmahnen*. A *fristlose Kündigung* (dismissal without notice) is only possible for a serious reason, such as theft, and must come within two weeks of the employer learning of it.
- Sick pay. An employee who is *arbeitsunfähig* (unable to work because of illness) continues to get their pay from the employer for up to six weeks: *die Lohnfortzahlung im Krankheitsfall*. *die Arbeitsunfähigkeit* has to be reported at once and, after three days, confirmed by a doctor; for people with statutory health insurance the certificate now goes to the employer electronically.
- Holiday. The legal minimum is 24 working days on a six-day week, which is 20 days for a five-day week. Many contracts and collective agreements give more, often 28 to 30 days. That is the *Urlaubsanspruch* (holiday entitlement).
- Minimum wage. Germany has had a statutory *Mindestlohn* since 2015. Since 1 January 2026 it has been 13.90 euros an hour, and the same regulation already sets a further rise to 14.60 euros from 1 January 2027.

## Works councils and collective agreements

Two institutions shape German workplaces more than any single law.

*Der Betriebsrat* (works council) is elected by the employees of a business; it can be set up in any business that normally has at least five permanent employees entitled to vote (three of whom can stand for election). It has a right to be consulted and, on many questions, a right of co-determination (*die Mitbestimmung*): working hours, overtime, monitoring technology, holiday planning. Before any dismissal the works council must be heard; a dismissal without that hearing is invalid. The Betriebsrat is the most common form of *Arbeitnehmervertretung* (employee representation) at company level.

*Der Tarifvertrag* (collective agreement) is negotiated between a union (*die Gewerkschaft*, B1) and an employers' association (*der Arbeitgeberverband*) or a single company. It sets pay scales, working hours and holiday for a whole sector or region. The negotiations, *die Tarifverhandlungen*, are followed in the news, and strikes are legal only in connection with them. Pay set by such an agreement is *tariflich* (*tarifliche Bezahlung*), and an employer who is bound by one is *tarifgebunden*. The freedom of unions and employers to negotiate without the state is protected by the Grundgesetz (Article 9).

In Austria the equivalent agreement is called *der Kollektivvertrag*, and there is no general statutory minimum wage: minimum pay is set in these agreements, which cover almost all employees.

## Reading strategy for contracts

1. Read the headings of the paragraphs first: they tell you where each topic is.
2. In each sentence, find the obligation: *ist … zu*, *hat … zu*, *muss*, *darf nicht*. Ask who must do what.
3. When a sentence starts with a verb and has a comma later, it's a condition: put *wenn* in front of it in your head.
4. Paraphrase in plain German: *Der Urlaub ist rechtzeitig zu beantragen* → *Ich muss meinen Urlaub früh genug beantragen.*

## Pronunciation

- *der Tarifvertrag*: ta-REEF-fer-trahk. *tariflich*: ta-REEF-lich.
- *die Abmahnung*: AP-mah-nung; *b* at the end of a syllable sounds like *p*.
- *arbeitsunfähig*: AR-baits-un-fä-ich.
- *fristlos*: FRIST-lohs, with a short *i*.

## Common mistakes

- Reading *ist zu* as "is closed" or "is too": *Die Kündigung ist schriftlich zu erklären* means "must be given in writing". The *zu* belongs to the infinitive.
- Reading a verb-first conditional as a question: *Wird der Vertrag nicht gekündigt, …* is not "Is the contract not terminated?". The comma and the second verb show the condition.
- Confusing *kündigen* (to give notice) with *die Kündigung erhalten* (to be given notice). *Ich habe gekündigt* means you quit; *Mir wurde gekündigt* means you were dismissed (with the dative).
- Translating *das Arbeitsrecht* as "right to work": it is labour law, the body of law.
- Thinking *fristlos* means "without a deadline". It means without a notice period, immediately.

## Key points

- Contracts use the present as rule, the passive, *sein + zu* (must be done) and *haben + zu* (the subject must do).
- Verb-first conditionals replace *wenn*: *Wird der Vertrag nicht gekündigt, verlängert er sich.* *Sollte …* makes the condition sound less likely.
- Notice must be in writing on paper; *Kündigungsschutz* after six months in larger businesses; an *Abmahnung* usually comes before dismissal for misconduct; *fristlos* only for a serious reason.
- Sick pay for up to six weeks; at least 20 days' holiday on a five-day week; minimum wage 13.90 euros per hour since 2026.
- The *Betriebsrat* represents employees in a business; the *Tarifvertrag* between union and employers sets pay for a sector.

lessons.title: Sprachmittlung: passing on what you read and heard
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Much of the German you will use at work isn't your own opinion. It is something you pass on: you tell a colleague what a long notice from HR says, you summarize a client's voicemail for your manager, you explain an English e-mail to a German team, or a German meeting to an English-speaking partner. This is **[[Sprachmittlung]]** (mediation): passing on the content of a text or a conversation to someone who can't or won't read it themselves, in the form that suits them.

Mediation is not translation. A translation keeps every sentence; mediation keeps what matters to this reader and changes everything else: length, order, register, sometimes the language. This lesson gives you a method for it, the grammar that helps (nominal phrases for condensing, reporting verbs and the Konjunktiv I for other people's positions), and a look at the workplace conventions you need to adapt to: *du* and *Sie*, hierarchy and directness.

## A method in four steps

1. Who is the reader, and what do they need? A new colleague needs to know what to do; a manager needs the decision and the deadline; a client needs the result, not the internal discussion.
2. Find the essential points (*das Wesentliche*). In most texts it is two or three facts. Ask: what changes for the reader? Leave out background, politeness formulas and repetition.
3. Main point first. Start with the most important thing, then the details the reader needs to act. A summary that begins with "First the e-mail says thank you for …" has already lost the reader.
4. Adapt the register. An official notice becomes a chat message; a colleague's chat message becomes a sentence in a formal e-mail. Pass the content on *sinngemäß* (in substance), not word for word.

## Condensing: nominal phrases and short clauses

A good mediation is short. Two tools from this course help most:

- nominal phrases (lesson 13) pack a whole clause into a few words: *wegen der Bauarbeiten* instead of *weil im Gebäude gebaut wird*; *nach Rücksprache mit der IT* instead of *nachdem wir mit der IT gesprochen haben*;
- the passive and *man* (lessons 06–08) let you leave out who does what when it doesn't matter.

In informal mediation, the opposite: unpack the nominal style of an official text into plain verbs. *Eine Inanspruchnahme der Parkplätze ist ab dem 1. März nur nach vorheriger Anmeldung möglich* becomes *Ab März musst du dich anmelden, wenn du auf dem Firmenparkplatz parken willst.*

## Reporting someone else's position

When you pass on what a person said or wrote, you show that it's their view, not yours. In writing, use a reporting verb and the Konjunktiv I (lessons 01–02 and 05):

| reporting verb | what it signals | example |
|---|---|---|
| *mitteilen* | neutral information | *Herr Ruiz teilt mit, die Lieferung verzögere sich um eine Woche.* |
| *betonen* | the person stresses it | *Sie betont, der Termin sei verbindlich.* |
| *einräumen* | the person admits it | *Er räumt ein, dass ein Fehler passiert sei.* |
| *vorschlagen* | a proposal | *Sie schlägt vor, das Treffen online abzuhalten.* |
| *bitten um* | a request | *Er bittet um eine Antwort bis Freitag.* |
| *sich beschweren über* | a complaint | *Die Kundin beschwert sich über die lange Wartezeit.* |

Two phrases introduce a summary: *Laut Herrn Ruiz …* (according to Mr Ruiz) and *Kurz gesagt: …* (in short). And *sinngemäß* marks a paraphrase of what someone said: *Er hat sinngemäß gesagt, wir sollten uns keine Sorgen machen.*

In speech, people report in the indicative or with *dass* and the Konjunktiv II: *Der Kunde hat gesagt, dass die Lieferung später kommt.* That is fine when you tell a colleague; in a written summary for a manager, the Konjunktiv I keeps the distance.

## Example 1: from an official notice to a colleague

Your company's HR department has sent out this notice. Your new colleague Sam, who has just started and whose German is still at A2, asks you in the team chat what it means.

> Information der Personalabteilung
>
> Aufgrund der Umstellung des Zeiterfassungssystems ist eine Buchung von Arbeitszeiten über das bisherige Portal ab dem 1. Oktober nicht mehr möglich. Sämtliche Beschäftigten werden gebeten, bis zum 30. September die Registrierung im neuen System vorzunehmen. Bei Fragen steht Ihnen das Team der Personalabteilung zur Verfügung. Bereits beantragte Urlaubstage bleiben von der Umstellung unberührt.

Your answer in the chat:

> Hi Sam, kurz gesagt: Wir bekommen ein neues System für die Arbeitszeiten. Ab 1. Oktober funktioniert das alte Portal nicht mehr. Du musst dich bis 30. September im neuen System registrieren. Dein Urlaub, den du schon beantragt hast, ist sicher. Wenn du Fragen hast, schreib der Personalabteilung oder frag mich!

In English, the notice and the chat message:

> Information from the HR department
>
> Owing to the changeover of the time recording system, it will no longer be possible to book working hours via the previous portal from 1 October. All employees are requested to complete their registration in the new system by 30 September. The HR team is available for any questions. Holiday days already applied for are unaffected by the changeover.

> Hi Sam, in short: we're getting a new system for working hours. From 1 October the old portal won't work any more. You have to register in the new system by 30 September. The holiday you've already applied for is safe. If you have questions, write to HR or ask me!

The chat message starts with the main point, keeps all four facts (new system, old portal ends, deadline, holiday safe), and turns the nominal style into short main clauses with *du*: *eine Buchung … ist nicht mehr möglich* becomes *funktioniert nicht mehr*, *die Registrierung vorzunehmen* becomes *dich registrieren*. *Sämtliche Beschäftigten werden gebeten* disappears: Sam is one of them.

## Example 2: from a voicemail to your manager

A supplier leaves this voicemail for your manager, who is in a meeting:

> Ja, guten Tag, Ruiz hier von der Firma Klimatec. Es geht um die Klimaanlagen für Ihr neues Büro. Also, wir haben leider ein Problem mit unserem Lieferanten, die Geräte kommen nicht diese Woche, sondern frühestens am 14. Das tut mir wirklich leid. Wir könnten aber übergangsweise zwei mobile Geräte bringen, kostenlos natürlich. Wenn Sie das wollen, rufen Sie mich bitte bis Donnerstag zurück, unter 0341 55 82 90. Danke, tschüss!

Your e-mail to your manager:

> Betreff: Klimaanlagen – Lieferung verzögert sich
>
> Liebe Frau Albers,
>
> Herr Ruiz von Klimatec hat angerufen: Die Klimaanlagen für das neue Büro werden frühestens am 14. geliefert, weil sein Lieferant Probleme habe. Er bietet an, übergangsweise zwei mobile Geräte kostenlos aufzustellen. Falls Sie das Angebot annehmen möchten, bittet er bis Donnerstag um Rückruf (0341 55 82 90).
>
> Viele Grüße
>
> Daniel Krüger

The voicemail is spoken (*Also*, *Ja*, *tschüss*, an apology); the e-mail keeps the facts in order of importance: problem and new date, offer, what the manager must do and by when. The supplier's reason is reported in Konjunktiv I (*habe*), the offer and the request with reporting verbs (*bietet an, bittet um*).

## Working across cultures

Mediation also means passing on the unwritten rules. *Interkulturell* competence is knowing that the same words can work differently in another workplace. Here are some tendencies in German-speaking workplaces; they vary a lot by company, sector, region and generation, so treat them as starting points, not rules.

### du or Sie?

Traditional companies, public administration, law firms and banks mostly use *Sie*, often with surnames, sometimes for years. Start-ups, IT companies, many retailers and creative agencies often use *du* with everyone, including the managing director. Some companies mix: *du* within the team, *Sie* with clients and senior managers.

The switch from *Sie* to *du* is a small ritual. Traditionally the older or more senior person offers it: *jemandem das Du anbieten*. You might hear *Wollen wir uns nicht duzen? Ich bin Petra.* It is hard to refuse without offending, and hard to go back. So if you are not sure, use *Sie* and wait; the other person will offer *du* if they want it. Using *du* unasked with a superior or a client is a classic *Fauxpas*.

In Austria and Bavaria, the *du* comes sooner in some settings, but titles matter more: *Frau Magister*, *Herr Diplomingenieur* and *Frau Doktor* are used in address in Austria more often than in Germany.

### Hierarchy and formality

Many German companies describe their hierarchies as flat. Still, decisions often follow a clear path: you go to your team leader before you go to their manager. Skipping a level can be read as going behind someone's back. *Die Förmlichkeit* (formality) is higher in writing than in speech: an e-mail to a manager you call *du* in the kitchen may still begin *Hallo Petra* and be well structured. *Hierarchisch* organized companies use the term *Dienstweg* for the official channel.

### Directness

German speakers are often described as direct, and in work matters this is often true: *Das funktioniert so nicht* or *Da sehe ich ein Problem* is normal in a meeting and usually not meant personally. The idea behind it is to separate the matter (*die Sachebene*) from the relationship. Small talk tends to be shorter, and *Wie geht's?* is a real question, not a greeting. On the other hand, many people find written criticism without any softening rude, so the Konjunktiv II forms of lesson 26 are still the norm in e-mails.

What is *kulturbedingt* (culturally determined) and what is just one person's style is often hard to tell. The *Mentalität* of a whole country is a cliché; the *Gepflogenheiten* (customs, practices) of a company are real, and you learn them by watching. That takes *Fingerspitzengefühl*: tact, a feel for the situation.

## Pronunciation

- *die Sprachmittlung*: SHPRAHKH-mit-lung.
- *die Hierarchie*: hi-e-rar-CHIE, stress at the end, with the soft *ch* of *ich*; *hierarchisch*: hi-e-RAR-chisch.
- *der Fauxpas* is French: fo-PA, the *x* and the *s* are silent; the plural is spelled the same, *die Fauxpas*, and said fo-PAS.
- *die Mentalität*: men-ta-li-TÄT.
- *das Fingerspitzengefühl*: FIN-ger-shpi-tsen-ge-fühl.

## Common mistakes

- Translating everything. Mediation leaves out what the reader doesn't need: politeness formulas, background, repetition.
- Keeping the source's order. Put the main point first, even if the original hides it at the end.
- Keeping the source's register. An official notice passed on to a colleague in chat should sound like a chat message.
- Presenting someone's claim as fact. *Der Lieferant habe Probleme* (Konjunktiv I) or *Laut Herrn Ruiz …* shows it's his statement.
- Offering *du* to your superior. The more senior person offers it; you wait.
- Writing *Fauxpas* with an ending in the plural: ~~die Fauxpase~~ → *die Fauxpas*.

## Key points

- Sprachmittlung passes on the essential content of a text or conversation for a particular reader, in a suitable form; it is not word-for-word translation.
- Method: reader and purpose → *das Wesentliche* → main point first → adapt the register.
- Condense with nominal phrases and the passive; for an informal reader, unpack nominal style into short main clauses.
- Report positions with reporting verbs (*mitteilen, betonen, einräumen, vorschlagen, bitten um*) and Konjunktiv I in writing; *sinngemäß* marks a paraphrase.
- Workplace conventions: *Sie* until *du* is offered (usually by the senior person); respect the *Dienstweg*; directness on the matter, politeness in writing.
