lessons.title: Kafka, Die Verwandlung: narrative perspective and erlebte Rede
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This honors module takes your B2 grammar out of the textbook and into the texts German speakers argue about: literature, the theatre, politics and the language itself. It starts with what may be the most famous first sentence in German literature, the opening of Franz Kafka's *Die Verwandlung* (*The Metamorphosis*).

You'll learn who Kafka was and why a Prague insurance clerk wrote in German, read the first lines of the story with notes, and look closely at how the story is told: the **[[narrative perspective]]** (*die Erzählperspektive*), and above all a technique German literature uses constantly, the **[[free indirect speech]]** (*die erlebte Rede*). You'll see why the Konjunktiv II and *würde* turn up in narration that isn't hypothetical at all. At the end you write an *Inhaltsangabe* (plot summary) at B2 level, with Konjunktiv I for what the characters say.

The quotations from *Die Verwandlung* are short and come from the text first published in 1915. Kafka died in 1924, so the work is in the public domain. Editions differ slightly in spelling (*ungeheueren* or *ungeheuren*, old or new *ß*); the quotations here follow modern spelling.

## Kafka and Prague German literature

Franz Kafka was born in Prague in 1883, when the city belonged to Austria-Hungary. Most people in Prague spoke Czech, but a minority, many of them Jewish families like Kafka's, spoke German, went to German schools and read German newspapers. Out of this small, tightly packed world came a remarkable group of writers, often called **[[Prague German literature]]** (*die Prager deutsche Literatur*): Rainer Maria Rilke, Franz Werfel, Max Brod and Kafka himself.

Kafka studied law and spent most of his working life at a semi-state insurance institute for workers' accidents. He wrote at night. Only a few of his texts appeared in his lifetime, among them *Das Urteil* and *Die Verwandlung*. When he died of tuberculosis in 1924, near Vienna, he asked his friend Max Brod to burn his manuscripts. Brod didn't, and published the novels *Der Process* (also spelled *Der Prozess*; *The Trial*), *Das Schloss* and *Der Verschollene* (also known as *Amerika*).

Kafka's German is famously clear: correct, almost official sentences, often long but never chaotic. The content is what unsettles the reader. Ordinary people are caught in situations that make no sense, and nobody in the story seems surprised. That combination gave the language a new adjective: *kafkaesk*.

- *Die Behörde verlangt ein Formular, das man nur mit einer Bescheinigung bekommt, für die man das Formular braucht. Das ist wirklich kafkaesk.* — The authority wants a form that you only get with a certificate for which you need the form. That's truly Kafkaesque.

In everyday German *kafkaesk* describes bureaucratic absurdity and a situation that is threatening but hard to explain. It's a little bookish, but you'll hear it in the news and in complaints about offices.

## The story in brief

*Die Verwandlung* was written in 1912 and published in 1915. It is usually called an *Erzählung* (a story, longer than a Kurzgeschichte); some critics call it a **[[Novelle]]** (*die Novelle*), a classic German form: a prose text of middle length that centres on one extraordinary event. Goethe once described the Novelle as the telling of an *unerhörte Begebenheit*, an unheard-of occurrence. A man waking up as an insect certainly qualifies.

Gregor Samsa is a travelling salesman for a cloth company. He hates his job but keeps it to pay off his parents' debts and to support them and his younger sister Grete. One morning he wakes up transformed into a huge insect. The story has three parts:

1. Gregor tries to get out of bed and go to work. The *Prokurist* (a senior manager) from his firm arrives to ask why he's late. When Gregor finally opens the door, the manager runs away, and Gregor's father drives him back into his room.
2. Grete feeds him and cleans his room; the family doesn't know what to do. When Gregor appears in the living room, his father throws apples at him; one sticks in his back and badly injures him.
3. The family has to earn money and takes in three lodgers. One evening Grete plays the violin, Gregor crawls out to listen, and the lodgers see him. Grete declares that the creature must go. Gregor dies that night. Relieved, the family takes a tram trip into the countryside and makes plans for the future.

Kafka never says what kind of animal Gregor is. The text uses *Ungeziefer*, a collective word for vermin (lice, bedbugs, cockroaches: creatures people want to get rid of). Late in the story the cleaning woman calls him a *Mistkäfer* (dung beetle), which is an insult, not a description. When the book first came out, Kafka asked the publisher not to show the insect on the cover.

## The opening

Here is the first sentence, in modern spelling:

> „Als Gregor Samsa eines Morgens aus unruhigen Träumen erwachte, fand er sich in seinem Bett zu einem ungeheueren Ungeziefer verwandelt.“

> "When Gregor Samsa woke one morning from troubled dreams, he found himself transformed in his bed into a monstrous vermin."

Look at the grammar, all of it B1–B2:

- *Als … erwachte*: *als* for a single event in the past, Präteritum in a subordinate clause.
- *eines Morgens*: genitive of time, "one morning" (like *eines Tages*).
- *fand er sich … verwandelt*: *sich finden* + Partizip II, "found himself transformed". *verwandelt* describes a state (compare the Zustandspassiv: *Er war verwandelt*). The transformation has already happened when the story begins; we never see it.
- *ungeheuer*: monstrous, enormous. *ungeheueren* is Kafka's spelling, with the full ending, and most editions keep it; in today's German you would normally write *ungeheuren*.

The second and third sentences describe what Gregor sees:

> „Er lag auf seinem panzerartig harten Rücken und sah, wenn er den Kopf ein wenig hob, seinen gewölbten, braunen, von bogenförmigen Versteifungen geteilten Bauch, auf dessen Höhe sich die Bettdecke, zum gänzlichen Niedergleiten bereit, kaum noch erhalten konnte.“

> "He lay on his back, hard as armour, and saw, when he lifted his head a little, his domed brown belly, divided by arch-shaped stiffenings, on top of which the blanket, ready to slide off completely, could barely stay in place."

This is exactly the B2 grammar of module 3: an extended participle attribute (*seinen gewölbten, braunen, von bogenförmigen Versteifungen geteilten Bauch* = his belly, which was domed, brown and divided by …), a genitive relative pronoun (*auf dessen Höhe* = on top of which), and a participle-like phrase set off by commas (*zum gänzlichen Niedergleiten bereit*). Kafka describes a nightmare in the precise, nominal German of a report.

> „Seine vielen, im Vergleich zu seinem sonstigen Umfang kläglich dünnen Beine flimmerten ihm hilflos vor den Augen.“

> "His many legs, pitifully thin compared with the rest of his body, flickered helplessly before his eyes."

Another extended attribute: *im Vergleich zu seinem sonstigen Umfang kläglich dünnen* sits between *seine vielen* and *Beine*.

Then comes a change of voice:

> „Was ist mit mir geschehen?“, dachte er. Es war kein Traum.

> "What has happened to me?" he thought. It was no dream.

## Who is telling the story?

Every narrative has a narrator, and German school analysis asks first about the narrative perspective: from where, and with how much knowledge, the story is told. Three types are the standard toolkit:

| type | German | what it does | typical sign |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[[omniscient narrator]]** | *der auktoriale Erzähler* | stands above the story, knows everything, comments, may address the reader | *Unser Held ahnte nicht, dass …* |
| **[[figural narrator]]** | *der personale Erzähler* | third person, but tied to one character: we see and know only what this character sees and knows | thoughts without comment, limited view |
| first-person narrator | *der Ich-Erzähler* | a character tells the story as *ich* | *Ich erinnere mich, dass …* |

*Die Verwandlung* is the textbook case of the figural narrator. The text says *er*, not *ich*, but almost everything is filtered through Gregor: we only know what happens in the next room when Gregor hears it through the door; we never learn what the family really thinks; nobody explains the transformation. The narrator doesn't comment, judge or reassure. That is a large part of the story's effect: we're locked in the room with Gregor.

Only after Gregor's death does the perspective change. The last pages follow the family from outside, in a cooler tone, and the reader notices how quickly they recover.

Now look again at *Es war kein Traum.* Is this the narrator stating a fact, or Gregor realizing it? It could be both, and that ambiguity is typical of the figural narrator. The technique that creates it has its own name.

## Erlebte Rede: thoughts in the narrator's voice

German narrative has several ways to present what a character thinks. Take a modern example: Lena is late for work again.

| technique | example |
|---|---|
| direct thought | *„Ich komme schon wieder zu spät“, dachte Lena. „Was wird der Chef sagen?“* |
| indirect thought | *Lena dachte, dass sie schon wieder zu spät komme, und fragte sich, was der Chef sagen werde.* |
| **[[free indirect speech]]** (*erlebte Rede*) | *Sie kam schon wieder zu spät. Was würde der Chef sagen? Nein, diesmal würde sie sich nicht entschuldigen!* |
| **[[interior monologue]]** (*innerer Monolog*) | *Schon wieder zu spät. Was sagt der Chef? Nein, diesmal entschuldige ich mich nicht.* |

In the erlebte Rede, the content and the tone are the character's (questions, exclamations, *nein*, emotion), but the grammar is the narrator's: third person and the past tense of the story. There is no *dachte sie* and no quotation marks. The reader slips inside the character's head without being told.

How to recognize erlebte Rede:

- third person (*sie, er*) and Präteritum, like the narration around it;
- no verb of thinking or saying, no quotation marks;
- the character's way of speaking: questions, exclamations, modal particles (*doch, ja, wohl*), colloquial words, incomplete sentences;
- time and place words from the character's point of view: *heute, morgen, jetzt, hier* stay as they are, even with a past verb (*Morgen musste sie es ihm sagen*). In indirect speech they would shift (*am nächsten Tag*).

The interior monologue goes one step further: first person, present tense, often fragments and jumps, as if we were hearing the thoughts directly. Writers such as Arthur Schnitzler (*Leutnant Gustl*, 1900) used it for whole stories.

### würde in erlebte Rede: the future seen from the past

Notice *Was würde der Chef sagen?* This *würde* isn't hypothetical. Lena's thought was *Was wird der Chef sagen?* (future); moved into the narrator's past tense, *wird* becomes *würde*: "What would the boss say?" in the sense of "was going to say". English does exactly the same with *will → would*. So in narration, *würde* + infinitive often means the future from a past point of view, not a condition:

- *Bald würde sie die Wohnung verlassen müssen.* — Soon she would have to leave the flat. (= that was going to happen)
- *Der Zug würde nicht warten.* — The train wouldn't wait.

### Konjunktiv II in narration: imagined possibilities

Real Konjunktiv II appears when a character imagines alternatives, and in erlebte Rede these thoughts are especially common. Early in *Die Verwandlung*, Gregor wonders whether he could simply report sick. In paraphrase, his thoughts run like this:

- *Wenn er sich krankmeldete, käme der Chef sicher mit dem Arzt der Krankenkasse.* — If he reported sick, the boss would certainly come with the health insurance doctor.
- *Der Arzt hielte ihn für einen gesunden, aber faulen Menschen.* — The doctor would consider him a healthy but lazy person.

(These two sentences are a paraphrase for this course, not Kafka's words.) The one-word forms (*käme, hielte*) are typical of literary German; in speech you'd say *würde kommen, würde halten*. Gregor's thinking is tragically practical: he has just turned into an insect, and his worry is the doctor's opinion of his work ethic.

Konjunktiv II also carries the many *als ob* comparisons of narrative prose:

- *Die Familie lebte weiter, als wäre nichts geschehen.* — The family went on living as if nothing had happened.

## A text in Kafka's manner

To see erlebte Rede in action, read this short original text, written for the course in the style of the figural narrator. A woman arrives at an office for an appointment.

> Als Frau Berger um neun Uhr das Amt betrat, war der Warteraum leer. Sie zog eine Nummer: 214. Auf der Anzeige stand 17.
>
> Sie setzte sich. Niemand kam, niemand ging. Hatte sie den falschen Eingang genommen? Nein, auf dem Brief stand ja deutlich: Zimmer 3, neun Uhr. Und doch gab es hier kein Zimmer 3, nur Zimmer 2 und Zimmer 4.
>
> Nach einer Stunde öffnete sich eine Tür. Ein Beamter sah sie freundlich an, als hätte er sie erwartet, und fragte, ob sie die Nummer 17 sei. Sie zeigte ihm ihren Zettel. Er nickte, als bestätige das alles, und schloss die Tür wieder.
>
> Was sollte das bedeuten? Würde man sie aufrufen, wenn die 214 an der Reihe war? Und wann würde das sein? Morgen? Nächste Woche? Sie blieb sitzen. Gehen konnte sie jetzt nicht mehr, das wäre unhöflich gewesen.

> When Frau Berger entered the office at nine o'clock, the waiting room was empty. She took a number: 214. The display said 17.
>
> She sat down. No one came, no one left. Had she taken the wrong entrance? No, the letter clearly said: Room 3, nine o'clock. And yet there was no Room 3 here, only Room 2 and Room 4.
>
> After an hour a door opened. An official looked at her kindly, as if he had been expecting her, and asked whether she was number 17. She showed him her slip. He nodded, as if that confirmed everything, and closed the door again.
>
> What was that supposed to mean? Would they call her when 214 was up? And when would that be? Tomorrow? Next week? She stayed seated. She couldn't leave now; that would have been impolite.

Find the techniques:

- Narration: *Sie setzte sich. Nach einer Stunde öffnete sich eine Tür.*
- Erlebte Rede: *Hatte sie den falschen Eingang genommen? Nein, auf dem Brief stand ja deutlich …* (a question, *nein*, the particle *ja*); *Morgen? Nächste Woche?* (*morgen* from her point of view).
- Future from the past: *Würde man sie aufrufen …? Und wann würde das sein?*
- Konjunktiv II: *als hätte er sie erwartet* (as if), *das wäre unhöflich gewesen* (her reasoning).
- Indirect speech with Konjunktiv I: *fragte, ob sie die Nummer 17 sei.* And a Konjunktiv I after *als*: *als bestätige das alles*. After *als* (= as if) with verb second, you will find both Konjunktiv II (*als hätte er*) and, in written style, Konjunktiv I (*als bestätige das*).
- The absurd, *rätselhaft* situation is told calmly; the character's fear is never named. The atmosphere is *beklemmend* (oppressive), and her situation feels *ausweglos* (without a way out). Her alienation (*die Entfremdung*) from the institution that is supposed to serve her is the real topic.

## Interpreting: Deutung and Motiv

German literature lessons distinguish between what happens (*die Handlung*) and what it might mean (*die Deutung*, from *deuten*, to interpret). *Die Verwandlung* has been read in many ways, and a good German essay presents a reading as a reading:

- *Man kann die Verwandlung als Bild für die Entfremdung des modernen Menschen in der Arbeitswelt deuten.* — The transformation can be interpreted as an image of modern people's alienation in the world of work.
- *Eine biografische Deutung verweist auf Kafkas schwieriges Verhältnis zu seinem Vater.* — A biographical interpretation points to Kafka's difficult relationship with his father.
- *Andere Interpreten lesen die Erzählung als Geschichte einer Familie, die sich von einem kranken Mitglied befreit.* — Other interpreters read the story as the story of a family freeing itself from a sick member.

Useful phrases for interpretation: *kann man als … deuten / verstehen / lesen; steht für; ist ein Bild für; verweist auf; legt nahe, dass …; es lässt sich nicht eindeutig sagen, ob …*. Kafka is a good author to practise hedging with, because his texts refuse a single meaning.

A **[[motif]]** (*das Motiv*) is an element that recurs and carries meaning: in *Die Verwandlung*, the door (Gregor's room has three, and who opens or locks them matters), food, the picture of a woman in furs that Gregor protects, and money (the debts, the father's hidden savings, the lodgers' rent). A *Leitmotiv* is a motif that runs through a whole work. Note that *das Motiv* also means "motive" (for a crime) and "subject, motif" (of a photo or painting).

## Writing an Inhaltsangabe at B2

German schools teach the **[[plot summary]]** (*die Inhaltsangabe*) as a fixed text type. At B2 you write it in the present tense, without quotations, in your own neutral words, and you report what characters say with the Konjunktiv I or a nominal phrase.

Structure:

1. *Einleitungssatz*: author, title, text type, year, and the core theme in one sentence, often with a relative clause.
2. *Hauptteil*: the plot in chronological order, the main steps only, present tense (Perfekt for what happened before).
3. Optional *Schluss*: a short, clearly marked interpretation or open question.

Example (original, for the course):

> In Franz Kafkas Erzählung „Die Verwandlung“, die 1915 erschien, geht es um einen jungen Handlungsreisenden, der sich eines Morgens in ein riesiges Insekt verwandelt hat und von seiner Familie immer mehr verstoßen wird.
>
> Gregor Samsa, der mit seinem Gehalt die ganze Familie ernährt, wacht in seinem Bett als Ungeziefer auf. Er will trotzdem zur Arbeit fahren, kann aber kaum aufstehen. Ein Vertreter der Firma erscheint und wirft ihm vor, seine Leistungen seien in letzter Zeit unbefriedigend. Als Gregor die Tür öffnet, flieht der Mann entsetzt. Von nun an lebt Gregor eingeschlossen in seinem Zimmer. Seine Schwester Grete versorgt ihn zunächst, doch der Vater verletzt ihn schwer, als er ihn mit Äpfeln bewirft. Da die Familie Geld braucht, vermietet sie Zimmer an drei Untermieter. Als diese Gregor entdecken, kündigen sie. Grete erklärt, man müsse das Tier loswerden; es könne nicht Gregor sein. In derselben Nacht stirbt Gregor. Erleichtert macht die Familie einen Ausflug und schmiedet Pläne für die Zukunft.

Notice:

- Present tense throughout: *wacht auf, erscheint, flieht, stirbt*. The Präteritum of the story is not copied.
- Perfekt for what happened before the story starts: *der sich … verwandelt hat*.
- Konjunktiv I for reported words: *wirft ihm vor, seine Leistungen seien …; erklärt, man müsse … es könne …*. No direct speech.
- Neutral words. Not "Gregor is a poor man", but what he does.
- Connectors that show order and cause: *von nun an, zunächst, doch, da, als, in derselben Nacht*.

Phrases for the Einleitungssatz: *In … geht es um …; … handelt von …; Im Mittelpunkt steht …; Thema der Erzählung ist …*. Note *handeln von + dative* (*Die Erzählung handelt von einem Mann, der …*); *es geht um + accusative* (*Es geht um einen Mann, der …*).

## Pronunciation

- *Kafka*: stress on the first syllable, KAF-ka. *kafkaesk*: kaf-ka-ESK, stress on the end.
- *die Novelle*: no-WEL-le, *v* as in English *v* (a loanword from Italian). The same *v* in *das Motiv* (mo-TIEF, final *v* sounds like *f*).
- *das Ungeziefer*: UN-ge-zie-fer, stress on *un-*.
- *absurd*: ap-SURT, stress on the second syllable.

## Common mistakes

- Writing the Inhaltsangabe in the past because the story is in the past: ~~Gregor wachte als Käfer auf.~~ → *Gregor wacht als Käfer auf.*
- Copying direct speech into a summary: ~~Grete sagt: „Wir müssen es loswerden.“~~ → *Grete erklärt, man müsse es loswerden.*
- Reading every *würde* in a story as a condition. *Was würde der Chef sagen?* in narration usually means "was going to say".
- Shifting time words in erlebte Rede: in *Morgen musste sie es ihm sagen*, *morgen* stays; only indirect speech changes it to *am nächsten Tag*.
- Confusing the narrator with the author. In *Die Verwandlung*, the narrator is a voice tied to Gregor; Kafka is the writer.
- *deuten* vs *bedeuten*: *Was bedeutet das?* (what does it mean?) vs *Wie deutest du das?* (how do you interpret it?). *deuten auf* also means "to point to": *Alles deutet darauf hin, dass …*.
- *Verwandlung* vs *Veränderung*: *verwandeln* is a complete change into something else (*in einen Käfer verwandelt*); *verändern* is any change (*Die Stadt hat sich verändert*).

## Key points

- Kafka (1883–1924) belonged to the German-speaking minority of Prague; *Die Verwandlung* (1915) is told in calm, precise German about an absurd event.
- The figural narrator (*personaler Erzähler*) tells the story in the third person but limits it to one character's view; the omniscient narrator (*auktorialer Erzähler*) knows and comments on everything.
- Erlebte Rede: a character's thoughts in third person and Präteritum, without *dachte er* or quotation marks, with the character's questions, exclamations, particles and *heute/morgen/hier*.
- In narration, *würde* + infinitive often means the future seen from the past; real Konjunktiv II shows imagined alternatives and *als ob* comparisons.
- An Inhaltsangabe is in the present tense, neutral, without quotations, with Konjunktiv I for what characters say, and starts with a sentence naming author, title, text type, year and theme.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Das Drama: reading a scene from Schiller and Büchner
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

German-speaking countries have one of the densest theatre landscapes in the world: Germany alone has well over a hundred publicly funded theatres, many cities have their own ensemble, and the classics of the 18th and 19th centuries are performed every season. Almost every pupil who takes the Abitur or the Matura reads at least one classical play.

This lesson gives you the vocabulary to talk about a play (*das Drama*), shows how a classical drama is built, and then reads two short passages from plays that are still on every school list: the opening of Friedrich Schiller's *Kabale und Liebe* (1784) and a speech from Georg Büchner's *Woyzeck* (written 1836–37). Both authors died long ago (Schiller in 1805, Büchner in 1837), so their texts are in the public domain. The quotations follow modern spelling, as most school editions do.

The language is more than two hundred years old, so you'll also learn to recognize the old and spoken forms you meet in these texts: *hätt, ihm's, ward, dem Manne*. You don't need to use them; you need to read them.

## Talking about a play

| German | English | note |
|---|---|---|
| *das Drama, die Dramen* | play, drama | also a dramatic situation: *Das ist doch kein Drama!* (It's not a big deal!) |
| *die Tragödie / das Trauerspiel* | tragedy | *Trauerspiel* is the older German word, used in titles |
| *die Komödie / das Lustspiel* | comedy | |
| *der Dramatiker, die Dramatikerin* | playwright | |
| *der Akt / der Aufzug* | act | a classical play has five, a comedy often three |
| *die Szene / der Auftritt* | scene | *Auftritt* also means an entrance or a stage appearance |
| *die Regieanweisung* | stage direction | printed in italics or brackets |
| *der Dialog / der Monolog* | dialogue / monologue | a monologue is one character speaking alone |
| *die Hauptrolle / die Nebenrolle* | leading role / supporting role | *Sie spielt die Hauptrolle.* |
| *das Bühnenbild* | set, stage design | |
| *die Intrige* | intrigue, plot (scheme) | |
| *der Bösewicht* | villain | a little old-fashioned or humorous today |

A few examples in context:

- *In der Regieanweisung steht, dass die Mutter am Fenster sitzt.* — The stage direction says that the mother is sitting at the window.
- *Im dritten Akt spinnt der Sekretär eine Intrige gegen das Liebespaar.* — In the third act the secretary hatches a plot against the lovers.
- *Das Bühnenbild war sehr reduziert: ein Tisch, zwei Stühle, eine Tür.* — The set was very minimal: a table, two chairs, a door.
- *Im zweiten Akt hat Lady Milford ihren ersten Auftritt.* — In the second act Lady Milford makes her first appearance.

**[[Act]]** (*der Akt*) and **[[scene]]** (*die Szene*) are the units of a printed play. In older German plays a new scene, called *Auftritt*, begins whenever a character enters or leaves. A **[[stage direction]]** (*die Regieanweisung*) tells the actors what to do and describes the setting; in the reading below it's in italics. A **[[monologue]]** (*der Monolog*) is a speech by a character alone on stage, often at a moment of decision.

## How a classical drama is built

A **[[tragedy]]** (*die Tragödie*) ends in catastrophe, usually the death of the main character; a comedy ends happily, often with a wedding. In the 19th century the writer Gustav Freytag described the "classical" five-act tragedy as a pyramid, and German schools still use his terms:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: The five parts of a classical tragedy
  accDescr: Act 1 is the exposition, which introduces the characters and the conflict. Act 2 is the rising action, where the conflict grows. Act 3 is the climax or turning point. Act 4 is the falling action, which delays the end. Act 5 is the catastrophe, the tragic ending.
  A["1. Exposition: characters and conflict"] --> B["2. Steigende Handlung: the conflict grows"]
  B --> C["3. Höhepunkt / Wendepunkt: the climax"]
  C --> D["4. Fallende Handlung: delay"]
  D --> E["5. Katastrophe: the tragic end"]
```

This model fits a **[[closed drama]]** (*das geschlossene Drama*): five acts, a small number of characters, one main plot, a short span of time, a strict cause-and-effect chain and elevated language. Schiller's plays are close to it. The **[[open drama]]** (*das offene Drama*) breaks these rules: many short scenes that can stand on their own, jumps in time and place, ordinary or dialect language, and often no clear ending. *Woyzeck* is the classic example.

An older rule, the **[[Ständeklausel]]** (the "rule of rank"), said that only kings and nobles could be the heroes of a tragedy; ordinary people belonged in comedy. In the 18th century German writers broke this rule with the **[[bourgeois tragedy]]** (*das bürgerliche Trauerspiel*): a tragedy about middle-class people, their families, their morals and their conflict with the nobility. Gotthold Ephraim Lessing wrote the first famous ones; *Kabale und Liebe* is subtitled *Ein bürgerliches Trauerspiel*.

## Two periods in two paragraphs

**[[Sturm und Drang]]** (Storm and Stress, about 1765–1785) was a movement of young writers who rebelled against the rule-bound literature of the Enlightenment and against the absolutist princes of their day. They celebrated feeling, nature, freedom and the "genius" who makes his own rules. The young Goethe (*Die Leiden des jungen Werthers*, 1774) and the young Schiller (*Die Räuber*, 1781; *Kabale und Liebe*, 1784) are its best-known names. Their characters speak in passionate, broken, exclamatory prose.

**[[Vormärz]]** ("before March", roughly 1830–1848) is the name for the years before the March Revolution of 1848, when writers fought censorship and demanded political freedom and social justice. Georg Büchner (1813–1837) was a medical student who co-wrote a revolutionary pamphlet for the peasants of Hesse, *Der Hessische Landbote* (1834), with the slogan *Friede den Hütten! Krieg den Palästen!* (Peace to the huts! War on the palaces!). He had to flee to Strasbourg and died in Zurich of typhus at 23. *Woyzeck* stayed an unordered set of fragments; Karl Emil Franzos first published it in 1875 (in a periodical; in book form in 1879), and it was first performed in 1913.

## Schiller, Kabale und Liebe

*die Kabale* is an old word for an intrigue (*eine Intrige*). The play's original title was *Luise Millerin*. Its story in brief:

Ferdinand von Walter, a young major and the son of the powerful *Präsident* at a small German court, loves Luise Miller, the daughter of a town musician. His father wants him to marry Lady Milford, the prince's mistress, for political reasons. The father's secretary Wurm, who wants Luise for himself, invents an intrigue: Luise's parents are arrested, and to save them she must write a love letter to a ridiculous courtier and swear to say she wrote it freely. Ferdinand finds the letter and believes it. He poisons a glass of lemonade, and they both drink. Only as she is dying does Luise tell him the truth. Wurm is the play's *Bösewicht*, and the class barrier between the nobleman and the musician's daughter is the real tragic force.

### Erster Akt, erste Szene

The play opens in the musician's house. Miller has heard the gossip about his daughter and the young nobleman.

> *Zimmer beim Musikus. Miller steht eben vom Sessel auf, und stellt seine Violoncell auf die Seite. An einem Tisch sitzt Frau Millerin noch im Nachtgewand, und trinkt ihren Kaffee.*
>
> MILLER (*schnell auf und ab gehend*). Einmal für allemal. Der Handel wird ernsthaft. Meine Tochter kommt mit dem Baron ins Geschrei. Mein Haus wird verrufen. Der Präsident bekommt Wind, und – kurz und gut, ich biete dem Junker aus.
>
> FRAU. Du hast ihn nicht in dein Haus geschwatzt – hast ihm deine Tochter nicht nachgeworfen.
>
> MILLER. Hab ihn nicht in mein Haus geschwatzt – hab ihm's Mädel nicht nachgeworfen; wer nimmt Notiz davon? – Ich war Herr im Haus. Ich hätt meine Tochter mehr koram nehmen sollen. Ich hätt dem Major besser auftrumpfen sollen – oder hätt gleich alles Seiner Exzellenz dem Herrn Papa stecken sollen. Der junge Baron bringt's mit einem Wischer hinaus, das muss ich wissen, und alles Wetter kommt über den Geiger.
>
> FRAU (*schlürft eine Tasse aus*). Possen! Geschwätz! Was kann über dich kommen? Wer kann dir was anhaben? Du gehst deiner Profession nach, und raffst Scholaren zusammen, wo sie zu kriegen sind.

(Friedrich Schiller, *Kabale und Liebe*, 1784, act I, scene 1, modern spelling.)

Notes on the language:

- *der Musikus*: old word for a musician; *das Violoncell* = das Cello; *das Nachtgewand* = nightdress.
- *Einmal für allemal*: "once and for all" (today *ein für alle Mal*).
- *Der Handel wird ernsthaft*: here *der Handel* means "the affair, the business", not "trade".
- *ins Geschrei kommen*: to get talked about (today *ins Gerede kommen*).
- *Wind bekommen* (von etwas): to get wind of something; still used today.
- *ich biete dem Junker aus*: old usage, roughly "I'll show the young gentleman the door". *der Junker* = a young nobleman.
- *in sein Haus schwatzen*: to talk someone into the house; *jemandem etwas nachwerfen*: to throw something at someone's feet (here: to push his daughter on him).
- *koram nehmen*: from Latin *coram*, "to take to task, to call to account".
- *auftrumpfen*: here, to stand up to someone forcefully.
- *jemandem etwas stecken*: to tip someone off (still colloquial today: *Wer hat dir das gesteckt?*).
- *mit einem Wischer hinausbringen*: to get off with a mere telling-off (*der Wischer* = a reprimand).
- *alles Wetter kommt über den Geiger*: the whole storm will break over the fiddler, i.e. over me.
- *Possen!*: nonsense! *was anhaben*: to harm you (*jemandem etwas anhaben können*). *die Scholaren*: pupils (here: music pupils).

### The same scene in today's German

A modern paraphrase, written for this course:

> MILLER. Jetzt reicht es. Die Sache wird ernst. Die Leute reden schon über meine Tochter und den Baron, und unser Haus bekommt einen schlechten Ruf. Wenn der Präsident davon erfährt … Kurz gesagt: Ich werfe den jungen Herrn raus.
>
> FRAU. Du hast ihn doch nicht eingeladen und hast ihm deine Tochter auch nicht angeboten.
>
> MILLER. Ja, ich habe ihn nicht eingeladen und ihm das Mädchen nicht angeboten, aber wen interessiert das? Ich war der Herr im Haus. Ich hätte meine Tochter strenger zur Rede stellen sollen. Ich hätte dem Major deutlicher die Meinung sagen sollen, oder ich hätte gleich alles seinem Vater erzählen sollen. Der junge Baron kommt mit einer Ermahnung davon, das weiß ich genau, und der ganze Ärger landet bei mir, dem Musiker.
>
> FRAU. Unsinn! Gerede! Was soll dir denn passieren? Wer kann dir schon etwas tun? Du machst deine Arbeit und suchst dir Schüler, wo du sie findest.

English:

> MILLER. That's enough now. This is getting serious. People are already talking about my daughter and the baron, and our house is getting a bad name. If the President hears about it … In short: I'm throwing the young gentleman out.
>
> WIFE. You didn't invite him, and you didn't offer him your daughter either.
>
> MILLER. Yes, I didn't invite him and I didn't offer him the girl, but who cares? I was the master of the house. I should have taken my daughter to task more strictly. I should have told the major plainly what I thought, or I should have told his father everything straight away. The young baron will get off with a warning, I know that for sure, and all the trouble will land on me, the musician.
>
> WIFE. Nonsense! Gossip! What could happen to you? Who can do anything to you? You do your job and find pupils wherever you can.

Look at the grammar Miller uses: *Ich hätt meine Tochter mehr koram nehmen sollen* is the Konjunktiv II past of a modal verb with the double infinitive, exactly the structure of modern *Ich hätte … zur Rede stellen sollen* (I should have …). Regret in the 18th century sounds like regret today.

The scene is a perfect exposition: in a few lines we learn the social setting (a musician's household), the conflict (a nobleman and a middle-class girl), the danger (the President) and Miller's character (proud, hot-tempered, afraid). The wife's sharp, practical answers create the contrast that keeps the dialogue alive.

## Old and spoken forms you'll meet

Classical texts show a few forms that look strange today. Here are the most common.

### Dropped e and apostrophes (elision)

Spoken German swallows unstressed *e* and short words, and older texts write this down: *hätt* = *hätte*, *hab* = *habe*, *glaub'* = *glaube*, *Leut'* = *Leute*, *ihm's* = *ihm das*, *bringt's* = *bringt es*, *hast's* = *hast es*. Modern German still does this in speech and informal writing (*Wie geht's? Ich hab's!*). This shortening is called **[[elision]]**.

### Dative -e

Older German often adds *-e* to masculine and neuter nouns in the dative singular: *dem Manne, dem Kinde, im Hause, am Tage, auf dem Lande*. Today it survives in set phrases: *nach Hause, zu Hause, im Grunde, im Laufe der Zeit, zum Tode verurteilt, auf dem Lande* (slightly formal).

### ward

An old Präteritum of *werden*, for *wurde* in the singular: *Es ward Nacht* (Night fell). *Er ward gefangen genommen* (He was taken prisoner). You'll find it in poems, fairy tales and the Bible; nobody uses it in normal speech.

### Other old forms

The genitive object after some verbs (*Er bedarf der Ruhe* = He needs rest; *Sie gedachten der Toten* = They remembered the dead), and old words: *das Mädel* (girl, today regional), *der Junker*, *die Profession* (trade, occupation).

## Büchner, Woyzeck

Franz Woyzeck is a poor soldier who earns extra money by shaving his captain and by letting a doctor use him for nutrition experiments (he must eat only peas). He has a child with Marie, but they aren't married. When Marie begins an affair with a drum major, Woyzeck, humiliated and increasingly confused, kills her. The play is based on a real case: in 1821 a former soldier called Johann Christian Woyzeck killed his lover in Leipzig and was executed in 1824 after a long dispute about whether he was of sound mind.

In an early scene the captain, whom Woyzeck is shaving, lectures him about morality: Woyzeck has a child "without the blessing of the Church". Woyzeck answers:

> WOYZECK. Wir arme Leut'. Sehn Sie, Herr Hauptmann, Geld, Geld. Wer kein Geld hat. – Da setz einmal einer seinesgleichen auf die Moral in der Welt. Man hat auch sein Fleisch und Blut. Unsereins ist doch einmal unselig in der und der andern Welt, ich glaub', wenn wir in Himmel kämen, so müssten wir donnern helfen.

(Georg Büchner, *Woyzeck*, scene with the captain, modern spelling; the order and wording of the fragments vary between editions.)

> WOYZECK. Us poor people. You see, Captain, money, money. Whoever has no money. – Just try bringing people like us into the world morally. We're flesh and blood too. People like us are wretched in this world and the next; I think if we went to heaven, we'd have to help with the thunder.

Notes:

- *Wir arme Leut'*: today's standard would usually be *Wir armen Leute* (after *wir*, the weak ending *-en* is the more common one), and *Leut'* drops the final *e*: Woyzeck speaks a regional, spoken German.
- *Sehn Sie* = *Sehen Sie*; *ich glaub'* = *ich glaube*; *in Himmel* = *in den Himmel*.
- *seinesgleichen*: people like him (*unseresgleichen*, *Ihresgleichen*: people like us, like you). The sentence is broken and hard to translate; it means something like "just try to bring up people of our kind according to morality".
- *unsereins*: people like us, the likes of us (colloquial, still used).
- *in der und der andern Welt*: in this world and in the next.
- *wenn wir in Himmel kämen, so müssten wir donnern helfen*: Konjunktiv II for an imagined situation, with the old *so* introducing the main clause after a *wenn* clause (today simply *dann* or nothing).

Compare the two plays. Schiller's Miller is angry but articulate; his sentences are complete and rhetorical. Woyzeck's sentences break off (*Wer kein Geld hat. –*), repeat (*Geld, Geld*) and jump. Büchner gives a poor man's broken speech the dignity of tragedy, which no German play had done so radically before.

## A conversation after the theatre

Two friends have just seen a modern production of *Woyzeck*.

> SINA: Und? Wie fandest du es?
>
> MALTE: Ehrlich gesagt hat mich das Bühnenbild mehr beeindruckt als das Stück. Diese leere, graue Fläche, nur eine Tür, durch die alle kommen und gehen …
>
> SINA: Das passt doch zum offenen Drama. Es gibt ja keine richtigen Akte, nur Szenen, die man beinahe beliebig ordnen kann.
>
> MALTE: Stimmt, aber ich hatte manchmal Mühe, der Handlung zu folgen. Im Original ist Woyzeck kein Bösewicht, und hier wirkte er von Anfang an gefährlich.
>
> SINA: Das fand ich gerade gut. Der Schauspieler in der Hauptrolle hat gezeigt, wie die anderen ihn kaputtmachen: der Hauptmann mit seiner Moral, der Doktor mit seinen Experimenten.
>
> MALTE: Tragisch ist es jedenfalls. Und erschreckend aktuell, wenn man an Leute denkt, die drei Jobs haben und trotzdem kein Geld.

English:

> SINA: So? What did you think?
>
> MALTE: Honestly, the set impressed me more than the play. That empty grey surface, just one door that everyone comes and goes through …
>
> SINA: That fits the open drama, though. There aren't any real acts, only scenes you can arrange almost any way you like.
>
> MALTE: True, but sometimes I found it hard to follow the plot. In the original Woyzeck isn't a villain, and here he seemed dangerous from the start.
>
> SINA: That's exactly what I liked. The actor in the lead role showed how the others destroy him: the captain with his morals, the doctor with his experiments.
>
> MALTE: It's tragic, anyway. And frighteningly relevant, when you think of people who have three jobs and still no money.

*tragisch* (tragic) is the adjective to *die Tragödie*. In everyday German it's used for any sad event, but in a literature class it means the hero's fall is unavoidable: whatever Luise or Woyzeck do, the world around them destroys them.

## Pronunciation

- *das Drama*: DRAH-ma, long *a*. Plural *die Dramen*. *der Dramatiker*: dra-MAH-ti-ker.
- *die Tragödie*: tra-GÖ-dje, three syllables (the final *-ie* sounds like *-je*); *die Komödie*: ko-MÖ-dje.
- *die Intrige*: in-TRIE-ge, a French loan with a long *i*.
- *der Monolog*: mo-no-LOHK, stress on the end, final *g* like *k*.
- *Woyzeck*: VOI-tsek; *Büchner*: BÜCH-ner, with the *ch* of *ich*.

## Common mistakes

- *der Akt* vs *die Akte*: *der Akt* is an act of a play (plural *die Akte*); *die Akte* is a file (plural *die Akten*). *Im dritten Akt*, but *Die Akte liegt auf dem Tisch.*
- *die Szene* in everyday German also means "the scene" in the sense of a subculture (*die Kunstszene*) or a row: *Mach keine Szene!* (Don't make a scene!).
- *das Drama* in everyday speech is a fuss: *Mach kein Drama daraus.* Don't confuse it with *der Dramatiker* (the playwright).
- Reading *ward* as a mistake for *war*. It means *wurde*.
- Reading *hätt* or *glaub'* as errors in an old text. They show spoken language, and writers used them on purpose.
- *Kabale und Liebe* is not "cable and love": *die Kabale* is an intrigue.

## Key points

- A play has acts (*Akte, Aufzüge*) and scenes (*Szenen, Auftritte*); stage directions (*Regieanweisungen*) describe the setting and actions.
- The closed drama (five acts, unity, elevated language) follows the pattern exposition – rising action – climax – falling action – catastrophe; the open drama (*Woyzeck*) uses loose, short scenes.
- The bourgeois tragedy put middle-class people at the centre of a tragedy and broke the old Ständeklausel. *Kabale und Liebe* (Sturm und Drang, 1784) is a classic example.
- Büchner's *Woyzeck* (Vormärz, fragment from 1836–37) gives the speech of a poor soldier tragic weight.
- Old and spoken forms: elision (*hätt, ihm's, glaub'*), dative *-e* (*dem Manne, nach Hause*), *ward* = *wurde*.

lessons.title: Europe and federalism: who decides what?
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Who decides when the summer holidays start in Munich? Who sets the tax rate in Zug? Who made mobile roaming free across Europe? In the German-speaking countries the answer is almost never simply "the government". Germany, Austria and Switzerland are all federal states, and Germany and Austria are also members of the European Union. Power is shared between several levels, and news reports constantly move between them.

This lesson explains the political structure of the three countries and of the EU, shows why the word *Bundesrat* means three different things, and practises the B2 grammar that texts about institutions are made of: the passive (*Das Parlament wird alle fünf Jahre gewählt*), relative clauses with prepositions (*das Gremium, in dem die Länder vertreten sind*) and the nominal style (*die Umsetzung der Richtlinie in nationales Recht*). In B1 you saw how a law passes through the Bundestag; here the focus is on the levels of power and who is responsible for what.

## Federalism: power on several levels

**[[Federalism]]** (*der Föderalismus*) means that a state is made up of member states that have their own parliaments, governments and areas of responsibility, while the federal level (*der Bund*) is responsible for the rest. The adjective is *föderal*: *Deutschland ist ein föderaler Staat* (Germany is a federal state). Its opposite is the centralized state (*der Zentralstaat*), such as France, where most decisions are made in the capital.

The member states are called *Länder* in Germany and Austria (*das Bundesland, die Bundesländer* in everyday speech) and *Kantone* in Switzerland. Each has its own government: *die Landesregierung* in Germany and Austria, usually *der Regierungsrat* in a Swiss canton. The government of the whole country is *die Bundesregierung* (Germany, Austria); in Switzerland, as you'll see, it has a different name.

The reasons for federalism differ. Switzerland grew out of an alliance of independent cantons, which still see themselves as the original holders of power. Germany's Länder are partly older than the German state, and after 1945 the Allies also wanted a decentralized Germany, so that power could never again be concentrated in one place. Austria is the most centralized of the three: its nine Länder have fewer powers than German Länder or Swiss cantons.

## Three countries side by side

| | Germany | Austria | Switzerland |
|---|---|---|---|
| member states | 16 Länder | 9 Länder | 26 Kantone |
| head of a member state | *Ministerpräsident(in)* (in Berlin, Hamburg, Bremen a mayor) | *Landeshauptmann / Landeshauptfrau* | a president of the cantonal government |
| parliament: chamber of the people | *der Bundestag* | *der Nationalrat* (183 members) | *der Nationalrat* (200 members) |
| parliament: chamber of the member states | *der Bundesrat* | *der Bundesrat* | *der Ständerat* (46 seats: 2 per canton, 1 for each of the six former half-cantons) |
| federal government | *die Bundesregierung*, led by the *Bundeskanzler(in)* | *die Bundesregierung*, led by the *Bundeskanzler(in)* | *der Bundesrat*: seven equal members |
| head of state | *Bundespräsident(in)*, elected by the Bundesversammlung | *Bundespräsident(in)*, elected directly by the people | none in the usual sense; the *Bundespräsident(in)* is one of the seven, for one year |

### One word, three institutions: der Bundesrat

The table hides a trap. *Der Bundesrat* exists in all three countries, but it isn't the same thing:

- In Germany the Bundesrat is the chamber through which the Länder take part in federal law-making. Its members aren't elected to it: they are members of the Land governments. Many laws need its consent.
- In Austria the Bundesrat is also the chamber of the Länder, but its members are sent by the Land parliaments (*Landtage*), and it is much weaker: in most cases the Nationalrat can override it.
- In Switzerland the Bundesrat is the federal government itself: seven ministers (*Bundesrätinnen und Bundesräte*) elected by parliament, who decide together as a college. One of them is *Bundespräsident(in)* for one year, mainly to chair the meetings and represent the country.

The Swiss and Austrian *Nationalrat* is the chamber elected by the people, comparable to the Bundestag. A member of it is also called *Nationalrat* or *Nationalrätin*: *Die Nationalrätin aus Bern hat einen Vorschlag eingebracht.* (The member of the National Council from Bern put forward a proposal.)

In Switzerland the two chambers together form the *Bundesversammlung* (Federal Assembly), and the people have the final word on many questions in referendums, several times a year. In Germany the *Bundesversammlung* is something else again: an assembly that meets only to elect the President.

## Who decides what?

In Germany, the Länder are responsible above all for schools and universities, the police and culture. That's why the school system differs from Land to Land, and why each Land sets its own school holidays. (A committee of the Länder education ministers coordinates the dates, so that not all families are on the motorway in the same week.) The Bund is responsible for foreign policy, defence, citizenship and most of the big laws on the economy, work and social security.

Swiss cantons have even more power: each has its own constitution, sets its own income tax rates (which is why rich people and companies are attracted to low-tax cantons such as Zug) and organizes its own schools. The municipalities (*Gemeinden*) also have considerable autonomy.

Behind this distribution stands the **[[subsidiarity principle]]** (*das Subsidiaritätsprinzip*): a task should be done at the lowest level that can do it well. The town decides about its swimming pool, the Land about its schools, the Bund about the army. The same principle appears in the EU treaties: the EU should act only when the member states can't achieve a goal as well on their own.

Language for describing responsibility:

- *Für die Schulen sind die Länder zuständig.* — The Länder are responsible for schools.
- *Die Polizei ist Ländersache.* — Policing is a matter for the Länder.
- *Das fällt in die Zuständigkeit des Bundes.* — That falls within the competence of the federal government.
- *Darüber entscheiden die Kantone selbst.* — The cantons decide that themselves.
- *Der Bund kann den Ländern hier nichts vorschreiben.* — The federal government can't tell the Länder what to do here.

## The European Union

The European Union (*die Europäische Union, die EU*) has 27 member states (*Mitgliedstaaten*). Germany is one of the six founding members: in 1957 it signed the Treaties of Rome with France, Italy and the Benelux countries. Austria joined in 1995 after a referendum. Switzerland isn't a member; it is linked to the EU by many bilateral treaties and takes part in the Schengen area. In 2020 the United Kingdom became the first member state to leave the EU (*aus der EU austreten*). The departure (*der Austritt*) is known everywhere by its English nickname, *der Brexit*.

The EU is neither a federal state nor an ordinary international organization. Its members have transferred part of their sovereignty (*die Souveränität*) to common institutions, especially for the single market (*der Binnenmarkt*): the area in which goods, services, capital and people can move freely. The free movement of people, *die Freizügigkeit*, means that EU citizens may live and work in any member state.

### The institutions

| institution | German | who sits there | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| European Parliament | *das Europäische Parlament* | 720 members, elected every five years (96 from Germany, 20 from Austria) | decides on laws and the budget together with the Council; elects the President of the Commission |
| European Commission | *die Europäische Kommission* | one commissioner per member state | proposes laws, carries out decisions, watches over the treaties |
| Council of the EU | *der Rat der Europäischen Union* | ministers of the member states, depending on the topic | decides on laws together with Parliament |
| European Council | *der Europäische Rat* | heads of state or government | sets the general direction; doesn't pass laws |
| Court of Justice | *der Gerichtshof der Europäischen Union* | judges from all member states (in Luxembourg) | interprets EU law |
| European Central Bank | *die Europäische Zentralbank* | (in Frankfurt am Main) | monetary policy for the euro |

Three councils are easily confused. The **[[Council of the EU]]** is made up of ministers (the agriculture ministers for agriculture, and so on); the **[[European Council]]** is the summit of heads of state and government. The *Europarat* (Council of Europe) in Strasbourg isn't part of the EU at all: it is an older organization with 46 member states, best known for the European Convention on Human Rights.

### How an EU law is made

The process is a good place to practise the passive:

1. *Ein Gesetzesvorschlag wird von der Kommission vorgelegt.* Only the Commission can formally propose a law.
2. *Der Vorschlag wird im Parlament und im Rat beraten.* Both can propose changes.
3. *Wenn sich beide einigen, wird das Gesetz verabschiedet.*
4. *Eine Verordnung gilt dann unmittelbar in allen Mitgliedstaaten. Eine Richtlinie muss erst in nationales Recht umgesetzt werden.*

The last step contains an important distinction. An **[[EU regulation]]** (*die Verordnung*) applies directly in every member state, like a national law: the end of mobile roaming charges in 2017 was achieved this way. An **[[EU directive]]** (*die Richtlinie*) sets a goal, and each member state must pass its own law to reach it by a deadline: the ban on some single-use plastic products, such as plastic straws, came as a directive, which was then implemented in national law.

In the nominal style of news reports: *Nach der Verabschiedung der Richtlinie haben die Mitgliedstaaten zwei Jahre Zeit für die Umsetzung.* (After the directive has been adopted, the member states have two years to implement it.) Or with *sein + zu*: *Die Richtlinie ist bis 2027 umzusetzen.* (The directive must be implemented by 2027.)

### Growing and shrinking

The EU has grown in several waves of enlargement (*die Erweiterung*). The biggest came in 2004, when ten countries, most of them in Central and Eastern Europe, joined at once; the most recent accession (*der Beitritt*) was Croatia's in 2013. Several countries are candidates.

- *Österreich ist der EU 1995 beigetreten.* — Austria joined the EU in 1995. (*beitreten* + dative, with *sein*)
- *Großbritannien ist 2020 aus der EU ausgetreten.* — Britain left the EU in 2020. (*austreten aus* + dative, with *sein*)
- *Der Beitritt neuer Mitgliedstaaten muss von allen bisherigen Mitgliedern gebilligt werden.* — The accession of new member states must be approved by all existing members.

*austreten* is also used for leaving any organization: *aus der Kirche austreten* (to leave the Church officially, which in Germany ends the church tax), *aus einem Verein austreten* (to leave a club). The noun is *der Austritt*: *Ich habe meinen Austritt aus dem Fitnessstudio erklärt.*

## Germany's role in the EU

Germany has the largest population and the largest economy in the EU, and so the most seats in Parliament. It pays more into the EU budget than it gets back (it is a *Nettozahler*, a net contributor). For decades, important steps in European integration were prepared jointly by Germany and France, often described as the "Franco-German engine" (*der deutsch-französische Motor*). At the same time, Germany's own federalism shapes its EU policy: the Bundesrat must be informed about EU matters, and on topics that belong to the Länder, such as education, the Länder have a say in the German position.

## Text: Ein Land, drei Ebenen

A radio programme explains to listeners why a simple question has a complicated answer. Original text for the course.

> Frau Yilmaz aus Köln möchte wissen, warum ihre Tochter in Nordrhein-Westfalen andere Sommerferien hat als die Cousine in Bayern. Die Antwort führt mitten in den deutschen Föderalismus.
>
> Für die Schulen sind in Deutschland die Länder zuständig. Jede Landesregierung entscheidet selbst über Lehrpläne, Schulformen und eben auch über die Ferien. Damit nicht alle Familien gleichzeitig in den Urlaub fahren, werden die Termine allerdings von den Kultusministern der Länder abgestimmt, und zwar für mehrere Jahre im Voraus. Bayern und Baden-Württemberg, die ihre Ferien traditionell spät beginnen, nehmen an diesem Wechsel nicht teil.
>
> Und was hat Brüssel damit zu tun? In diesem Fall nichts. Die Europäische Union hat in der Bildungspolitik kaum Kompetenzen; sie fördert zwar Austauschprogramme wie Erasmus, über Schulferien entscheidet sie aber nicht. Anders ist es beim Handy-Roaming, das die Familie im Urlaub in Italien nutzen wird: Dass dafür keine zusätzlichen Gebühren mehr anfallen, wurde durch eine EU-Verordnung geregelt, die in allen Mitgliedstaaten unmittelbar gilt.
>
> Man könnte also sagen: Wann die Familie fährt, bestimmt das Land. Was das Telefonieren am Strand kostet, bestimmt die EU.

English:

> Ms Yilmaz from Cologne would like to know why her daughter in North Rhine-Westphalia has different summer holidays from her cousin in Bavaria. The answer leads straight into German federalism.
>
> In Germany, the Länder are responsible for schools. Each Land government decides for itself on curricula, types of school and, indeed, the holidays. So that not all families go on holiday at the same time, though, the dates are coordinated by the Länder education ministers, several years in advance. Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg, which traditionally start their holidays late, don't take part in this rotation.
>
> And what does Brussels have to do with it? In this case, nothing. The European Union has hardly any powers in education policy; it does fund exchange programmes such as Erasmus, but it doesn't decide on school holidays. It's different for the mobile roaming the family will use on holiday in Italy: the fact that there are no longer any extra charges for it was settled by an EU regulation, which applies directly in all member states.
>
> So you could say: when the family goes is decided by the Land. What it costs to phone from the beach is decided by the EU.

Grammar to notice: the passive (*werden … abgestimmt; wurde … geregelt*), relative clauses (*die ihre Ferien traditionell spät beginnen; das die Familie … nutzen wird; die … gilt*), a *dass* clause as subject (*Dass … keine Gebühren mehr anfallen, wurde … geregelt*), *zwar … aber* for concession, and indirect questions in the Vorfeld (*Wann die Familie fährt, bestimmt das Land*). *Brüssel* is shorthand for the EU institutions, just as *Berlin* stands for the federal government and *Bern* for the Swiss one.

## Describing an institution in B2 style

When you describe an institution in an essay or a presentation, three structures do most of the work.

Passive for what is done:

- *Der Nationalrat wird alle fünf Jahre vom Volk gewählt.* — The National Council is elected by the people every five years. (Austria)
- *Die Mitglieder der Kommission werden von den Mitgliedstaaten vorgeschlagen.*

Relative clauses with prepositions to define:

- *Der Ständerat ist die Kammer, in der die Kantone vertreten sind.* — The Council of States is the chamber in which the cantons are represented.
- *Die Kommission ist das Organ, von dem die Gesetzesvorschläge kommen.*

Nominal style for compact information:

- *Seit dem Beitritt Österreichs zur EU …* — Since Austria's accession to the EU …
- *Die Wahrung der Souveränität der Kantone ist in der Schweiz ein zentrales Anliegen.* — Preserving the sovereignty of the cantons is a central concern in Switzerland.

## Pronunciation

- *der Föderalismus*: fö-de-ra-LIS-mus; *föderal*: fö-de-RAHL.
- *die Souveränität*: su-ve-rä-ni-TÄT, from French: *ou* sounds like *u*, *v* like English *v*.
- *die Kommission*: ko-mi-SJOHN.
- *die Freizügigkeit*: FREI-tsü-gich-keit; the *-ig-* is said like *ich*.

## Common mistakes

- Assuming *der Bundesrat* is the same everywhere. In Switzerland it's the government; in Germany and Austria it's the chamber of the Länder.
- Confusing *der Europäische Rat* (heads of government, EU), *der Rat der EU* (ministers, EU) and *der Europarat* (Council of Europe, not EU).
- *die EU* is feminine (*die Union*): *in der EU, aus der EU, der EU beitreten.*
- Wrong case and auxiliary with *beitreten* and *austreten*: ~~Österreich hat die EU beigetreten~~ → *Österreich ist der EU beigetreten*; ~~aus die EU~~ → *aus der EU ausgetreten*.
- *der Mitgliedstaat* is the official spelling in EU texts; *der Mitgliedsstaat* with a linking *s* is also common and correct.
- *das Land* in German politics usually means a federal state (*das Land Hessen*), not a country. *Die Länder* in a German news report are the 16 states.
- *die Kompetenz* in politics means a power or area of responsibility (*Die Länder haben die Kompetenz für Bildung*), not "competence" in the sense of skill.

## Key points

- Germany (16 Länder), Austria (9 Länder) and Switzerland (26 cantons) are federal states; the subsidiarity principle says tasks belong at the lowest level that can handle them.
- *Bundesrat*: in Germany and Austria the chamber of the Länder; in Switzerland the seven-member federal government. *Nationalrat* is the people's chamber in Austria and Switzerland.
- The EU (27 member states) shares sovereignty in the single market with free movement of goods, services, capital and people (*Freizügigkeit*).
- The Commission proposes laws; Parliament and the Council of the EU decide them. A regulation (*Verordnung*) applies directly; a directive (*Richtlinie*) must be implemented in national law.
- Describe institutions with the passive, relative clauses with prepositions and nominal phrases: *Das Parlament wird direkt gewählt; die Kammer, in der …; nach dem Beitritt zur EU.*

lessons.title: One language, three standards: Austrian and Swiss German
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You have learned the German of Germany: *Januar, Tomate, Fahrrad, parken*. Travel to Vienna and the menu offers *Paradeiser* and *Marillenknödel*; in Zurich you lock your *Velo* on the *Trottoir*, and the newspaper writes *Strasse* without *ß*. None of this is dialect or slang. It is standard German, just not the standard of Germany.

This lesson explains why German is a **[[pluricentric language]]** (*eine plurizentrische Sprache*), introduces the most useful words, pronunciation features and grammar of standard Austrian and Swiss German, and looks at the special language situation in German-speaking Switzerland, where almost everyone speaks dialect but writes standard German. The listening practice uses Austrian and Swiss voices where your device has them; otherwise you'll hear a standard German voice and can read the transcript.

## One language, several centres

English is the model case of a pluricentric language: British and American English are both correct, each with its own spelling (*colour, color*), words (*lorry, truck*) and pronunciation, and each country has its own dictionaries. German works the same way. It has several centres with their own standard, and none of them is "the real one":

- Germany;
- Austria;
- Switzerland;
- with smaller variants of their own: Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, South Tyrol in Italy and the German-speaking Community of Belgium.

Each national variety of the standard language is called a **[[standard variety]]** (*die Standardvarietät*). The general term **[[variety]]** (*die Varietät*) is the linguists' neutral word for any form of a language: a dialect, the standard of a country, the language of young people. A word or feature typical of one centre has its own name:

| term | German | example |
|---|---|---|
| **[[Austriacism]]** | *der Austriazismus, die Austriazismen* | *der Jänner, die Marille, die Matura* |
| **[[Helvetism]]** | *der Helvetismus, die Helvetismen* | *das Velo, parkieren, das Trottoir* |
| **[[Teutonism]]** | *der Teutonismus* (also *Deutschlandismus*) | *die Sahne, der Bürgersteig, das Abitur* |

The last row is important: words like *Sahne* or *Abitur* aren't "normal German" that Austrians and Swiss replace with local words. They are Germany's variants, just as *Schlagobers* is Austria's. Many speakers in Germany are surprised to learn that.

Each country also has reference works. In Austria the *Österreichisches Wörterbuch* is the official reference for schools and offices. Duden, published in Germany, marks Austrian and Swiss forms (*österr.*, *schweiz.*) and accepts them as standard.

## Words: a small comparison

| Germany | Austria | Switzerland | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| *der Januar* | *der Jänner* | *der Januar* | January |
| *die Tomate* | *der Paradeiser* (also *die Tomate*) | *die Tomate* | tomato |
| *die Aprikose* | *die Marille* | *die Aprikose* | apricot |
| *die Kartoffel* | *der Erdapfel* (also *die Kartoffel*) | *die Kartoffel* | potato |
| *die Sahne* | *das Obers, das Schlagobers* | *der Rahm* | cream |
| *der Quark* | *der Topfen* | *der Quark* | quark (soft cheese) |
| *das Brötchen* | *die Semmel* | *das Brötchen*, regional words | bread roll |
| *das Fahrrad* | *das Fahrrad* | *das Velo* | bicycle |
| *parken* | *parken* | *parkieren* | to park |
| *der Bürgersteig, der Gehweg* | *der Gehsteig* | *das Trottoir* | pavement, sidewalk |
| *das Abitur* | *die Matura* | *die Matura* (also *die Matur*) | school-leaving exam |
| *das Krankenhaus* | *das Krankenhaus, das Spital* | *das Spital* | hospital |
| *die Fahrkarte* | *der Fahrschein, die Fahrkarte* | *das Billett* | ticket |
| *der Stuhl* | *der Sessel* | *der Stuhl* | chair |
| *dieses Jahr* | *heuer* | *dieses Jahr, heuer* | this year |

Notes:

- Many Austrian food words are protected by EU law. When Austria joined the EU in 1995, its accession treaty included a protocol listing 23 Austrian food terms, among them *Erdäpfel, Marillen, Paradeiser, Topfen* and *Obers*, which have the same status in EU texts as the terms used in Germany and may be used alongside them.
- *der Erdapfel* (plural *die Erdäpfel*) and *der Paradeiser* are typical of eastern Austria, especially Vienna; in the west you'll also hear *Kartoffel* and *Tomate*. Austrian menus show them in dishes: *Erdäpfelsalat, Paradeisersuppe, Marillenmarmelade*.
- *der Sessel* is a false friend: in Austria it's an ordinary chair, in Germany an armchair.
- Swiss German has many words from French, which is also a national language: *das Velo* (from *vélocipède*), *das Trottoir, das Billett, merci* (thanks), *der Coiffeur* (hairdresser), and verbs in *-ieren* where Germany has a shorter form: *parkieren, grillieren* (to grill).
- *die Matura* is the name of the final school exam in both Austria and Switzerland; *maturieren* (Austria) means to pass it.

## Grammar differences

The grammar of the three standards is almost identical. A few differences come up all the time.

### sein in the perfect of sitzen, stehen, liegen

In Austria, Switzerland and southern Germany these verbs form the perfect with *sein*; in northern and central Germany with *haben*. Both are standard in their regions:

- *Ich bin den ganzen Tag im Büro gesessen.* (AT, CH, south) = *Ich habe den ganzen Tag im Büro gesessen.* (north) — I sat in the office all day.
- *Wir sind lange an der Haltestelle gestanden.* = *Wir haben lange … gestanden.*
- *Das Buch ist auf dem Tisch gelegen.* = *Das Buch hat auf dem Tisch gelegen.*

The same goes for *hängen* in the sense of "to be hanging": *Das Bild ist lange dort gehangen* (south) = *Das Bild hat lange dort gehangen* (north).

### Gender

Some nouns have a different gender:

- *das Cola* (Austria, Switzerland, south) vs *die Cola* (Germany): *Ein Cola, bitte!*
- *das E-Mail* (Austria, Switzerland) vs *die E-Mail* (Germany).
- *das Tram* (Switzerland) vs *die Tram* or *die Straßenbahn* (Germany).

### Diminutives

Austrian colloquial German uses *-erl* (*das Sackerl* = small bag, *das Packerl* = small parcel, *das Stamperl* = a small glass for schnapps) where Germany has *-chen* (*das Tütchen*). Swiss words with *-li* (*das Müesli, das Rüebli* = carrot) come from the dialect and have partly entered the standard: *das Müesli* gave the world *muesli*.

### Small differences in phrasing

Austrians go *auf Urlaub* (Germany: *in den Urlaub*), and in Switzerland you can *einen Entscheid fällen* (Germany: *eine Entscheidung treffen*).

## Spelling: no ß in Switzerland

In Switzerland and Liechtenstein *ß* isn't used at all; *ss* is written in every case: *die Strasse, gross, der Fuss, heissen, Grüsse*. Swiss schools stopped teaching *ß* during the 20th century, and Swiss newspapers gave it up one after another. The official rules of German spelling allow this explicitly for Switzerland. A side effect: *Masse* can mean both *Maße* (measurements) and *Masse* (mass); the context decides.

## Pronunciation

Standard Austrian and Swiss German have their own pronunciation norms too. A few features you will notice:

- *-ig* at the end of a word: in Germany it's pronounced like *ich* (*König* ends like *ich*); in Austria and Switzerland it's pronounced with *k* (*König* sounds like "Könik"). Both are standard.
- *ch* and *k* in loanwords: *Chemie, China* begin with a *k* sound in Austria and southern Germany, with the *ich* sound in the north.
- *s* before a vowel at the start of a word is voiced (like English *z*) in northern Germany, voiceless (like English *s*) in Austria, Switzerland and the south: *Sonne, sagen*.
- Stress in loanwords: *der Kaffee* is stressed on the second syllable in Austria (ka-FEE), on the first in Germany (KAF-fee). Swiss speakers often stress the first syllable of French loans: *das Büro* sounds like BÜ-ro.
- Swiss speakers keep long and short vowels very distinct and pronounce *r* often at the tip of the tongue; the *ch* in words like *ich* is often a harder sound at the back of the mouth. This is a strong sign of a Swiss accent even in standard German.

## Diglossia: dialect and standard in Switzerland

In Germany and Austria the language people speak forms a continuum: from broad dialect via regional colloquial speech (*Umgangssprache*) to the standard, and most speakers move along it depending on the situation. German-speaking Switzerland is different. There are two clearly separate forms, each with its own domain. Linguists call this **[[diglossia]]** (*die Diglossie*).

- **[[Swiss German]]** (*das Schweizerdeutsch*, also *die Mundart* or *der Dialekt*) is spoken by everyone, in every social class, in almost every situation: at home, at work, with the boss, on local radio and TV, and in many cantonal parliaments. It isn't one dialect but a group: Zurich, Bern, Basel and Valais German differ clearly from each other. People increasingly write it too, in text messages and social media, without fixed spelling.
- Standard German (*die Standardsprache*; in Switzerland often called *Hochdeutsch* or *Schriftdeutsch*) is the language of writing: newspapers, books, official letters, most school lessons, news on national TV. People also speak it with those who don't understand dialect.

Swiss German is not a dialect of German Standard German in the sense of a "bad" version: it is the everyday language with high prestige, and the standard is felt by many Swiss as a slightly formal, learned language. As a learner, you aren't expected to speak Schweizerdeutsch. Speak standard German; many Swiss will switch to standard for you (sometimes with visible effort), and some will prefer English or French.

Austria has no diglossia of the Swiss kind, but Austrian speakers move constantly between dialect, colloquial speech and standard, and many feel that Austrian standard German is under pressure from German TV and online media: children who say *Tüte* and *lecker* instead of *Sackerl* and *gut* are a regular topic of newspaper columns.

## Listening: two short conversations

Two everyday scenes in standard Austrian and standard Swiss German, written for the course. (If your device has no Austrian or Swiss voice, the lines are read by a standard German voice.)

```dialogue lang=de-AT
# Am Markt in Wien
Verkäuferin: Grüß Gott! Was darf's sein?
= Hello! What can I get you?
Kunde: Ein Kilo Erdäpfel, bitte, und ein halbes Kilo Paradeiser.
= A kilo of potatoes, please, and half a kilo of tomatoes.
Verkäuferin: Gern. Die Marillen sind heuer übrigens besonders gut. Möchten Sie welche kosten?
= Of course. The apricots are especially good this year, by the way. Would you like to try some?
Kunde: Ja, danke. Mhm, die sind wirklich süß. Dann nehme ich ein Kilo für Marillenknödel.
= Yes, thanks. Mm, they're really sweet. Then I'll take a kilo for apricot dumplings.
Verkäuferin: Brauchen Sie ein Sackerl?
= Do you need a bag?
Kunde: Nein, danke, ich hab eine Tasche mit. Bis zum nächsten Mal!
= No, thanks, I've got a bag with me. See you next time!
```

```dialogue lang=de-CH
# Vor dem Bahnhof in Zürich
Passantin: Entschuldigung, darf man hier das Velo parkieren?
= Excuse me, are you allowed to park your bike here?
Polizist: Auf dem Trottoir leider nicht. Gleich um die Ecke gibt es einen Veloparkplatz.
= Not on the pavement, I'm afraid. There's a bike park just around the corner.
Passantin: Merci! Und wo kann ich ein Billett nach Bern lösen?
= Thanks! And where can I buy a ticket to Bern?
Polizist: Am Automaten in der Halle oder mit der App. Der Zug fährt auf Gleis sieben.
= At the machine in the hall or with the app. The train leaves from platform seven.
Passantin: Super, vielen Dank. Ich bin nämlich schon eine halbe Stunde am falschen Ort gestanden.
= Great, thank you very much. You see, I've been standing in the wrong place for half an hour already.
```

Notice *Grüß Gott* (the standard greeting in Austria and southern Germany), *was darf's sein?* (the shop assistant's standard question), *heuer*, *das Sackerl*; and in the Swiss scene *Velo, parkieren, Trottoir, Merci, ein Billett lösen* (to buy a ticket; *lösen* in this sense is also used in Germany and Austria, but more formal there) and *bin … gestanden*. In real Zurich, of course, the conversation would almost certainly be in Swiss German, unless the woman were a tourist.

## Text: Ein Deutscher in Wien

A forum post, original for the course.

> Ich wohne seit drei Monaten in Wien und dachte, Sprachprobleme würde ich hier keine haben. Ein Irrtum! Am ersten Tag habe ich im Supermarkt nach Sahne gefragt. Die Verkäuferin hat freundlich gelächelt und mir Schlagobers gegeben. Im Büro hat mir eine Kollegin einen Sessel angeboten, und ich habe mich gewundert, warum sie mir einen ganz normalen Stuhl hinschiebt. Und als ich im Januar – pardon, im Jänner – gesagt habe „Ich habe zwei Stunden beim Arzt gesessen“, hat mein Kollege gegrinst: „Du meinst, du bist gesessen.“
>
> Mittlerweile sage ich selbst „Servus“ und bestelle Topfenstrudel. Was ich gelernt habe: Österreichisches Deutsch ist kein Dialekt, sondern eine eigene Standardsprache. Mein Deutsch aus Hannover ist hier genauso eine Varietät wie das Wienerische, nur eben eine andere.

English:

> I've been living in Vienna for three months and thought I wouldn't have any language problems here. Wrong! On the first day I asked for Sahne (cream) in the supermarket. The shop assistant smiled kindly and gave me Schlagobers. At the office a colleague offered me a Sessel, and I wondered why she was pushing a completely normal chair towards me. And when I said in Januar – sorry, in Jänner – "I sat at the doctor's for two hours" (with haben), my colleague grinned: "You mean bist gesessen."
>
> In the meantime I say "Servus" myself and order Topfenstrudel. What I've learned: Austrian German isn't a dialect but a standard language of its own. My German from Hanover is just as much a variety here as the Viennese dialect, just a different one.

## Pronunciation of the lesson words

- *plurizentrisch*: plu-ri-TSEN-trisch.
- *der Austriazismus*: aus-tri-a-TSIS-mus; *der Helvetismus*: hel-ve-TIS-mus (*v* like English *v*).
- *die Diglossie*: di-glo-SIE, stress on the last syllable.
- *der Jänner*: JÄN-ner, short *ä*.
- *das Trottoir*: tro-TWAHR, French pronunciation.
- *das Velo*: VEE-lo, *v* like English *v*, stress on the first syllable.

## Common mistakes

- Calling Austrian or Swiss standard German "dialect". *Jänner* and *parkieren* are standard; dialect is something else (*Härdöpfel* for potatoes in Swiss German, for example).
- Treating German-from-Germany words as neutral: *Sahne* and *Abitur* are Germany's variants.
- Using Swiss German yourself to be friendly. As a learner, speak standard German; imitating dialect can easily sound odd.
- *das Schweizerdeutsch* (the dialects) vs *das Schweizer Hochdeutsch* (the Swiss standard). They are different things.
- *der Sessel* in Austria is a chair, not an armchair; *der Stuhl* is understood too.
- Correcting *ich bin gesessen* as wrong. In Austria, Switzerland and southern Germany it is the standard form.

## Key points

- German is pluricentric: Germany, Austria and Switzerland each have their own standard variety, with Austriacisms, Helvetisms and Teutonisms.
- Typical Austrian words: *Jänner, Paradeiser, Marille, Erdapfel, Topfen, Obers, Matura, heuer*; typical Swiss words: *Velo, parkieren, Trottoir, Billett, Spital, Matura*.
- In the south (AT, CH, southern Germany) *sitzen, stehen, liegen* take *sein* in the perfect: *ich bin gesessen*. Some genders differ: *das Cola, das E-Mail*.
- Switzerland writes *ss* for *ß*: *Strasse, gross*.
- German-speaking Switzerland has diglossia: Swiss German dialects for speaking, standard German mainly for writing and formal speech.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

sections.name: Working life and the B2 exam
Honors: Sprache, Literatur und Öffentlichkeit (language, literature and public life)

questions.stem: Which technique is used here? "Sie kam schon wieder zu spät. Was würde der Chef sagen? Nein, diesmal würde sie sich nicht entschuldigen!"
questions.explanation: Third person (sie) and the past tense of the narration, but the character's own questions and exclamations, with no "dachte sie" and no quotation marks: that is erlebte Rede. Direct thought would need quotation marks and ich; indirect speech would need an introducing verb and a dass or ob clause; an interior monologue would be in the first person and present tense.

questions.stem: Lena thinks: "Ich komme schon wieder zu spät. Was sagt der Chef?" Which version is an interior monologue?
choices: Schon wieder zu spät. Was sagt der Chef?
Sie kam schon wieder zu spät. Was würde der Chef sagen?
Lena dachte, dass sie schon wieder zu spät komme.
„Ich komme schon wieder zu spät“, dachte Lena.
questions.explanation: The interior monologue gives the thoughts directly, in the first person and present tense, often as fragments and without any narrator: "Schon wieder zu spät. Was sagt der Chef?" The second version is erlebte Rede (third person, past), the third indirect speech, the fourth direct thought with "dachte Lena".

questions.stem: In a story told in the past tense: "Sie wartete am Bahnsteig. Würde er wirklich kommen?" What does "würde ... kommen" express here?
choices: An unreal condition (he would come if ...)
The future seen from a past point of view (was he going to come?)
questions.explanation: Her thought was "Wird er wirklich kommen?" (future). Moved into the past tense of the narration, wird becomes würde, just as English will becomes would. There is no condition here, so it isn't a hypothetical Konjunktiv II, and würde + infinitive is never a passive.

questions.stem: Complete the Inhaltsangabe in the correct tense: "Gregor ___ eines Morgens als Ungeziefer auf." (aufwachen)
questions.explanation: An Inhaltsangabe is written in the present tense, even when the story is told in the Präteritum: Gregor wacht auf. "wachte" would copy the story's past tense.

questions.stem: Report Grete's words in the Inhaltsangabe with the Konjunktiv I: "Grete erklärt, man ___ das Tier loswerden." (müssen)
questions.explanation: The Konjunktiv I of müssen for man (er/sie/es form) is "müsse": stem müss- + -e. "muss" would be the indicative, and "müsste" the Konjunktiv II, which is used only when the Konjunktiv I looks like the indicative.

questions.stem: Which sentence belongs in a B2 Inhaltsangabe of Die Verwandlung?
choices: Der Prokurist sagt: „Ihre Leistungen sind unbefriedigend.“
Der Vertreter der Firma wirft Gregor vor, seine Leistungen seien unbefriedigend.
Der Vertreter der Firma warf Gregor vor, dass seine Leistungen unbefriedigend waren.
Der arme Gregor muss sich auch noch die gemeinen Vorwürfe dieses Mannes anhören.
questions.explanation: An Inhaltsangabe uses the present tense, no direct speech and neutral words; what characters say is reported with the Konjunktiv I: "wirft ... vor, seine Leistungen seien ...". The first choice quotes directly, the third is in the past tense, and the last one judges ("der arme Gregor", "gemein").

questions.stem: Match each type of narrator or technique with its description.
choices: knows everything and may comment on the story
third person, limited to what one character sees and knows
a character tells the story and says "ich"
a character's thoughts in third person and past tense, without "dachte er"
the author's own opinion in the preface
questions.explanation: The omniscient narrator (auktorial) stands above the story; the figural narrator (personal) stays with one character, as in Die Verwandlung; the first-person narrator is a character who says ich; erlebte Rede renders thoughts in the narrator's grammar. A preface by the author isn't a narrative perspective.

questions.stem: Listen to the start of a lecture. What did Max Brod do with Kafka's manuscripts?
