questions.explanation: Ich bin manchmal ungeduldig, wenn Entscheidungen lange dauern: she is impatient when decisions take long. She then says what she does about it, which is the recommended way to answer. Teamwork, English and deadlines aren't mentioned as weaknesses.

questions.stem: Listen to the voicemail from HR. What should Ms Okafor bring to the interview?

audio.text: Guten Tag, Frau Okafor, hier spricht Lisa Brandt aus der Personalabteilung der Firma Solartec. Vielen Dank für Ihre Bewerbung. Wir würden Sie gern zu einem Vorstellungsgespräch einladen, am Dienstag, dem 14., um zehn Uhr. Bitte bringen Sie Ihr Abschlusszeugnis im Original mit. Rufen Sie mich doch kurz zurück, ob der Termin passt. Danke!

choices: her final certificate in the original
a letter of reference from her current employer
questions.explanation: Bitte bringen Sie Ihr Abschlusszeugnis im Original mit: the original of her final certificate. Ms Brandt also asks her to call back to confirm the date. CV, references and a passport aren't mentioned.

questions.stem: Listen and type the sentence you hear.

audio.text: Ich habe mich regelmäßig weitergebildet.

questions.explanation: sich weiterbilden (to do further training) is separable and reflexive: ich bilde mich weiter; Perfekt: ich habe mich weitergebildet.

questions.stem: Build the interview question.
questions.prompt: I'd be interested to know what the induction looks like.
questions.explanation: Mich würde interessieren, … is a polite frame for a question; the indirect question with wie sends the verb (aussieht, separable aussehen joined again) to the end.

questions.stem: Build the sentence for a cover letter.
questions.prompt: For three years I have been leading a team of five.
questions.explanation: seit + present: Seit drei Jahren leite ich … or Ich leite seit drei Jahren … The verb stays in position 2, so the subject comes after it when seit drei Jahren starts the sentence. habe … geleitet would be the English-style mistake.

questions.stem: What is an "Initiativbewerbung"?
choices: an application for a management position
an application to a company that hasn't advertised a job
an application through a temp agency
questions.explanation: Eine Initiativbewerbung (unsolicited application) is sent on your own initiative, without a job ad. It has nothing to do with the level of the job, the channel or Zeitarbeit (agency work).

questions.stem: "Die neue Kollegin ist Quereinsteigerin." What does this mean?
choices: She has just finished her vocational training.
She works for the company through a temp agency.
She is moving from one department to another.
She has come into this job from a different profession.
questions.explanation: A Quereinsteiger / eine Quereinsteigerin is a career changer, someone who enters a field without the usual training for it. Moving between departments isn't Quereinstieg, and an agency worker is in Zeitarbeit.

questions.stem: Match the qualities from job ads to their meanings.
questions.explanation: Teamfähigkeit is being a team player, Belastbarkeit the ability to work under pressure (from belastbar), Eigeninitiative acting on your own initiative, Fachkompetenz specialist knowledge, as opposed to Sozialkompetenz (social skills).

questions.stem:
Read the job ad. What must applicants include in their application?

"Für unser Team in Graz suchen wir ab sofort eine Sachbearbeiterin / einen Sachbearbeiter (m/w/d) im Einkauf. Sie bringen eine kaufmännische Ausbildung und gute Englischkenntnisse mit; Erfahrung im Einkauf ist von Vorteil, aber keine Voraussetzung. Bitte senden Sie Ihre Bewerbungsunterlagen unter Angabe Ihrer Gehaltsvorstellung und Ihres frühestmöglichen Eintrittstermins an personal@beispiel-graz.at."
choices: their salary expectations and their earliest start date
an English certificate and a photo
a letter of motivation and two references
questions.explanation: unter Angabe Ihrer Gehaltsvorstellung und Ihres frühestmöglichen Eintrittstermins: stating your salary expectations and earliest start date. Purchasing experience is von Vorteil, aber keine Voraussetzung (an advantage, not a requirement); no certificate, photo or references are asked for.

questions.stem: Which first sentence of a cover letter makes the best impression?
choices: Hiermit bewerbe ich mich um die Stelle als Einkäufer.
Seit zwölf Jahren arbeite ich mit Lebensmitteln, bisher allerdings in der Küche.
Ich habe Ihre Anzeige gesehen und will die Stelle.
Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, ich bin der Richtige für Sie.
questions.explanation: A specific fact about you and the job catches the reader's attention. Hiermit bewerbe ich mich … is correct but so common that recruiters skip it; will die Stelle is too direct, and an unsupported claim sounds boastful.

questions.stem: "Sie hat eine sehr positive Einstellung zur Arbeit." What does "Einstellung" mean here?
questions.explanation: die Einstellung has two meanings in job contexts: the hiring of staff (die Einstellung neuer Mitarbeiter) and an attitude (eine positive Einstellung zu etwas). With zur Arbeit and positiv, it can only be attitude.

questions.stem: Which sentence fits a formal written notice from a school?
choices: Wegen dem Streik ist am Montag kein Unterricht.
Montag fällt Schule aus, wegen Streik.
Am Montag ist halt kein Unterricht, weil die streiken.
Aufgrund des Streiks entfällt der Unterricht am Montag.
questions.explanation: aufgrund + genitive, entfallen and the nominal style are typical of formal notices. wegen + dative is colloquial; the second option uses ellipsis and Ausklammerung, and the third uses halt and a vague die. All three are fine in speech, not in a notice.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct in written standard German?
choices: Ich komme heute nicht, weil ich keine Zeit habe.
Ich komme heute nicht, weil ich habe keine Zeit.
Ich komm heute nicht, weil – hab keine Zeit.
Ich komme heute nicht, weil habe ich keine Zeit.
questions.explanation: In writing, weil sends the verb to the end. weil + main-clause order (weil ich habe …) is very common in speech, but not standard in writing. The last option has question order, which is wrong everywhere.

questions.stem: In casual speech someone says: "Weiß ich nicht." What is the full sentence?
questions.explanation: Spoken German often drops a pronoun in position 1 (here das): Das weiß ich nicht → Weiß ich nicht. It's still a statement, not a question, and still the present tense.

questions.stem: In which region would you most expect the tag question "gell?"
questions.explanation: gell (also gelle) is southern and Austrian. In Berlin you hear wa?, in the north ne? or nich?; oder? is used everywhere, and nicht wahr? is the formal one.

questions.stem: Complete with the article: "___ Meeting beginnt um zehn."
questions.explanation: Meeting is neuter: das Meeting, like its German equivalent das Treffen. Borrowed nouns often take the gender of a German word with the same meaning, and -ing nouns are usually neuter (das Training, das Marketing).

questions.stem: Complete with the participle: "Ich habe gestern zwei Stunden mit meiner Schwester ___." (chatten)
questions.explanation: English verbs become weak German verbs: chatten, ich chatte, hat gechattet, with ge- and -t (here -et after the stem ending in t). The English -ed (gechatted) is the common mistake.

questions.stem: An English colleague asks what "das Handy" is. What do you say?
choices: It's an English word for a small tool.
It means something practical, like English "handy".
It means a mobile phone; the word isn't used like that in English.
questions.explanation: das Handy is a German creation that looks English (a pseudo-Anglicism). In English it would be a mobile or a cell phone. Similar cases are der Beamer (projector) and das Homeoffice.

questions.stem: Which form refers to a mixed group with a participle?
questions.explanation: die Studierenden is a participle (studierend) used as a noun, so it covers everyone without a gender ending. Student*innen uses the asterisk, Studentinnen und Studenten is the Doppelnennung, and die Studenten is the generic masculine.

questions.stem: You are writing to the whole team in a traditional company and are unsure about gender-inclusive forms. Which greeting is the safe choice?
questions.explanation: The Doppelnennung (naming both forms) is widely accepted, also by people who reject the asterisk. Kolleg*innen is debated and not part of official spelling; Kollegen alone is the generic masculine, which some readers find exclusive; Hallo Leute is too casual.

questions.stem: Listen to the conversation. What is the first speaker's argument?

audio.text: Ich finde, die vielen englischen Wörter in der Werbung nerven. – Echt? Ich finde das normal. Sprache verändert sich halt. – Schon, aber meine Oma versteht die Hälfte nicht mehr.

choices: English words are always shorter than German ones.
Older people no longer understand many advertising words.
Advertising should be in English only.
questions.explanation: A says the English words in advertising annoy her, and when B says language just changes, she replies: meine Oma versteht die Hälfte nicht mehr (my grandma doesn't understand half of it). Her point is about understanding, not about length or English-only ads.

questions.stem: Listen to the lecture extract. What makes a word a "Lehnwort"?

audio.text: Unter einem Lehnwort versteht man ein Wort, das aus einer anderen Sprache übernommen wurde und sich in Aussprache und Schreibung so angepasst hat, dass es nicht mehr als fremd empfunden wird.

choices: It is a foreign word that keeps its original spelling.
It is a German word that other languages have borrowed.
It is an old German word that is no longer used.
It was borrowed and has adapted so far that it no longer feels foreign.
questions.explanation: The lecturer defines a Lehnwort as a word taken from another language that has adapted in pronunciation and spelling so much that it is no longer felt to be foreign (Fenster, Mauer). A word that still looks foreign is a Fremdwort.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the second speaker mean?

audio.text: Kommst du heute Abend mit ins Kino? – Geht nicht, muss noch arbeiten.

choices: I can't, I still have to work.
It's not going well at work.
I'd like to come, but the film is bad.
questions.explanation: Geht nicht, muss noch arbeiten is spoken ellipsis for Das geht nicht, ich muss noch arbeiten: the pronouns are dropped. It is a refusal with a reason, not a promise to come later.

questions.stem: Build the written report of what the researcher said.
questions.prompt: The researcher stresses that language change is completely normal.
questions.explanation: A written report of someone's view uses a reporting verb and the Konjunktiv I: sei. Without dass, the reported clause keeps main-clause order (verb in position 2). seien is the plural form and doesn't agree with Sprachwandel.

questions.stem: Build the sentence.
questions.prompt: Many children in Germany grow up bilingual.
questions.explanation: aufwachsen is separable: the prefix auf goes to the end of the main clause, and wachsen stays in position 2. In Deutschland can also start the sentence (In Deutschland wachsen viele Kinder zweisprachig auf).

questions.stem: "Türkisch ist meine Herkunftssprache." What does Leonie mean?
choices: Turkish is the only language she speaks.
Turkish is the language of her family's origin.
She learned Turkish at school as a foreign language.
Turkish is the official language where she lives.
questions.explanation: die Herkunftssprache (heritage language) is the language of the family's origin, often spoken at home alongside the language of the country. It says nothing about being the only language; a school language would be a Fremdsprache, an official one an Amtssprache.

questions.stem: Match each sentence to its register.
left: Wir bitten, die Verspätung zu entschuldigen.
questions.explanation: The formal version uses bitten + infinitive group, typical of notices. The neutral one is a normal polite sentence with Sie. The colloquial one drops the pronoun (bin) and uses an English word and an idiom (spät dran sein).

questions.stem: Complete: "Sie ___ fünf Sprachen, drei davon fließend." (has a command of, present)
questions.explanation: beherrschen (to have a full command of) is weak and inseparable: sie beherrscht, sie hat beherrscht. The be- never separates.

questions.stem:
Read the forum post. What is the writer's opinion?

"Meine Tochter ist 15 und redet mit ihren Freundinnen in einer Sprache, die ich oft nicht verstehe. Am Anfang hat mich das gestört. Inzwischen sehe ich es anders: Als ich jung war, haben meine Eltern auch über unsere Wörter den Kopf geschüttelt. Jugendsprache gehört einfach dazu, und in der Schule und im Praktikum spricht meine Tochter ganz normal. Problematisch fände ich es nur, wenn sie nicht mehr zwischen den Situationen unterscheiden könnte."
choices: Youth slang is a danger to the German language.
Parents should forbid youth slang at home.
Youth slang is normal, as long as young people can switch register when needed.
questions.explanation: The writer was annoyed at first but now sees youth slang as normal (gehört einfach dazu), and would only find it a problem if her daughter couldn't tell situations apart. The idea of danger is what she rejects; banning or teaching slang isn't mentioned.

questions.stem: Which is the written version of "Ich hab sie getroffen gestern, beim Bäcker"?
choices: Ich habe getroffen sie gestern beim Bäcker.
Ich habe sie getroffen gestern beim Bäcker.
Gestern ich habe sie beim Bäcker getroffen.
Ich habe sie gestern beim Bäcker getroffen.
questions.explanation: In writing, the time and place phrases go back inside the verb bracket, before the participle at the end, and hab becomes habe. Leaving them after getroffen is spoken Ausklammerung. Ich habe getroffen sie puts the participle before the object, and Gestern ich habe … puts two elements before the verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a mistake?
choices: Die Meeting findet morgen im Raum 3 statt.
Ich schicke dir die E-Mail gleich.
Das Team hat das Update installiert.
questions.explanation: Meeting is neuter: das Meeting, like das Treffen. die E-Mail, das Team, das Update and der Workshop are all correct.

questions.stem: How long is the Lesen module of the Goethe-Zertifikat B2 for adults?
questions.explanation: Lesen takes 65 minutes for 5 parts and 30 items. About 40 minutes is Hören, and 75 minutes is Schreiben.

questions.stem: What do you write in the Schreiben module?
choices: an informal e-mail, a forum post and a formal letter of about 80 words each
a forum post of about 150 words and a message to a superior of about 100 words
a summary of a lecture and a letter of complaint
questions.explanation: B2 Schreiben has two parts: Teil 1, a forum post giving your opinion (about 150 words), and Teil 2, a formal message in a work context to a superior (about 100 words), in 75 minutes. Three shorter texts (two e-mails and a forum post) are the B1 format.

questions.stem: How many points do you need to pass a module?
questions.explanation: Each module is scored out of 100 and passed with 60 (ausreichend). 70 is the start of befriedigend.

questions.stem: Which parts of the Hören module are heard only once?
questions.explanation: Teil 1 (short texts) and Teil 3 (a discussion) are played once; Teil 2 (an interview) and Teil 4 (a short lecture) are played twice. So in Teil 1 and 3 answer immediately and move on.

questions.stem: What happens in the Sprechen module?
choices: Each candidate gives a short talk and answers questions, then the two candidates discuss a question together.
Each candidate reads a text aloud and summarizes it.
The two candidates plan an event together, then each presents a photo.
Each candidate is interviewed alone about their CV.
questions.explanation: B2 Sprechen is done in pairs: Teil 1 is a talk of about four minutes followed by questions, Teil 2 a discussion of about five minutes on a controversial question. Planning something together is a B1 task.

questions.stem: You score 82 points in Hören. Which Notenstufe is that?
questions.explanation: The grades are 90–100 sehr gut, 80–89 gut, 70–79 befriedigend, 60–69 ausreichend. 82 is in the gut band.

questions.stem: In Lesen Teil 2 you have to put sentences into gaps in a text. Two of the sentences are "überzählig". What does that mean?
questions.explanation: überzählig means extra, one too many: two sentences don't belong in the text at all. Forcing them into a gap is a common way to lose two points.

questions.stem: Review (lesson 01): complete the news sentence with the Konjunktiv I: "Der Minister sagte, er ___ keine Zeit für ein Interview." (haben)
questions.explanation: Indirect speech in news uses the Konjunktiv I: er habe. It shows the report doesn't vouch for the statement. hat would be the indicative, hätte is only needed where the Konjunktiv I looks like the indicative (sie haben → sie hätten).

questions.stem: Review (lesson 02): "Die Ärzte sagten, sie ___ zu wenig Personal." Which form is correct in a written report?
questions.explanation: The Konjunktiv I of haben for sie (plural) is haben, identical to the indicative, so the replacement rule switches to the Konjunktiv II: hätten. habe is singular, and hatten is the Präteritum indicative.

questions.stem: Review (lesson 07): "Das Formular ist bis Freitag abzugeben." What does it mean?
choices: The form must be handed in by Friday.
The form was handed in on Friday.
The form can't be handed in until Friday.
The form is being handed in on Friday.
questions.explanation: sein + zu + infinitive is a passive with a modal meaning, here müssen: Das Formular muss bis Freitag abgegeben werden. It isn't a past or a progressive form.

questions.stem: Review (lesson 11): which relative clause means the same as "die seit Jahren steigenden Mieten"?
choices: die Mieten, die seit Jahren gestiegen sind
die Mieten, die seit Jahren steigen
die Mieten, die seit Jahren erhöht werden müssen
die Mieten, die seit Jahren gleich geblieben sind
questions.explanation: A Partizip I (steigend) means something happening at the same time and is active: the rents that have been rising for years and still are (German uses the present with seit). A Partizip II would give gestiegen, and müssen would need the gerundive (die zu erhöhenden Mieten).

questions.stem: Review (lesson 03): "Der neue Chef soll sehr streng sein." What does this mean?
choices: The new boss claims to be very strict.
I'm certain the new boss is very strict.
People say the new boss is very strict.
The new boss used to be very strict.
questions.explanation: sollen with a subjective meaning reports hearsay: it is said that … A claim by the boss himself would use wollen (Er will streng sein), the speaker's own certainty would be muss (Er muss sehr streng sein), and nothing here is in the past.

questions.stem: Review (lesson 04): "Sie ist noch nicht da. Sie wird den Bus verpasst haben." What does the speaker mean?
choices: She is going to miss the bus.
She had missed the bus before.
She will have to take another bus.
She has probably missed the bus.
questions.explanation: Futur II (wird … verpasst haben) is used mainly for assumptions about the past: she has probably missed the bus. A real future would be Sie wird den Bus verpassen.

questions.stem: Listen to the instructions. How often will you hear the interview?

audio.text: Sie hören nun den zweiten Teil. Sie hören ein Interview. Dazu sollen Sie sechs Aufgaben lösen. Sie haben zunächst neunzig Sekunden Zeit, die Aufgaben zu lesen. Sie hören das Interview zweimal.

questions.explanation: Sie hören das Interview zweimal: twice. That fits Hören Teil 2, the interview, which is played twice; you first get ninety seconds to read the tasks.

questions.stem: Listen to the discussion. What does the first speaker finally propose?

audio.text: Ich finde, Homeoffice sollte für alle möglich sein. – Das sehe ich anders. Gerade neue Kolleginnen und Kollegen lernen im Büro viel schneller. – Da hast du recht. Wie wäre es dann mit zwei Tagen Homeoffice pro Woche?

choices: working from home two days a week
no working from home for new colleagues
questions.explanation: After her partner's objection (new colleagues learn faster in the office), she concedes (Da hast du recht) and proposes a compromise: Wie wäre es mit zwei Tagen pro Woche? Reacting and proposing a compromise is exactly what the discussion task rewards.

questions.stem: Listen to the end of a lecture. What does the speaker's first phrase tell you?

audio.text: Zusammenfassend lässt sich sagen, dass Mehrsprachigkeit für Kinder kein Nachteil ist, sondern eher ein Vorteil.

choices: The speaker is going to give an example.
A summary of the main points follows.
The speaker disagrees with an earlier point.
questions.explanation: Zusammenfassend lässt sich sagen, … (in summary, it can be said …) signals the conclusion. In Hören Teil 4, such signposts help you follow the structure of the lecture.

questions.stem: Build the sentence (lesson 27).
questions.prompt: Many believe that the problem could have been solved.
questions.explanation: Konjunktiv II past of a modal passive: hätte … gelöst werden können. With the double infinitive (werden können) in a subordinate clause, the finite hätte goes in front of the cluster.

questions.stem: Build the report sentence (lessons 01 and 05).
questions.prompt: The company announces that the delivery is delayed.
questions.explanation: mitteilen is separable (teilt … mit). The reported statement without dass keeps verb-second order and uses the Konjunktiv I verzögere to show it's the company's information.

questions.stem:
This paragraph comes from a set of rules (Lesen Teil 5). Which heading fits it?

"§ 6 Fahrräder dürfen nur in den dafür vorgesehenen Ständern im Hof abgestellt werden. Im Treppenhaus und in den Fluren ist das Abstellen aus Brandschutzgründen nicht gestattet. Räder, die länger als vier Wochen nicht bewegt werden, können nach vorheriger Ankündigung entfernt werden."
questions.explanation: The whole paragraph is about where bicycles may be left (abgestellt) and what happens to abandoned ones. Fire safety (Brandschutz) is only the reason for one rule, which makes it a tempting but too narrow heading; repairs and parties aren't mentioned.

questions.stem: Match each structure from the course to an example.
questions.explanation: The Zustandspassiv (sein + Partizip II) describes a state (lesson 06); a Funktionsverbgefüge pairs a noun with a light verb (lesson 09); the gerundive is zu + Partizip I as an attribute (lesson 12); doch and mal are modal particles (lesson 16).

questions.stem: "Die Kündigung ist schriftlich zu erklären." What does this contract clause mean?
choices: Notice has already been given in writing.
Notice must be given in writing.
Notice is too complicated to explain in writing.
Notice can be given orally or in writing.
questions.explanation: sein + zu + infinitive in a rule means "must be done": Die Kündigung muss schriftlich erklärt werden. zu belongs to the infinitive; it isn't "too". There's no choice of oral notice: German law requires written form for termination.

questions.stem: "Der Arbeitnehmer hat seine Arbeitsunfähigkeit unverzüglich mitzuteilen." Which sentence means the same?
choices: Der Arbeitnehmer hat seine Arbeitsunfähigkeit sofort mitgeteilt.
Der Arbeitnehmer darf seine Arbeitsunfähigkeit mitteilen.
Der Arbeitnehmer muss seine Arbeitsunfähigkeit sofort mitteilen.
Der Arbeitnehmer kann seine Arbeitsunfähigkeit später mitteilen.
questions.explanation: haben + zu + infinitive is the active partner of sein + zu: the subject must do something. hat … mitgeteilt would be the perfect (he has reported it), and darf / kann change the obligation into permission or possibility.

questions.stem: "Wird der Vertrag nicht bis zum 30. Juni gekündigt, verlängert er sich um ein Jahr." What does it say?
choices: Will the contract not be terminated by 30 June? Then it is extended.
The contract will be terminated on 30 June and then extended.
Because the contract was terminated on 30 June, it is extended by a year.
If the contract isn't terminated by 30 June, it is extended by a year.
questions.explanation: A finite verb in first position followed by a comma and a second clause is a verb-first conditional: Wird … nicht gekündigt = Wenn … nicht gekündigt wird. It is not a question (no question mark) and not a cause.

questions.stem: Which sentence means the same as "Wenn das Arbeitsverhältnis endet, ist der Laptop zurückzugeben"?
choices: Endet das Arbeitsverhältnis, ist der Laptop zurückzugeben.
Das Arbeitsverhältnis endet, ob der Laptop zurückzugeben ist.
Ist das Arbeitsverhältnis zu enden, gibt man den Laptop zurück.
Das Arbeitsverhältnis endet, wenn der Laptop zurückgegeben ist.
questions.explanation: Leaving out wenn, the finite verb endet moves to the front of the conditional clause. The other options change the meaning: ob makes a question, ist … zu enden is not German, and the last one makes returning the laptop the condition.

questions.stem: In Germany, an employer sends you your dismissal by e-mail. Is it valid?
choices: Yes, if it is sent from the company's official address.
No: a notice of termination must be in written form on paper with a signature.
Yes, an e-mail always counts as written form.
Only if the works council agrees.
questions.explanation: German law requires written form (Schriftform) for any notice of termination, meaning a signed paper document; e-mail, fax and text messages don't count. The sender's address doesn't change that, and the works council's hearing is a separate requirement.

questions.stem: For how long does an employer in Germany normally continue to pay wages when an employee is ill?
choices: until the employee is well again, however long
questions.explanation: Die Lohnfortzahlung im Krankheitsfall lasts up to six weeks. Three days is when a doctor's certificate is normally needed; after six weeks, people with statutory insurance get sick pay from their health insurer instead.

questions.stem: What is "eine Abmahnung"?
choices: a reminder to pay a bill
an agreement to end a contract by mutual consent
a formal warning that misconduct must stop, or dismissal may follow
questions.explanation: An Abmahnung (from abmahnen) names a specific breach of duty and warns of consequences; before a dismissal for misconduct, it is usually required. A dismissal without notice is eine fristlose Kündigung. In everyday use, a payment reminder is eine Mahnung.

questions.stem: Match the terms to their meanings.
choices: employees' elected council in a business
agreement between a union and employers
the number of days off you are entitled to
questions.explanation: The Betriebsrat represents the employees of one business; the Tarifvertrag is negotiated by a union and an employers' association for a sector; the Mindestlohn is the statutory minimum wage; the Urlaubsanspruch is your holiday entitlement.

questions.stem: Listen to the radio news. What will happen on Thursday?

audio.text: Die Tarifverhandlungen für die Beschäftigten im Einzelhandel sind auch in der dritten Runde gescheitert. Die Gewerkschaft fordert sieben Prozent mehr Lohn, der Arbeitgeberverband bietet drei Prozent. Für Donnerstag sind in mehreren Städten Warnstreiks angekündigt.

choices: The union will accept the offer of three per cent.
A new minimum wage will come into force.
questions.explanation: Für Donnerstag sind Warnstreiks angekündigt: warning strikes have been announced for Thursday. The talks have just failed in the third round; the union demands seven per cent and the employers offer three.

questions.stem: Listen to the clause. What does it mean?

audio.text: Sollte der Arbeitnehmer krank werden, hat er dies sofort zu melden.

choices: The employee should try not to fall ill.
If the employee falls ill, he must report it immediately.
Should the employee report his illness immediately?
The employee reported his illness immediately.
questions.explanation: Sollte in first position, followed by a comma and a second clause, is a verb-first conditional: Sollte der Arbeitnehmer krank werden = Wenn der Arbeitnehmer krank werden sollte. hat … zu melden expresses the obligation.

questions.stem: Build the contract clause.
questions.prompt: If the employee is ill, he must report it immediately.
questions.explanation: The verb-first conditional starts with Ist; the main clause can start with so, followed by the finite verb hat. haben + zu puts the infinitive with zu at the end: mitzuteilen (separable mitteilen).

questions.stem: A colleague says: "Mir wurde gekündigt." What happened?
questions.explanation: kündigen + dative of the person (jemandem kündigen) means to dismiss someone, so Mir wurde gekündigt is "I was dismissed". Ich habe gekündigt would mean she resigned; a warning is eine Abmahnung.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between Sprachmittlung and translation?
choices: Mediation is always oral, translation always written.
Mediation always goes from German into English.
Mediation passes on what matters to a particular reader, in a suitable form; translation renders the whole text.
Mediation keeps every sentence but changes the register.
questions.explanation: Sprachmittlung selects and adapts: it keeps das Wesentliche for this reader and changes length, order, register and sometimes language. It can be written or oral and in any direction, and it doesn't keep every sentence.

questions.stem: You summarize a long e-mail for your manager. How should your summary start?
choices: with the thanks and greetings from the original e-mail
with the background, in the order of the original
with your own opinion of the writer
with the most important point: what has changed or what she has to decide
questions.explanation: Main point first: a busy reader needs the decision or the change at once. Politeness formulas and background are usually left out, and your opinion doesn't belong in a summary of someone else's text.

questions.stem: HR writes: "Sämtliche Beschäftigten werden gebeten, bis zum 30. September die Registrierung im neuen System vorzunehmen." Which chat message passes this on best to a new colleague?
choices: Du musst dich bis 30. September im neuen System registrieren.
Sämtliche Beschäftigten werden gebeten, die Registrierung vorzunehmen.
HR hat eine Mail geschickt, irgendwas mit dem System.
Es wird um Vornahme der Registrierung gebeten.
questions.explanation: Good mediation keeps the facts (what, by when) and changes the register for the reader: short, with du and a plain verb (sich registrieren instead of die Registrierung vornehmen). Copying the notice doesn't help, and the vague version loses the deadline.

questions.stem: Complete the summary: "Der Lieferant räumt ___, dass ein Fehler passiert sei."
questions.explanation: einräumen (to admit, concede) is separable: er räumt ein. It signals that the speaker admits something unfavourable, which is useful information for the reader of a summary.

questions.stem: In a written summary for your manager you want to make clear that the delay is the supplier's claim, not a fact you checked. Which sentence does that?
choices: Laut Herrn Ruiz habe sein Lieferant Probleme.
Herr Ruiz hat Probleme mit seinem Lieferanten, das ist klar.
Ich glaube, der Lieferant hat Probleme.
questions.explanation: laut + the source and the Konjunktiv I (habe) mark the statement as reported. The plain indicative presents it as a fact, das ist klar adds your own certainty, and Ich glaube turns it into your opinion.

questions.stem: In a traditional German company, who usually offers "das Du"?
choices: whoever has been in the company longer
the older or more senior person
nobody: you simply start using du
questions.explanation: Traditionally the older or more senior person offers the du (jemandem das Du anbieten), and the other accepts. Simply switching to du with a superior or client is a classic Fauxpas. Many start-ups use du from the first day, so watch the company's practice.

questions.stem: "Das war ein ziemlicher Fauxpas." What happened?
choices: Someone broke an unwritten social rule.
questions.explanation: der Fauxpas (from French, said fo-PA) is a social blunder, a breach of manners or etiquette. Forgetting an appointment or a calculation error is just a mistake (ein Fehler, ein Versehen).

questions.stem: "Für dieses Gespräch braucht man viel Fingerspitzengefühl." What do you need?
choices: tact and a feel for the situation
a lot of patience to wait
questions.explanation: das Fingerspitzengefühl is literally "fingertip feeling": sensitivity and tact in a delicate situation. It has nothing to do with typing or with technical knowledge.

questions.stem: Listen to the voicemail. Which summary for your manager is best?

audio.text: Hallo, hier ist Sabine Lange von Bürotec. Es geht um die drei Drucker für Ihre Abteilung. Die kommen leider erst am Montag, unser Lager hatte einen Engpass. Das tut mir sehr leid. Wenn Sie wollen, bringen wir Ihnen bis dahin ein Ersatzgerät. Geben Sie mir bitte bis morgen Bescheid, ob Sie das möchten. Danke!

choices: Frau Lange von Bürotec hat angerufen. Sie hat sich entschuldigt und gesagt, dass es ihr sehr leidtut.
Die Lieferung der Drucker verzögert sich bis Montag. Frau Lange bittet um Rückruf bis morgen, ob ein Ersatzgerät gebracht werden soll.
Die Drucker sind kaputt. Bürotec bringt morgen neue.
Frau Lange hat wegen der Drucker angerufen. Bitte rufen Sie zurück.
questions.explanation: The best summary keeps the essential facts: the delay and the new date, the offer and what the manager must decide by when. The first option keeps only the apology, the third gets the facts wrong (nothing is broken; the delivery is late), and the fourth leaves the reader without information.

questions.stem: Listen to your colleague. Why has the meeting been postponed?

audio.text: Also, kurz gesagt: Das Treffen mit den Kunden aus Lyon wird auf nächste Woche verschoben, weil ihr Flug gestrichen wurde. Den neuen Termin schickt uns Frau Martin noch.

choices: The clients want to change the agenda.
questions.explanation: weil ihr Flug gestrichen wurde: because their flight was cancelled (streichen: to cancel). Frau Martin is only the person who will send the new date.

questions.stem: Build the sentence.
questions.prompt: In substance he said that we should wait.
questions.explanation: sinngemäß (in substance) marks a paraphrase; it stands in the Mittelfeld before the participle gesagt or starts the sentence (Sinngemäß hat er gesagt, …). In the dass-clause the modal sollen goes to the end, after the infinitive warten.

questions.stem: In a company with a clear hierarchy, you go straight to your team leader's manager with a problem, without talking to your team leader first. How may this be read?
choices: as a sign of good Eigeninitiative that everyone expects
as completely normal in every German company
as a request for a transfer
as going behind your team leader's back
questions.explanation: Even in companies that call their hierarchies flat, decisions often follow a path (der Dienstweg). Skipping a level can look as if you are going behind someone's back. Initiative is valued, but usually through the right channel.

glossary.definition: Literature written in German by the German-speaking minority of Prague around 1900, many of them Jewish: Franz Kafka, Max Brod, Franz Werfel and Rainer Maria Rilke are its best-known names.

A classic German prose form of middle length that centres on one extraordinary event; Goethe called its subject an "unerhörte Begebenheit" (an unheard-of occurrence). Kafka's Die Verwandlung is usually called an Erzählung, sometimes a Novelle.
From where, and with how much knowledge, a story is told: the standard types are the omniscient narrator, the figural narrator and the first-person narrator.
A narrator (der auktoriale Erzähler) who stands above the story, knows the thoughts of all characters and what will happen, and may comment or address the reader.

A third-person narrator (der personale Erzähler) tied to one character: the reader sees and knows only what this character sees and knows, without comment. Die Verwandlung is told this way, close to Gregor.

A character's thoughts given in the narrator's grammar (third person, past tense) but in the character's words and tone, without "he thought" or quotation marks: Sie kam schon wieder zu spät. Was würde der Chef sagen? Time words such as heute and morgen stay unchanged.

A character's thoughts given directly, in the first person and present tense, often in fragments, with no narrator in between: Schon wieder zu spät. Was sagt der Chef? Arthur Schnitzler's Leutnant Gustl (1900) is told entirely this way.
An element that recurs in a text and carries meaning (das Motiv), such as the door in Die Verwandlung. A Leitmotiv runs through a whole work.

The German school text type die Inhaltsangabe: an introductory sentence (author, title, text type, year, theme), then the main events in order, in the present tense, in neutral words, without quotations; what characters say is reported with the Konjunktiv I.
One of the large parts of a play (der Akt, also der Aufzug). A classical tragedy has five acts.
A smaller unit of a play (die Szene). In older German plays a new scene, called Auftritt, begins whenever a character enters or leaves.
Text in a play that isn't spoken (die Regieanweisung): it describes the setting and what the actors do, usually printed in italics or brackets.
A speech by one character alone on stage (der Monolog), often at a moment of decision; the opposite of dialogue between characters.
A play that ends in catastrophe, usually the death of the main character (die Tragödie, older das Trauerspiel); its counterpart is the comedy (die Komödie, das Lustspiel).

A play built on the classical model (das geschlossene Drama): usually five acts, few characters, one main plot, a short span of time, strict cause and effect and elevated language, following the pattern exposition – rising action – climax – falling action – catastrophe.

A play that breaks the classical rules (das offene Drama): many short, loosely connected scenes, jumps in time and place, everyday or dialect language and often an open ending. Büchner's Woyzeck is the classic example.
The old rule of poetics that only kings and nobles could be the heroes of a tragedy, while ordinary people belonged in comedy. The bourgeois tragedy of the 18th century broke it.

An 18th-century type of tragedy (das bürgerliche Trauerspiel) about middle-class people, their families and morals, often in conflict with the nobility: Lessing's Emilia Galotti, Schiller's Kabale und Liebe.

A literary movement of young writers in about 1765–1785 who celebrated feeling, nature, freedom and genius against the rules of the Enlightenment and the power of the princes; the young Goethe and the young Schiller are its best-known names.
"Before March": the years before the March Revolution of 1848 (roughly 1830–1848), when writers such as Georg Büchner fought censorship and demanded political freedom and social justice.
Leaving out an unstressed sound or short word, often marked with an apostrophe: hätt for hätte, glaub' for glaube, geht's for geht es. Common in speech and in plays that imitate it.

A system in which a state is made up of member states (Länder, Kantone) that have their own parliaments, governments and areas of responsibility, while the federal level (der Bund) handles the rest. Germany, Austria and Switzerland are all federal.
The rule that a task should be handled at the lowest level that can do it well (town, Land or canton, federal state, EU). It is written into the EU treaties.

The EU institution in which the ministers of the member states meet, depending on the topic (der Rat der Europäischen Union); it decides on EU laws together with the European Parliament. Not the same as the European Council or the Council of Europe (Europarat).
The summit of the heads of state or government of the EU member states (der Europäische Rat). It sets the general political direction but doesn't pass laws.
An EU law (die Verordnung) that applies directly in all member states without a national law, such as the end of mobile roaming charges in 2017.
An EU law (die Richtlinie) that sets a goal; each member state must implement it (umsetzen) in its own national law by a deadline.

A language with several centres, each with its own standard (like British and American English). German has standard varieties in Germany, Austria and Switzerland, with smaller ones in Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, South Tyrol and East Belgium.
Linguists' neutral word for any form of a language (die Varietät): a dialect, a national standard, the language of a social group.
The standard language of one centre of a pluricentric language: Austrian standard German, Swiss standard German, the standard German of Germany. All are equally correct.
A word or feature typical of standard German in Austria (der Austriazismus): der Jänner, die Marille, der Topfen, ich bin gesessen.
A word or feature typical of standard German in Switzerland (der Helvetismus): das Velo, parkieren, das Trottoir, ss instead of ß.
A word or feature typical of standard German in Germany but not in Austria or Switzerland (der Teutonismus): die Sahne, der Bürgersteig, das Abitur.

A situation in which a community uses two clearly separate forms of a language for different purposes (die Diglossie). In German-speaking Switzerland, Swiss German dialects are spoken in almost every situation, while standard German is used mainly for writing and formal speech.

The Alemannic dialects spoken in German-speaking Switzerland (das Schweizerdeutsch, die Mundart), such as Zurich or Bern German. Not the same as Swiss standard German (Schweizer Hochdeutsch), the standard language used in writing.

A verb form made from the infinitive stem + -e, -est, -e, -en, -et, -en, with no vowel change: er komme, sie habe, es gebe, man könne; sein: ich sei, wir seien. Its main use is indirect speech in news, reports and formal writing, where it marks a statement as someone else's. It also appears in old-style instructions (Man nehme …), in maths (Gegeben sei …) and in set phrases (Gott sei Dank). Not to be confused with the Konjunktiv II (wäre, hätte, würde).

Someone's exact words, in quotation marks and in the indicative: Sie sagte: „Ich bin müde.“ German quotation marks open low and close high. After a quotation, the reporting verb comes before the subject: „…“, sagte sie.

Passing on what someone said without quoting their exact words, in a clause after a verb of saying: Sie sagte, sie sei müde. In formal German the verb goes into the Konjunktiv I (or its replacement), pronouns shift to the reporter's point of view, and the tense of the reporting verb doesn't matter. In everyday speech the indicative or Konjunktiv II is common: Sie hat gesagt, dass sie müde ist / sie wäre müde.

In indirect speech, a Konjunktiv I that looks like the indicative is replaced by the Konjunktiv II (sie haben → sie hätten, wir kommen → wir kämen); if the Konjunktiv II also looks like the indicative, as with weak verbs, würde + infinitive is used (sie zahlten → sie würden zahlen). sei and seien are always distinct and never need replacing.

A question reported in a subordinate clause, introduced by ob (yes/no questions) or a question word, with the verb at the end and no question mark: Sie fragte, ob er komme. Er wollte wissen, wann das Urteil falle. In formal reports the verb is in the Konjunktiv I.

An order or request in indirect speech. Because an imperative can't be reported, German uses sollen (instruction: Er sagte, sie solle warten) or, more politely and formally, mögen (Sie bat, er möge Platz nehmen), or an infinitive with zu after bitten, auffordern, raten (Sie bat ihn, Platz zu nehmen).

The use of a modal verb to show how sure the speaker is, or where the information comes from, rather than what the subject can, must or wants to do. sollen = it is said (Er soll reich sein); wollen = the subject claims (Sie will nichts gesehen haben); muss = very sure, dürfte = probably, kann/könnte = possibly, kann nicht = impossible. Usually in the present or Konjunktiv II, often with a perfect infinitive for the past: Er soll gelogen haben. Its opposite is the objective use (Er muss arbeiten = he has to work).

Partizip II + haben or sein: gesehen haben, gegangen sein (passive: gesehen worden sein). Used after subjective modal verbs for the past (Sie muss den Termin vergessen haben), in the Futur II (Er wird gegangen sein) and in zu-infinitives (Er behauptet, nichts gesehen zu haben).

werden + perfect infinitive: Wir werden die Wohnung abbezahlt haben. Sie wird gegangen sein. It expresses an action completed before a point in the future (Bis 2041 werden wir … abbezahlt haben; in speech usually the perfect: Bis 2041 haben wir … abbezahlt) and, more often, an assumption about the past (Er wird den Bus verpasst haben = he probably missed the bus). In a subordinate clause werden goes last: …, dass er es vergessen haben wird.

A verb that introduces what someone said: sagen, erklären, mitteilen (neutral); betonen (stress), einräumen (concede), bestreiten (deny), versichern (assure), bekräftigen (reaffirm), ankündigen (announce in advance), verkünden (make public), warnen vor (warn of), behaupten (claim, suggesting doubt). The choice of verb tells the reader the speaker's attitude, and sometimes the writer's.

A word that works like a preposition but stands after its noun: dem Bericht zufolge (according to the report), meiner Meinung nach (in my opinion), der Vereinbarung gemäß (in accordance with the agreement). zufolge follows its noun (with the dative; a rare formal variant puts it before a genitive); nach and gemäß can go before or after.

The present tense used for past events to make them vivid, as if happening now: in live tickers and sports commentary (Novak tritt an … und trifft!), at the dramatic moment of a story, in jokes and in history writing (1989 fällt die Mauer). In a formal written report the simple past is the norm.

Leaving out words the reader or listener can supply: verbs, articles or whole clauses. Typical in headlines (Bayern weiter souverän), tickers (Gelb für Lenz.), notes and casual speech (Kommst du mit? – Keine Zeit.). Not used in essays or formal letters.

A sentence form in which the subject is the person or thing the action is done to. German has two: the Vorgangspassiv with werden (Die Brücke wird gesperrt: an action) and the Zustandspassiv with sein (Die Brücke ist gesperrt: the resulting state). Used for processes, rules, news and when the doer is unknown or unimportant.

The passive with werden + past participle, describing an action or process: Die Brücke wird am Montag gesperrt. It exists in every tense (wurde gesperrt, ist gesperrt worden, war gesperrt worden, wird gesperrt werden) and with modal verbs (muss gesperrt werden). The agent can be added with von.

sein + past participle, describing the state that results from an action: Die Brücke ist gesperrt (it is closed now) vs Die Brücke wird gesperrt (someone is closing it). Past: war gesperrt; with a modal: muss gesperrt sein. Only verbs whose action leaves a lasting result have one (bauen, sperren, verkaufen; not sehen or lieben), and it rarely names an agent.

A passive with a modal verb: modal + past participle + werden. Das Formular muss abgegeben werden. In a subordinate clause the modal goes last: …, weil es ersetzt werden muss. Past: Das Werk musste geschlossen werden. Shorter alternatives are sein + zu, sich lassen and -bar adjectives.

sein + zu + infinitive, a formal alternative to the modal passive meaning "must be done" (Das Formular ist bis Freitag abzugeben = muss abgegeben werden) or "can be done", often with leicht, kaum or nicht (Das ist leicht zu reparieren = kann leicht repariert werden). Typical of regulations, official letters and labels (zu verbrauchen bis …).

sich lassen + infinitive, a neutral alternative to the passive with können: Der Fleck lässt sich entfernen = kann entfernt werden. The thing is the subject and lassen agrees with it (Die Flecken lassen sich entfernen). Not to be confused with lassen meaning "have something done": Ich lasse das Auto reparieren.

A passive in which the person who receives something (the dative object of the active sentence) becomes the subject: bekommen + past participle. Die Kundin bekommt den Kaufpreis erstattet = Der Kundin wird der Kaufpreis erstattet. Colloquially kriegen, formally erhalten: Sie erhalten die Unterlagen zugeschickt.

A passive without a subject, made from verbs without an accusative object, saying that an activity takes place: Hier wird nicht geraucht. Den Mitarbeitern wurde gekündigt. werden is always singular. If nothing else is in position 1, es fills it (Es wird verhandelt); otherwise es disappears (Heute wird verhandelt).

A fixed combination of a noun (often with a preposition) and a verb that has lost most of its own meaning, so that the noun carries the meaning: eine Entscheidung treffen (= entscheiden), in Betracht ziehen (= erwägen), zur Sprache bringen (= ansprechen). Preposition, article and verb are fixed. Typical of formal writing; some express a state (zur Verfügung stehen), a beginning (in Gang kommen) or a passive (Anwendung finden).

The verb in a Funktionsverbgefüge, which adds little meaning of its own: bringen, kommen, nehmen, stellen, stehen, setzen, treffen, ziehen, finden, üben. It still adds nuance: stehen expresses a state, stellen or bringen a cause, kommen that something happens (zur Sprache kommen / bringen).

A stressed verb prefix that splits off in main clauses and goes to the end: aufladen → Er lädt das Auto auf. The participle has ge- in the middle (aufgeladen) and the zu-infinitive has zu inside (aufzuladen). Examples: ab-, an-, auf-, aus-, ein-, mit-, vor-, zu-, zurück-.

An unstressed verb prefix that never separates and takes no ge- in the participle: be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss-, ver-, zer- (verladen → er verlädt, hat verladen). Many have typical meanings: be- makes a verb transitive, ver- can mean "wrongly" or a change, zer- "into pieces", ent- "away", miss- "badly".

A prefix that can be separable or inseparable depending on the verb: über-, unter-, um-, durch-, wieder-. As a rule of thumb the separable verb is literal with the stress on the prefix (ÜBERsetzen, to ferry across; hat übergesetzt), the inseparable one figurative with the stress on the stem (überSETZen, to translate; hat übersetzt).

An instruction given with the bare infinitive at the end, typical of signs, labels, manuals and recipes: Vor Gebrauch schütteln. Nicht berühren! Bitte anschnallen. It addresses nobody in particular; nicht goes before the infinitive, sich and often articles are dropped.

A description of how something is done or made, step by step: in the present tense, impersonal (passive or man), in strict order with words such as zunächst, anschließend, sobald and nachdem, and precise about quantities and times. Zuerst wird das Malz geschrotet. Anschließend wird es mit Wasser gemischt.

A participle used as an adjective before a noun, with other words in front of it: die seit Jahren steigenden Mieten, der von der Stadt geplante Neubau. It packs a relative clause in front of the noun: article, then the words of the clause in clause order, then the participle with an adjective ending, then the noun. Partizip I is active and simultaneous; Partizip II of a transitive verb is passive, of a sein-verb active and completed. Typical of written German.

The infinitive + -d: steigend, wohnend, wachsend. As an attribute it takes adjective endings (die steigenden Mieten) and is active, describing something happening at the same time as the main verb. With zu in front it becomes the gerundive (das zu lösende Problem).

zu + Partizip I + adjective ending before a noun: das zu lösende Problem = das Problem, das gelöst werden muss (or kann). It is the attribute form of sein + zu: usually "must", "can" with kaum, leicht or nicht (eine kaum zu überschätzende Bedeutung). Separable verbs take zu inside: die einzusparenden Emissionen. Only transitive verbs form it.

Writing that turns actions into nouns and links them with prepositions and genitives: wegen des Lehrkräftemangels, zur Verbesserung der Schulen, nach dem Abschluss. Short, precise and impersonal; typical of reports, official letters, CVs, headlines and academic texts. Piled up, it becomes hard to read.

Writing and speaking that builds sentences around verbs and subordinate clauses: weil viele Lehrkräfte fehlen, damit die Schulen besser werden, nachdem sie die Schule abgeschlossen hatte. Typical of speech and personal writing; the opposite of nominal style.

Making a noun from another word, especially from a verb: fördern → die Förderung (-ung, feminine), lernen → das Lernen (infinitive, neuter), abschließen → der Abschluss (stem noun), suchen → die Suche (-e). Also the process of turning a clause into a noun phrase: wenn man ankommt → bei der Ankunft.

An infinitive used as a noun: always neuter and written with a capital letter: das Lernen, das Sitzenbleiben, beim Schreiben. It names the activity itself and can be formed from any verb, so it is the safe choice when no other noun exists.

A noun in the genitive after another noun, saying whose it is or what it belongs to: das Ende des Films. In nominal style the object of the original verb (die Reform des Schulsystems) or the subject of an intransitive verb (die Ankunft der Schüler) becomes a genitive attribute. Without an article or adjective, von + dative replaces it: die Einstellung von Lehrkräften.

A relative clause with no noun before it, starting with wer (whoever) or was (whatever): Wer zu spät kommt, den bestraft das Leben. The main clause usually picks it up with der/das (or a da-word) in the case the main clause needs; the pick-up word can be left out only when both cases are the same (Wer A sagt, muss auch B sagen).

The present tense used in laws and rules to say what must be the case, not what is: Die Wohnung ist unverletzlich (the home must not be violated); Eine Zensur findet nicht statt (censorship is forbidden). English laws often use "shall" for the same job.

A word that makes an adjective stronger or weaker: äußerst, höchst, überaus (extremely), ausgesprochen (decidedly), durchaus (definitely, often before a "but"), ziemlich, recht (fairly), eher (rather), etwas (a bit, mostly with negative adjectives), wenig (not very), alles andere als (anything but).

A small, unstressed word such as ja, doch, mal, halt, eben, schon, denn, wohl, etwa, eigentlich, ruhig, bloß or nur that adds the speaker's attitude (shared knowledge, surprise, urging, resignation, softening) without changing the facts: Das ist ja teuer. Komm doch mit! Was ist denn los? Modal particles can be left out, never stand in position 1, sit in the middle of the sentence (usually after pronouns and before nicht), and depend on the sentence type. Most of them also exist as ordinary adverbs or conjunctions with another meaning.

A subordinate clause that says by what means something is done, introduced by indem or dadurch, dass (English: by + -ing): Man baut Stress ab, indem man Sport treibt. Man baut Stress dadurch ab, dass man Sport treibt. It answers the question Wie? or Wodurch?

A clause that admits a fact which would normally lead to a different result: Obwohl sie die Beste war, bekam sie die Stelle nicht. German introduces it with obwohl (everyday), obgleich and wenngleich (formal), auch wenn or selbst wenn (even if), or the pattern so … auch / wie … auch (Sosehr ich mich auch bemühe, …). Concession is different from contrast, which only sets two facts side by side (während, wohingegen).

A comparison with something that isn't (or probably isn't) true, introduced by als ob or als wenn (verb at the end) or by als with the verb straight after it, usually with the Konjunktiv II: Er tut so, als ob er nichts gehört hätte = Er tut so, als hätte er nichts gehört. Formal writing also uses the Konjunktiv I (als habe er nichts gehört); casual speech sometimes uses the indicative.

Making a claim only as strong as the evidence allows, with phrases such as es scheint, dass …, vieles spricht dafür, dass …, in der Regel, tendenziell, eher, or a subjective modal verb (Das dürfte der Hauptgrund sein). Typical of good argumentative and academic writing.

A rhetorical device: several sentences or clauses begin with the same word or words, which creates rhythm and stresses the key idea: Wir wollen eine Stadt, in der … Wir wollen eine Stadt, in der … (Not the same as the grammatical sense of anaphora, a word that refers back.)

A rhetorical device: three parallel words, phrases or clauses, often growing in length or weight: Wir haben geplant, wir haben gestritten, und am Ende haben wir gemeinsam gebaut. Three parts feel complete to listeners.
In rhetoric, a series of words or clauses that rises step by step in intensity and ends on the strongest point: Das kostet uns Zeit, es kostet uns Geld, und es kostet uns das Vertrauen der Menschen.

A question to which the speaker expects no answer, because the answer is obvious or the speaker gives it straight away: Wollen wir wirklich eine Stadt ohne Bäume? Used in speeches and arguments to involve the audience.

The "let's" form: the verb in first position followed by wir: Gehen wir! Machen wir uns nichts vor. For sein it uses the Konjunktiv I form: Seien wir ehrlich! (Sind wir ehrlich? would be a question). The alternative is lass uns / lasst uns / lassen Sie uns + infinitive: Lassen Sie uns anfangen.

A signal in a text or in speech that the words are not meant literally: exaggeration, particles of obviousness (natürlich, ja, doch) where nothing is obvious, an inappropriately formal style, distancing words such as sogenannt and angeblich, quotation marks around a single word, an over-polite Konjunktiv, or (in speech) the tone of voice.

The ways a language makes new words from existing ones. German uses mainly derivation (adding a prefix or suffix: messen → die Messung) and compounding (joining words: die Forschung + das Ergebnis → das Forschungsergebnis).
Making a new word by adding a prefix or suffix to an existing one: frei → die Freiheit, lesen → lesbar, wichtig → unwichtig. The suffix often decides the word class and, for nouns, the gender.

A part added at the end of a word to make a new word: -ung, -heit, -keit, -bar, -los. Noun suffixes usually fix the gender: words in -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ität and -ion are feminine, words in -ismus and -ling masculine, words in -chen and -ment neuter.

A word made of two or more words written together: das Forschungsergebnis, die Datenbank, der Versuchsaufbau. The last part (the head) decides the gender, plural and basic meaning; the parts in front narrow it down. Read long compounds from the end.

The last part of a compound, which decides its word class, gender and plural: in die Versuchsperson the head is die Person, so the compound is feminine. The part in front is the modifier (Bestimmungswort).

A sound inserted between the parts of a compound without changing the meaning: Forschung-s-ergebnis, Sonne-n-energie, Kind-er-zimmer. After -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion and -ität there is always an -s-; a verb stem never keeps the infinitive -en (Messwert, but Wartezimmer); otherwise it has to be learned with the word.

A shortened word: clipped (die Uni, die Kita, der Azubi) or made of initials, spoken letter by letter (die EU, der Lkw, die KI) or as a word (die NATO). A short form takes the gender of the head noun of the full form: der Lkw because der Lastkraftwagen.

An adjective made of a noun, adjective or participle plus an adjective: benutzerfreundlich, fehleranfällig, energiesparend, hellblau. Like compound nouns, it is written as one word and read from the end.

A clause with zu + infinitive at the end and no subject of its own: Sie versucht, früher aufzustehen. Its subject is the subject (or sometimes the object) of the main clause; with a different subject German uses a dass clause. It can be in the perfect (gesehen zu haben) or the passive (ausgewählt zu werden).

A word in the main clause that points forward to a following clause: es (Es ist schwer, …) or da(r)- + preposition (Sie träumt davon, …; Es kommt darauf an, …). With some verbs it is required, with many optional; when it is there, the comma before the infinitive clause is required.

Phrases that tell listeners or readers where they are in a talk or text: Mein Vortrag besteht aus drei Teilen; Ich komme nun zu …; Wie bereits erwähnt; Zusammenfassend lässt sich sagen. In spoken German they replace the headings of a written text.

In a German clause, the part between the conjugated verb (position 2) and the other verb parts at the end. Its typical order: pronouns first (nominative – accusative – dative), then nouns with dative before accusative, adverbials roughly time – cause – manner – place, and known information before new information.

Position 1 in a German main clause, before the conjugated verb. It holds exactly one part of the sentence: the subject (neutral) or another part that links to the previous sentence or is emphasized (Dieser Rückgang hat mehrere Gründe; Den ersten Punkt habe ich erklärt). An unstressed es as object and the reflexive sich can't go there.

A memory aid for the usual order of adverbials in the Mittelfeld: temporal (when), kausal (why), modal (how), lokal (where): Sie hält morgen wegen der Prüfung ohne Folien im Seminar einen Vortrag. A tendency, not a strict rule: known information still comes before new.

The group of verbs at the end of a German clause. In a subordinate clause the finite verb is normally last and each verb depends on the one to its right, so it is read from the right: …, dass das Werk geschlossen werden muss (muss → werden → geschlossen).

The infinitive that replaces the participle of a modal verb (and of lassen) when it has another infinitive with it: Wir haben die Preise erhöhen müssen (not gemusst). In a subordinate clause the finite verb then goes in front of the whole cluster: …, weil wir die Preise haben erhöhen müssen; …, dass er hätte kommen sollen.

Placing a part of the sentence after the final verbs, outside the verb bracket. Comparisons with als and wie usually stand there even in writing (Der Umsatz ist stärker gestiegen als erwartet); other phrases there are typical of speech (Ich hab sie getroffen gestern, beim Bäcker).

The level of formality chosen for a reader or listener. German ranges from formal written (nominal style, passive, genitive: Aufgrund des Streiks entfällt der Unterricht) through neutral (Wegen des Streiks fällt der Unterricht aus) to colloquial (Wegen dem Streik ist heute kein Unterricht).

A short word or phrase added to the end of a statement to ask for agreement. German uses one fixed word instead of the English verb tags: oder? (everywhere), ne? or nich? (north), gell? (south and Austria), wa? (Berlin), nicht wahr? (formal).

The traditional use of the masculine form for a mixed group or for people in general: die Lehrer, alle Mitarbeiter. Many people find that it leaves women and non-binary people out, which is why gender-inclusive forms are used as alternatives.

Forms that refer to people of all genders instead of the generic masculine: Doppelnennung (Kolleginnen und Kollegen), the slash (Mitarbeiter/-innen), participles (die Studierenden), neutral nouns (die Lehrkraft) and signs such as the asterisk (Lehrer*innen). Usage is debated; the Doppelnennung and neutral nouns are widely accepted, while the asterisk is not part of official spelling.

aliases: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages
glossary.definition: The Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, which describes language ability in six levels: A1 and A2 (basic user), B1 and B2 (independent user), C1 and C2 (proficient user). Exams such as the Goethe-Zertifikat are named after its levels.
A description of what a learner at a given CEFR level can do with the language, for example: understand the main ideas of complex texts on concrete and abstract topics (B2).

The links between sentences that you can see in the text itself: pronouns (sie, dies), connectors (jedoch, außerdem, deshalb) and repeated or related words. Lesen Teil 2 of the Goethe B2 tests it by asking which sentence fits a gap.

Whether a text makes sense as a whole: a logical order of ideas, each point linked to the next, and a clear structure. It is one of the criteria for marking writing and speaking at B2; cohesion (connectors, pronouns) is one of the means to achieve it.

A condition expressed without wenn by putting the finite verb first: Wird der Vertrag nicht gekündigt, verlängert er sich (= Wenn der Vertrag nicht gekündigt wird, …). Typical of legal and formal texts; with sollte it makes the condition sound less likely: Sollte eine Bestimmung unwirksam sein, …

Passing on the content of a text or conversation to someone who can't or won't read or hear it themselves, in the form they need: the essential points, main point first, in a suitable register, sometimes in another language. Unlike translation, it selects and adapts.

references.title: Connectors at B2
references.body:
## Word order types

| Type | Word order | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Subordinating conjunction | conjugated verb at the end of its clause | *indem, sofern, soweit, ohne dass, (an)statt dass, als dass, wenngleich, obgleich, auch wenn, selbst wenn, während, wohingegen, als ob, als wenn* |
| Adverb (position 1 or middle) | verb straight after it in position 1 | *dagegen, hingegen, jedoch, allerdings, insofern, zwar* |
| Special | see the notes below | *es sei denn, je nachdem, als* + verb, *so … auch* |

## Means, condition and extent

| Connector | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *indem* | by (doing) | *Man lernt, indem man übt.* |
| *dadurch, dass* | by (doing); because | *Man lernt dadurch, dass man übt.* |
| *sofern* | provided that | *Sofern es dir passt, treffen wir uns um acht.* |
| *soweit* | as far as | *Soweit ich weiß, ist das kostenlos.* |
| *insofern …, als* | in that | *Er hat insofern recht, als …* |
| *je nachdem, ob/wie/wann* | depending on | *Je nachdem, wie es mir geht, komme ich mit.* |
| *je nach* + dative | depending on (+ noun) | *je nach Wetter* |
| *es sei denn* (+ verb second, or + *dass*) | unless (always second) | *Ich komme, es sei denn, es regnet.* |
| *außer wenn* | except when | *Ich schlafe gut, außer wenn ich grüble.* |
| *ohne dass* | without (different subject) | *Er ging, ohne dass es jemand merkte.* |
| *ohne … zu* | without (same subject) | *Er ging, ohne sich zu verabschieden.* |
| *(an)statt dass* | instead of (different subject) | *Statt dass er hilft, redet er.* |
| *(an)statt … zu* | instead of (same subject) | *Statt zu helfen, redet er.* |
| *zu* + adj. …, *als dass* + Konj. II | too … to | *Es ist zu komplex, als dass man es schnell lösen könnte.* |

## Concession

| Connector | Register | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *obwohl* | everyday | *Obwohl es regnet, gehen wir raus.* |
| *obgleich, wenngleich* | formal, written | *Wenngleich die Lücke kleiner ist, bleibt sie groß.* |
| *auch wenn* | even if / even though | *Auch wenn es unbequem ist, …* |
| *selbst wenn* | even if (stronger, often Konj. II) | *Selbst wenn wir wollten, könnten wir nicht.* |
| *wenn auch* (often without a verb) | albeit | *Es hat sich verbessert, wenn auch langsam.* |
| *so / wie* + adj. … *auch* | no matter how | *Sosehr ich mich auch bemühe, ich verstehe es nicht.* |
| *zwar …, aber / doch / jedoch* | admittedly …, but | *Das ist zwar teuer, aber gut.* |
| *trotzdem, dennoch* (B1) | nevertheless (adverbs) | *Es regnet. Trotzdem gehen wir raus.* |

## Contrast

| Connector | Type | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *während* | verb at the end | *Er arbeitet Vollzeit, während sie Teilzeit arbeitet.* |
| *wohingegen* | verb at the end, formal | *…, wohingegen heute viele Väter Elternzeit nehmen.* |
| *dagegen, hingegen* | adverb | *Ältere Bewerber hingegen sind oft benachteiligt.* |
| *jedoch* | adverb (formal *aber*) | *Jedoch fehlt das Geld. / Das Geld fehlt jedoch.* |
| *allerdings* | adverb, limits what was said | *Das ist modern, allerdings gibt es keinen Aufzug.* |
| *nicht A, sondern B* | replaces after a negation | *nicht dagegen, sondern dafür* |
| *nicht nur A, sondern auch B* | adds | *nicht nur jung, sondern auch alt* |

## Unreal comparison

| Pattern | Verb position | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *als ob* + Konj. II | end | *Er tut so, als ob er nichts gehört hätte.* |
| *als wenn* + Konj. II | end | *…, als wenn er nichts gehört hätte.* |
| *als* + Konj. II (or I) | straight after *als* | *…, als hätte er nichts gehört.* |

## Arguing and discussing

| Function | Phrases |
|---|---|
| Position | *Ich vertrete die Ansicht, dass …; Meines Erachtens …; Aus meiner Sicht …* |
| Adding reasons | *Dafür spricht vor allem, dass …; Hinzu kommt, dass …; Nicht zuletzt …* |
| Conceding, objecting | *Zwar …, aber …; Man könnte einwenden, dass …; Dem lässt sich entgegenhalten, dass …* |
| Hedging | *Es scheint, dass …; Vieles spricht dafür, dass …; in der Regel* |
| Concluding | *Zusammenfassend lässt sich sagen, dass …; Alles in allem …; Daraus folgt, dass …* |
| Proposing (Konj. II) | *Wäre es nicht sinnvoller, …? Wie wäre es, wenn …? Könnten wir uns darauf einigen, dass …?* |
| Taking and holding the floor | *Darf ich dazu kurz etwas sagen? Lassen Sie mich bitte ausreden.* |

references.title: Funktionsverbgefüge
references.body:
## Common Funktionsverbgefüge

The noun carries the meaning; preposition, article and verb are fixed.

| Funktionsverbgefüge | simple verb or paraphrase | English |
|---|---|---|
| *eine Entscheidung treffen* | *entscheiden* | to make a decision |
| *eine Frage stellen* | *fragen* | to ask a question |
| *einen Antrag stellen* | *beantragen* | to submit an application |
| *Kritik üben (an + dat.)* | *kritisieren* | to criticise |
| *Einfluss nehmen (auf + acc.)* | *beeinflussen* | to influence |
| *Bezug nehmen (auf + acc.)* | *sich beziehen auf* | to refer to |
| *Rücksicht nehmen (auf + acc.)* | *rücksichtsvoll sein* | to show consideration for |
| *Maßnahmen ergreifen / treffen* | *handeln* | to take measures |
| *eine Rolle spielen* | *wichtig sein* | to play a role, matter |
| *in Betracht ziehen* | *erwägen, berücksichtigen* | to consider |
| *in Frage (infrage) kommen* | *möglich sein* | to be an option |
| *in Anspruch nehmen* | *nutzen* | to make use of |
| *in Kraft treten* | *gültig werden* | to come into force |
| *zur Verfügung stehen* | *verfügbar sein* | to be available |
| *zur Verfügung stellen* | *bereitstellen* | to make available |
| *zum Ausdruck bringen* | *ausdrücken* | to express |
| *zur Sprache bringen* | *ansprechen* | to raise (a topic) |
| *zur Diskussion stellen* | *zur Diskussion vorschlagen* | to put up for discussion |
| *zum Abschluss bringen* | *abschließen* | to complete |
| *in Gang setzen* | *starten* | to set in motion |
| *sich in Verbindung setzen (mit)* | *kontaktieren* | to get in touch |
| *in Betrieb nehmen* | *einschalten, starten* | to put into operation |

## Pairs: state, happening, cause

| state (stehen / sein) | it happens (kommen / treten) | someone causes it (stellen / bringen / setzen) |
|---|---|---|
| *zur Verfügung stehen* | | *zur Verfügung stellen* |
| *zur Diskussion stehen* | | *zur Diskussion stellen* |
| *zur Wahl stehen* | | *sich zur Wahl stellen* |
| | *zur Sprache kommen* | *zur Sprache bringen* |
| | *zum Ausdruck kommen* | *zum Ausdruck bringen* |
| | *zum Abschluss kommen* | *zum Abschluss bringen* |
| *in Gang sein* | *in Gang kommen* | *in Gang setzen* |
| *in Kraft sein* | *in Kraft treten* | *außer Kraft setzen* (to repeal) |
| *in Betrieb sein* | | *in Betrieb nehmen* |

## Passive meaning without werden

| Funktionsverbgefüge | = passive |
|---|---|
| *Die Regel findet Anwendung.* | *Die Regel wird angewendet.* |
| *Der Vorschlag findet Zustimmung.* | *Dem Vorschlag wird zugestimmt.* |
| *Das Thema findet Beachtung.* | *Das Thema wird beachtet.* |
| *Das Projekt erhält Unterstützung.* | *Das Projekt wird unterstützt.* |
| *Der Punkt steht zur Diskussion.* | *Der Punkt wird diskutiert.* |

## Word order and negation

| | example |
|---|---|
| main clause | *Wir ziehen diese Lösung in Betracht.* |
| subordinate clause | *…, weil wir diese Lösung in Betracht ziehen.* |
| Perfekt | *Das Gesetz ist im Januar in Kraft getreten.* |
| negation, preposition type: *nicht* | *Das kommt nicht in Frage.* |
| negation, noun without article: *kein* | *Er übte keine Kritik.* |

references.title: Konjunktiv I and indirect speech
references.body:
## Forms

Infinitive stem + endings, no vowel change.

| | ending | kommen | haben | können | werden | fahren | sein |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | -e | *(komme)* | *(habe)* | könne | *(werde)* | *(fahre)* | sei |
| du | -est | kommest | habest | könnest | werdest | fahrest | seist |
| er / sie / es | -e | komme | habe | könne | werde | fahre | sei |
| wir | -en | *(kommen)* | *(haben)* | *(können)* | *(werden)* | *(fahren)* | seien |
| ihr | -et | kommet | habet | könnet | *(werdet)* | fahret | seiet |
| sie / Sie | -en | *(kommen)* | *(haben)* | *(können)* | *(werden)* | *(fahren)* | seien |

Forms in brackets are identical to the indicative and are replaced in indirect speech (see below). The du and ihr forms are correct but rare.

- Strong verbs: *er gebe, nehme, lese, fahre, schlage, trete* (indicative *gibt, nimmt, liest, fährt, schlägt, tritt*).
- Modals and *wissen*: *er könne, müsse, dürfe, solle, wolle, möge, wisse*.
- *es gibt* → *es gebe*. Separable verbs: *er rufe an, sie kündige an*.

## The replacement rule

1. Konjunktiv I, if it differs from the indicative: *er habe, sie komme, sie seien*.
2. Otherwise Konjunktiv II: *sie haben* → *sie hätten*; *wir können* → *wir könnten*; *sie kommen* → *sie kämen*.
3. If the Konjunktiv II also looks like the indicative (weak verbs), or sounds old-fashioned: *würde* + infinitive: *sie zahlen* → (*zahlten* = past) → *sie würden zahlen*.

## Time in indirect speech

| original | indirect speech | plural (replaced) |
|---|---|---|
| present: *„Ich bin krank.“* | *er sei krank* | *sie seien krank* |
| present: *„Ich habe Zeit.“* | *er habe Zeit* | *sie hätten Zeit* |
| any past: *„Ich sah / habe gesehen / hatte gesehen …“* | *er habe … gesehen* | *sie hätten … gesehen* |
| any past with sein: *„Ich ging / bin gegangen …“* | *er sei … gegangen* | *sie seien … gegangen* |
| past passive: *„Ich wurde gefragt.“* | *er sei gefragt worden* | *sie seien gefragt worden* |
| future: *„Ich werde kommen.“* | *er werde kommen* | *sie würden kommen* |
| Futur II: *„Ich werde es geschafft haben.“* | *er werde es geschafft haben* | *sie würden es geschafft haben* |

The tense of the reporting verb (*sagt, sagte, hat gesagt*) doesn't change the Konjunktiv.

## Questions, commands, requests

| original | indirect |
|---|---|
| *„Kommst du?“* | *Sie fragte, ob er komme.* |
| *„Wann kommst du?“* | *Sie fragte, wann er komme.* |
| *„Komm sofort!“* | *Sie sagte, er solle sofort kommen.* |
| *„Bitte warten Sie.“* | *Sie bat, er möge warten.* / *Sie bat ihn zu warten.* |

## Pronouns, place and time

*ich → er/sie, wir → sie, mein → sein/ihr; hier → dort; heute → an diesem Tag; gestern → am Tag zuvor; morgen → am nächsten Tag; jetzt → zu diesem Zeitpunkt* (only when the point of view changes).

## Register

| formal writing | neutral, spoken | everyday spoken |
|---|---|---|
| *Er sagte, er sei krank.* | *Er hat gesagt, er wäre krank.* | *Er hat gesagt, dass er krank ist.* |

## Naming the source

| | case | position | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *laut* | dative (formal also genitive) | before | *laut Polizei, laut dem Bericht* |
| *zufolge* | dative | after | *dem Bericht zufolge* |
| *nach* | dative | before (opinions: after) | *nach Angaben der Polizei; meiner Meinung nach* |
| *gemäß* | dative | before or after | rules only: *gemäß der Vereinbarung* |
| *wie … mitteilte* | clause + indicative | first | *Wie die Polizei mitteilte, ist …* |
| *so* | no verb | at the end | *…, so die Polizei.* |

## Other uses of the Konjunktiv I

- Instructions: *Man nehme 200 g Mehl. Man beachte … Wer Interesse hat, melde sich.*
- Maths: *Gegeben sei ein Dreieck ABC. Es sei x eine Zahl. Seien A und B zwei Punkte.*
- Wishes and set phrases: *Gott sei Dank. Es lebe … Wie dem auch sei. Sei es …, sei es … Koste es, was es wolle.*

## Subjective modal verbs and Futur II

| | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *soll* | it is said | *Er soll reich sein. Sie soll gelogen haben.* |
| *will* | the subject claims | *Er will nichts gesehen haben.* |
| *muss* | I'm sure | *Sie muss krank sein.* |
| *dürfte* | probably | *Das dürfte stimmen.* |
| *wird (wohl)* | assumption | *Er wird im Stau stehen. Er wird den Bus verpasst haben.* |
| *kann / könnte* | possibly | *Das könnte eine Fälschung sein.* |
| *kann nicht* | impossible | *Das kann nicht stimmen.* |
| *mag* | concession, estimate | *Das mag sein, aber … Sie mag vierzig sein.* |

Futur II: *werden* + Partizip II + *haben/sein*: *Bis 2041 werden wir die Wohnung abbezahlt haben* (completed future); *Sie wird den Termin vergessen haben* (assumption about the past). Subordinate clause: *…, dass er es vergessen haben wird.*

references.title: Nominal style and verbal style
references.body:
## Nouns from verbs

| type | gender | examples |
|---|---|---|
| stem + *-ung* | feminine | *fördern → die Förderung, versetzen → die Versetzung, prüfen → die Prüfung* |
| nominalized infinitive | neuter | *lernen → das Lernen, sitzenbleiben → das Sitzenbleiben* |
| stem noun (often a vowel change) | mostly masculine | *abschließen → der Abschluss, abbrechen → der Abbruch, beginnen → der Beginn, ausbauen → der Ausbau* |
| stem noun, feminine | feminine | *ankommen → die Ankunft, teilnehmen → die Teilnahme* |
| stem + *-e* | feminine | *suchen → die Suche, helfen → die Hilfe* |

## Clause → prepositional phrase

| conjunction | preposition | example |
|---|---|---|
| *wenn / als* | *bei* + dat. | *wenn man ankommt → bei der Ankunft* |
| *weil / da* | *wegen, aufgrund* + gen. | *weil es regnete → wegen des Regens* |
| *obwohl* | *trotz* + gen. | *obwohl er krank war → trotz seiner Krankheit* |
| *um … zu / damit* | *zu(r/m)* + dat. | *um die Schulen zu verbessern → zur Verbesserung der Schulen* |
| *nachdem* | *nach* + dat. | *nachdem sie abgeschlossen hatte → nach dem Abschluss* |
| *bevor* | *vor* + dat. | *bevor das Jahr beginnt → vor Beginn des Jahres* |
| *während* | *während* + gen. | *während er studierte → während seines Studiums* |
| *seit* | *seit* + dat. | *seit sie umgezogen ist → seit ihrem Umzug* |
| *indem / dadurch, dass* | *durch* + acc. | *indem man Lehrkräfte einstellt → durch die Einstellung von Lehrkräften* |
| *falls* | *im Fall* + gen., *bei* | *falls Unterricht ausfällt → bei Unterrichtsausfall* |
| *ohne dass* | *ohne* + acc. | *ohne dass die Eltern zustimmen → ohne Zustimmung der Eltern* |

## Where the parts of the clause go

| in the clause | in the phrase | example |
|---|---|---|
| accusative object | genitive after the noun | *das Schulsystem reformieren → die Reform des Schulsystems* |
| subject of an intransitive verb | genitive after the noun | *die Schüler kommen an → die Ankunft der Schüler* |
| subject + object | object in the genitive, doer with *durch* | *die Förderung begabter Kinder durch die Schulen* |
| pronoun | possessive | *sie kommt an → ihre Ankunft* |
